entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1865, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely, coming directly from Mexican Alta California (ceded under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854; previously San Jose, then Vallejo, then Benicia during the early 1850s)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** No U.S. federal territorial period preceded statehood; previously Alta California under Mexico
- **Population during period:** Approximately 300,000 migrants arrived during the Gold Rush (Wikipedia, California Gold Rush article). The 1850 federal census and 1852 California state census are the principal population snapshots for the decade.
- **Economy:** Gold mining (1848–1855 peak); supporting trades, shipping through San Francisco, and agriculture
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly male and transient; arrivals from eastern U.S. states, Latin America, China, Australia, and Europe; pre-Gold Rush Hispanic Californio population; indigenous peoples. The foreign miner population was substantial enough to prompt a dedicated Foreign Miners' Tax (1850 onward).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant in the pre-Gold Rush mission era); Methodist, Baptist, and other Protestant denominations established during and after the Gold Rush
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery at Sutter's Mill (January 24, 1848); California statehood (1850); rapid county organization throughout the 1850s; Civil War (1861–1865, California remained in the Union and contributed troops)

## Boundary changes
- California entered the Union in 1850 directly from Mexican territory — there are no preceding U.S. territorial records.
- County formation was rapid and ongoing throughout the 1850s; many counties were carved from a few original large counties. A locality's county may have changed within the decade.
- Always identify which county held jurisdiction over a specific locality at the event date before searching county-level records.

## Available record types

Record-holding levels vary by type: vital events were recorded at the **county** level from 1850; federal census was at the **national** level; mining claims were filed at the **county** recorder's office; ship arrivals were documented at the **federal** level.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** FamilySearch collections show county-level birth records (collection 2017276) and county marriage records (collection 1452832) from 1850. The specific year California required civil registration was not stated by any tool result in this survey — the California Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content. Do not assume registration was uniformly mandatory from 1850; county coverage within these collections likely varies.
- **What exists:** County-level birth records from 1850 (789,456 records; FamilySearch collection 2017276, indexed + images); county marriage records from 1850 (567,890 records / 1,135,780 persons; FamilySearch collection 1452832, indexed + images). No death collection was returned by collections_search for this period.
- **Where held:** Originals at county clerk offices. FamilySearch online: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276 (births); https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832 (marriages).
- **Gaps:** No statewide death collection for the 1850s appeared in collections_search. County coverage within the collections likely varies — not every county may have records from 1850.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** 1852 California state census (FamilySearch volume 006601001, 88% name-indexed); church records; newspaper notices; probate records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (mission era through the 1850s); Methodist, Baptist, Congregationalist, and Episcopal denominations established during the Gold Rush
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic); sacramental registers vary by denomination
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1804372 ("California, Mission Records, 1769-1850," 98,765 records, indexed + images) covers the Franciscan mission era. For Gold Rush-era Catholic and Protestant records, the California State Library and Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley hold extensive manuscript collections, per the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).
- **Gaps:** Mission Records (collection 1804372) end at 1850 — they are background context for the Gold Rush decade, not prime sources. Church records for the 1850s Gold Rush influx have uncertain online coverage; the California Church Records wiki page returned only generic content.
- **Language:** Mission-era records are in Spanish and Latin

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850 (California's first, but partially destroyed — some county returns are missing, per the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records); 1860 (next available, complete). Mortality schedules (deaths in the preceding year) accompanied both.
- **State census:** 1852 California state census — digitized, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable (FamilySearch volume 006601001, 522 images, date range 1850-1852). This is the most critical substitute for the damaged 1850 federal returns and the primary census source for the early Gold Rush years.
- **Access:** 1852 state census: indexed + images (FamilySearch volume 006601001). 1850 and 1860 federal censuses: Ancestry.com U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions; naturalizations (pre-1906, any court of record)
- **Date range:** From county formation; the earliest California counties were organized immediately after statehood in 1850
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); California State Archives (Sacramento). The California Probate Records wiki page returned only generic content and did not name specific holdings.
- **Note on naturalizations:** Before 1906, any court of record could process naturalizations. Gold Rush arrivals often naturalized in the county where they settled; search both county courts and the federal district court for the district.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular (public land) survey system for public domain lands; Spanish and Mexican land grants (ranchos) used metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal Bureau of Land Management (GLO) for public domain grants. California State Archives for Mexican-era land grant records. The California Land and Property wiki page returned only generic content.
- **Types:** BLM General Land Office patents (https://glorecords.blm.gov/), county deed books, mining claim registers (see below), Mexican-era rancho grants
- **Where held:** BLM GLO records online at https://glorecords.blm.gov/. County deed books at county recorders' offices. Mexican-era grants at the California State Archives.

### Mining claim records
- **Unique to the Gold Rush era.** Mining claim registers were filed at county recorders' offices per the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). They named the claimant and the location, date, and description of the claim — a direct record of a miner's presence.
- **FamilySearch volume 006601002** covers Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco, 1849-1855 (340 images) — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be browsed image-by-image.
- **Also consult:** Individual county recorders' offices and the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley for manuscript mining records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846-1848, just before the Gold Rush); Civil War (1861-1865, California units)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Mexican-American War era), Civil War draft and enrollment records
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA, https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; California State Archives for state adjutant general records

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online database; coverage of 1850s Gold Rush-era graves varies significantly by county. Many Gold Rush burials occurred in informal mining camp cemeteries with limited record-keeping.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual cemeteries; municipal cemeteries of San Francisco and Sacramento are primary for the urban centers.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Alta California (San Francisco, founded 1849) and Sacramento Union (founded 1851) were the principal papers of the period
- **Where held:** The California Digital Newspaper Collection (UC Riverside) and the Bancroft Library hold Gold Rush-era papers; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for additional digitized holdings
- **Content value:** Ship arrivals, mining company announcements, obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices were regularly published

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary port of entry by sea for Gold Rush arrivals
- **FamilySearch volume 006601003** covers Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento, 1849-1858 (298 images) — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)
- **Ship passenger manifests** for San Francisco arrivals are held at the National Archives, San Bruno facility, per the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). Also searchable via Ancestry.com and NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).
- **Overland arrivals:** Overland trail diaries and journals document the land route migrants; primarily held at the Bancroft Library and California State Library.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.
- **Naturalization:** Declarations of intention and final papers were filed at county-level courts pre-1906; search the county court of settlement.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax (from 1850), and Foreign Miners' Tax (1850 onward, applicable to non-citizen miners — a key source for Chinese, Latin American, and European miners)
- **Where held:** County assessors' offices and county archives; California State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls can substitute for missing census years and name men absent from indexed censuses

### Voter registration (Great Registers)
- **FamilySearch collection 1923340** ("California, Great Registers, 1866-1910," 1,345,678 records) — indexed + images
- **Important:** These begin in 1866 and do NOT cover the 1850s Gold Rush arrival years. They are valuable for identifying where a Gold Rush-era migrant eventually settled and whether he naturalized, but they postdate the target period.

### Other record types
- **Overland trail diaries / journals:** Manuscript records of overland migrants; Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and California State Library are the principal holders
- **Mining district records:** Some informal mining district organizations kept their own membership and claim records distinct from county recorder filings; held at the Bancroft Library or county archives
- **Foreign Miners' Tax records:** Generated by California's 1850 tax on non-citizen miners; physical records at county level, not known to be widely digitized

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | County Births 1850-1919 (2017276); County Marriages 1850-1952 (1452832); Mission Records 1769-1850 (1804372); State Census 1850-1852 (vol. 006601001, 88% indexed); Mining Claim Registers SF 1849-1855 (vol. 006601002, browse-only); Port Arrival Registers Sacramento 1849-1858 (vol. 006601003, browse-only) | Core county vital records; 1852 state census; mining and arrival records | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1850, 1860) | 1850 and 1860 federal censuses | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military service and pension records | Civil War and Mexican-American War records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records | Burial documentation not captured in vital records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical newspapers | Obituaries, ship arrivals, legal notices | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco); naturalization records; federal court records | Sea arrivals; citizenship filings | Free (in-person/request) |
| BLM GLO (https://glorecords.blm.gov/) | Federal land patents | Public domain land grants | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for 1848-1865; only 3 are detailed above (first page of results). The remaining 11 volumes were not examined — check further pages of volume_search results before concluding a record type is unavailable online.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives, San Bruno, CA | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco); federal court and naturalization records | In-person / NARA online request |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | State government records; Mexican-era land grants; California State Census; probate and court records; state adjutant general records | In-person / mail request |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Gold Rush manuscript collections; newspapers; county histories; overland trail materials | In-person |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections; overland trail diaries; mining records | In-person; some digitized |
| County courthouses (each Gold Rush county) | Deed books; mining claim registers; probate files; marriage registers; naturalizations | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online

- County probate and court files for most Gold Rush-era counties are not digitized and must be accessed in person at the county courthouse or California State Archives
- Foreign Miners' Tax records (1850 onward) — physical records at county level; not known to be digitized
- Mining district membership and informal organization records — manuscript form at the Bancroft Library or county archives
- County tax rolls for the 1850s — physical at county level; not widely digitized
- Overland trail diaries and journals — primarily manuscript collections at the Bancroft Library and California State Library
- Death records for the 1850s — no death collection appeared in collections_search for this period; county-level originals are the primary source

## Known record losses

- The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. This is stated by the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). The 1852 California state census (FamilySearch volume 006601001) is the primary substitute.
- No other specific record losses were stated by any tool result in this survey. Empty search results represent coverage gaps, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- Begin with the **1852 California state census** (FamilySearch volume 006601001, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable) before the 1850 federal census — it is more complete for California and covers the key early Gold Rush years. See the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records.
- **Mining claim registers** at county recorders' offices directly document a miner's presence and claim location. FamilySearch volume 006601002 (San Francisco, 1849-1855) is browse-only; also request records from individual county recorders and check the Bancroft Library.
- **Ship passenger manifests** for San Francisco arrivals are at the National Archives, San Bruno. Sea arrivals dominated for Latin American, Chinese, Australian, and many European miners — check these before assuming an ancestor arrived overland.
- Because **county boundaries shifted frequently** in the 1850s, always confirm which county governed a specific locality at the event date before routing a county record search.
- The **Great Registers** (FamilySearch collection 1923340, beginning 1866) are a bridge source: they do not cover the 1850s arrival years but can pinpoint where a Gold Rush migrant settled and whether he had naturalized by the late 1860s.
- The **FamilySearch Wiki California-specific pages** — all four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and the topical pages for Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate Records, Census, and Naming Customs — returned only generic fallback content during this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy directly before finalizing any research plan that depends on California-specific wiki guidance.

Record-holding levels vary by type: vital events were recorded at the **county** level from 1850; federal census was at the **national** level; mining claims were filed at the **county** recorder's office; ship arrivals were documented at the **federal** level.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** FamilySearch collections show county-level birth records (collection 2017276) and county marriage records (collection 1452832) from 1850. The specific year California required civil registration was not stated by any tool result in this survey — the California Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content. Do not assume registration was uniformly mandatory from 1850; county coverage within these collections likely varies.
- **What exists:** County-level birth records from 1850 (789,456 records; FamilySearch collection 2017276, indexed + images); county marriage records from 1850 (567,890 records / 1,135,780 persons; FamilySearch collection 1452832, indexed + images). No death collection was returned by collections_search for this period.
- **Where held:** Originals at county clerk offices. FamilySearch online: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276 (births); https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832 (marriages).
- **Gaps:** No statewide death collection for the 1850s appeared in collections_search. County coverage within the collections likely varies — not every county may have records from 1850.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** 1852 California state census (FamilySearch volume 006601001, 88% name-indexed); church records; newspaper notices; probate records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (mission era through the 1850s); Methodist, Baptist, Congregationalist, and Episcopal denominations established during the Gold Rush
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic); sacramental registers vary by denomination
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1804372 ("California, Mission Records, 1769-1850," 98,765 records, indexed + images) covers the Franciscan mission era. For Gold Rush-era Catholic and Protestant records, the California State Library and Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley hold extensive manuscript collections, per the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).
- **Gaps:** Mission Records (collection 1804372) end at 1850 — they are background context for the Gold Rush decade, not prime sources. Church records for the 1850s Gold Rush influx have uncertain online coverage; the California Church Records wiki page returned only generic content.
- **Language:** Mission-era records are in Spanish and Latin

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850 (California's first, but partially destroyed — some county returns are missing, per the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records); 1860 (next available, complete). Mortality schedules (deaths in the preceding year) accompanied both.
- **State census:** 1852 California state census — digitized, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable (FamilySearch volume 006601001, 522 images, date range 1850-1852). This is the most critical substitute for the damaged 1850 federal returns and the primary census source for the early Gold Rush years.
- **Access:** 1852 state census: indexed + images (FamilySearch volume 006601001). 1850 and 1860 federal censuses: Ancestry.com U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions; naturalizations (pre-1906, any court of record)
- **Date range:** From county formation; the earliest California counties were organized immediately after statehood in 1850
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); California State Archives (Sacramento). The California Probate Records wiki page returned only generic content and did not name specific holdings.
- **Note on naturalizations:** Before 1906, any court of record could process naturalizations. Gold Rush arrivals often naturalized in the county where they settled; search both county courts and the federal district court for the district.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular (public land) survey system for public domain lands; Spanish and Mexican land grants (ranchos) used metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal Bureau of Land Management (GLO) for public domain grants. California State Archives for Mexican-era land grant records. The California Land and Property wiki page returned only generic content.
- **Types:** BLM General Land Office patents (https://glorecords.blm.gov/), county deed books, mining claim registers (see below), Mexican-era rancho grants
- **Where held:** BLM GLO records online at https://glorecords.blm.gov/. County deed books at county recorders' offices. Mexican-era grants at the California State Archives.

### Mining claim records
- **Unique to the Gold Rush era.** Mining claim registers were filed at county recorders' offices per the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). They named the claimant and the location, date, and description of the claim — a direct record of a miner's presence.
- **FamilySearch volume 006601002** covers Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco, 1849-1855 (340 images) — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be browsed image-by-image.
- **Also consult:** Individual county recorders' offices and the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley for manuscript mining records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846-1848, just before the Gold Rush); Civil War (1861-1865, California units)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Mexican-American War era), Civil War draft and enrollment records
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA, https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; California State Archives for state adjutant general records

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online database; coverage of 1850s Gold Rush-era graves varies significantly by county. Many Gold Rush burials occurred in informal mining camp cemeteries with limited record-keeping.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual cemeteries; municipal cemeteries of San Francisco and Sacramento are primary for the urban centers.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Alta California (San Francisco, founded 1849) and Sacramento Union (founded 1851) were the principal papers of the period
- **Where held:** The California Digital Newspaper Collection (UC Riverside) and the Bancroft Library hold Gold Rush-era papers; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for additional digitized holdings
- **Content value:** Ship arrivals, mining company announcements, obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices were regularly published

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary port of entry by sea for Gold Rush arrivals
- **FamilySearch volume 006601003** covers Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento, 1849-1858 (298 images) — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)
- **Ship passenger manifests** for San Francisco arrivals are held at the National Archives, San Bruno facility, per the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). Also searchable via Ancestry.com and NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).
- **Overland arrivals:** Overland trail diaries and journals document the land route migrants; primarily held at the Bancroft Library and California State Library.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.
- **Naturalization:** Declarations of intention and final papers were filed at county-level courts pre-1906; search the county court of settlement.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax (from 1850), and Foreign Miners' Tax (1850 onward, applicable to non-citizen miners — a key source for Chinese, Latin American, and European miners)
- **Where held:** County assessors' offices and county archives; California State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls can substitute for missing census years and name men absent from indexed censuses

### Voter registration (Great Registers)
- **FamilySearch collection 1923340** ("California, Great Registers, 1866-1910," 1,345,678 records) — indexed + images
- **Important:** These begin in 1866 and do NOT cover the 1850s Gold Rush arrival years. They are valuable for identifying where a Gold Rush-era migrant eventually settled and whether he naturalized, but they postdate the target period.

### Other record types
- **Overland trail diaries / journals:** Manuscript records of overland migrants; Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and California State Library are the principal holders
- **Mining district records:** Some informal mining district organizations kept their own membership and claim records distinct from county recorder filings; held at the Bancroft Library or county archives
- **Foreign Miners' Tax records:** Generated by California's 1850 tax on non-citizen miners; physical records at county level, not known to be widely digitized

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | County Births 1850-1919 (2017276); County Marriages 1850-1952 (1452832); Mission Records 1769-1850 (1804372); State Census 1850-1852 (vol. 006601001, 88% indexed); Mining Claim Registers SF 1849-1855 (vol. 006601002, browse-only); Port Arrival Registers Sacramento 1849-1858 (vol. 006601003, browse-only) | Core county vital records; 1852 state census; mining and arrival records | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1850, 1860) | 1850 and 1860 federal censuses | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military service and pension records | Civil War and Mexican-American War records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records | Burial documentation not captured in vital records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical newspapers | Obituaries, ship arrivals, legal notices | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco); naturalization records; federal court records | Sea arrivals; citizenship filings | Free (in-person/request) |
| BLM GLO (https://glorecords.blm.gov/) | Federal land patents | Public domain land grants | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for 1848-1865; only 3 are detailed above (first page of results). The remaining 11 volumes were not examined — check further pages of volume_search results before concluding a record type is unavailable online.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives, San Bruno, CA | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco); federal court and naturalization records | In-person / NARA online request |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | State government records; Mexican-era land grants; California State Census; probate and court records; state adjutant general records | In-person / mail request |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Gold Rush manuscript collections; newspapers; county histories; overland trail materials | In-person |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections; overland trail diaries; mining records | In-person; some digitized |
| County courthouses (each Gold Rush county) | Deed books; mining claim registers; probate files; marriage registers; naturalizations | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online

- County probate and court files for most Gold Rush-era counties are not digitized and must be accessed in person at the county courthouse or California State Archives
- Foreign Miners' Tax records (1850 onward) — physical records at county level; not known to be digitized
- Mining district membership and informal organization records — manuscript form at the Bancroft Library or county archives
- County tax rolls for the 1850s — physical at county level; not widely digitized
- Overland trail diaries and journals — primarily manuscript collections at the Bancroft Library and California State Library
- Death records for the 1850s — no death collection appeared in collections_search for this period; county-level originals are the primary source

## Known record losses

- The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. This is stated by the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). The 1852 California state census (FamilySearch volume 006601001) is the primary substitute.
- No other specific record losses were stated by any tool result in this survey. Empty search results represent coverage gaps, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- Begin with the **1852 California state census** (FamilySearch volume 006601001, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable) before the 1850 federal census — it is more complete for California and covers the key early Gold Rush years. See the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records.
- **Mining claim registers** at county recorders' offices directly document a miner's presence and claim location. FamilySearch volume 006601002 (San Francisco, 1849-1855) is browse-only; also request records from individual county recorders and check the Bancroft Library.
- **Ship passenger manifests** for San Francisco arrivals are at the National Archives, San Bruno. Sea arrivals dominated for Latin American, Chinese, Australian, and many European miners — check these before assuming an ancestor arrived overland.
- Because **county boundaries shifted frequently** in the 1850s, always confirm which county governed a specific locality at the event date before routing a county record search.
- The **Great Registers** (FamilySearch collection 1923340, beginning 1866) are a bridge source: they do not cover the 1850s arrival years but can pinpoint where a Gold Rush migrant settled and whether he had naturalized by the late 1860s.
- The **FamilySearch Wiki California-specific pages** — all four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and the topical pages for Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate Records, Census, and Naming Customs — returned only generic fallback content during this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy directly before finalizing any research plan that depends on California-specific wiki guidance.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide for **New York City in the 1700s colonial period**:

---

## New York City (Manhattan), 1700–1799 — Locality Research Guide

### Key Context
- **No civil vital registration** existed anywhere in colonial New York during this period. Church registers are the functional equivalent of birth, marriage, and death records.
- "New York City" in the 1700s means **Manhattan only**. Ancestors in Brooklyn (Kings County), Queens, Staten Island (Richmond County), or the Bronx area fall under **separate county jurisdictions** with their own records.

---

### Church Records
The most critical records for this period:

| Denomination | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Dutch Reformed** | Registers from 1639; a Dutch-language volume covering 1700–1776 (211 images) is digitized on FamilySearch — browse-only, not name-indexed |
| **Anglican / Church of England** | Trinity Church registers from ~1698 |
| **Presbyterian** | Also present in the city by this era |

---

### Other Key Record Types

| Record Type | Details |
|---|---|
| **Probate Records** | Prerogative Court of New York; abstracts indexed by the New-York Historical Society (*Abstracts of Wills*) |
| **Land Records & Conveyances** | Land transactions document property-owning families |
| **Tax Assessment Lists** | Ward-level; substitute for census records through most of the century |
| **Militia Rolls** | Useful for adult male ancestors |
| **1790 Federal Census** | Only covers the last years of the century |

---

### FamilySearch Indexed Collections (New York State–Level)
- **Church Records 1640–1940** — Collection 1469062
- **Land Records 1630–1975** — Collection 2078654
- **Probate Records 1629–1971** — Collection 1542780

---

### Key Repositories
- **New York State Archives, Albany** — holds colonial probate, land, tax, and militia records
- **New-York Historical Society** — indexed *Abstracts of Wills*; strong colonial holdings
- **FamilySearch Wiki** — visit [New York City Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy) for current guidance

---

### Next Step
To build a targeted research plan, it helps to know which specific families or individuals you are tracing. Once you share names, locations (which ward or neighborhood), religion, or approximate dates, a focused search sequence can be developed from this survey.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700–1799)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam was founded by the Dutch West India Company in 1626; renamed New York City following the British takeover in 1664. During the 1700s the city served as the capital of the Province of New York.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City was itself the seat of New York County (the sole county constituting the city in this period).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colony, 1664–1776); State of New York (1776 onward).
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Merchant trade, maritime commerce, and crafts trades; one of the busiest colonial ports in North America.
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, French Huguenot, German, and enslaved and free African communities, per the Wikipedia article on the Province of New York.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous registers, beginning 1639), Anglican (Trinity Church, founded ca. 1698), Presbyterian, French Huguenot, and others — named in the FamilySearch Wiki search results for New York City Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Key historical events:** British military occupation of New York City throughout the Revolutionary War (1776–1783) disrupted civilian record-keeping; the city was a Loyalist center during this period.

## Boundary changes
- During the 1700s, "New York City" meant New York County — Manhattan island only. Brooklyn was in Kings County; Queens was Queens County; Staten Island was Richmond County; the Bronx area was in Westchester County. Each of these is a distinct jurisdiction with its own record series.
- The Province of New York became the State of New York in 1776. Records created before 1776 were made under colonial British authority; researchers must search both the provincial colonial record system and the post-1783 state record system for families spanning the Revolution.
- The five-borough consolidation of modern New York City did not occur until 1898 and does not apply to this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in New York City during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki page for New York Vital Records returned only generic content and did not supply a registration date; wiki search results confirm that church registers functioned as the de facto vital records for this era.
- **What exists:** No civil vital registers exist for New York City 1700–1799 at any government level.
- **Where held:** See Church Records below.
- **Gaps:** The complete absence of civil vital registration is the defining gap for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (Dutch Reformed, Anglican, Presbyterian); newspaper marriage and death notices (New-York Gazette, beginning 1725).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (registers beginning 1639), Anglican (Trinity Church, ca. 1698), Presbyterian, French Huguenot, and others, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials; some denominations also kept communion rolls and membership registers.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1469062, "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (2,345,678 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062). One digitized volume of Dutch Reformed Church Registers, New York City, 1700–1776 was returned by volume search (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 211 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only, must be navigated image by image). The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society also hold colonial church records, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **Gaps:** No digitized or indexed FamilySearch volumes were returned for Anglican (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, or French Huguenot registers for 1700–1799; these may be undigitized or held only at the denominational repository or the New York State Archives.
- **Language:** The Dutch Reformed volume (imageGroupNumber 007733180) is in Dutch; 18th-century Dutch script literacy is required. Anglican and Presbyterian registers are in English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census was conducted in 1790, at the very end of the 1700s. No federal census exists for 1700–1789.
- **State/provincial census:** No colonial or provincial census returns for New York City 1700–1799 were returned by any tool.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax assessment lists by ward survive for some years, and militia rolls list men of military age — both per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records. These are the primary substitutes for census records throughout most of the 1700s.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census for New York is indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Ward-level tax lists and militia rolls are not online as a named digitized collection; they are held at the New York State Archives in Albany.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, inventories, letters of administration, and guardianship files.
- **Jurisdictional note:** Colonial-era probate for New York was handled by the Prerogative Court of New York, not county-level probate courts. Wills proved in this court are indexed in the "Abstracts of Wills" series published by the New-York Historical Society, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1542780, "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (987,654 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) overlaps the 1700s period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1542780; the New-York Historical Society's published Abstracts of Wills; the New York State Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial British).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for New York Land and Property returned only generic content. Wikipedia confirms the Province of New York held land-grant authority under the British Crown; the New York State Archives in Albany holds colonial land records.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, and mortgages. Land conveyances are named as a key colonial source at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078654, "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (1,567,890 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) covers the 1700s.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2078654; New York State Archives in Albany.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), the French and Indian War (1754–1763), and the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls (listing men of military age by ward), Revolutionary War service records, and pension files — militia rolls named at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.
- **Where held:** Colonial militia rolls: New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives (Albany). Revolutionary War service records and pension files: National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Colonial-era burials were predominantly in church burial grounds (Trinity Church yard, Dutch Reformed churchyard).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) carries some transcriptions; coverage for 1700s graves is limited and variable.
- **Physical records:** Sexton and vestry burial registers held by the church archives; some published in 19th-century genealogical periodicals.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New-York Gazette began publication in 1725, making it the earliest sustained newspaper for genealogical use in New York City. Marriage notices and death notices appear from the colonial era.
- **Where held:** Digitized colonial newspapers available via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); the New York State Library and the New-York Historical Society hold microfilm.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, legal notices, estate and probate notices.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the primary colonial port of entry.
- **Record types:** Formal NARA passenger lists begin around 1820 and do not cover the 1700s. Colonial-era arrival records are scattered across British customs records, provincial court records, and private accounts.
- **Where held:** Colonial-era records: New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives; British colonial records at the UK National Archives. NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds post-1820 records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists as a standardized federal record type did not exist in the 1700s. Naturalization records filed in any court of record may document foreign-born residents; declarations of intention, affidavits, and alien registrations were generated inland, not only at ports.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Ward-level tax assessment rolls on real and personal estate.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1678432, "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (123,456 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432) begins at 1799 — the very end of the target period. Earlier ward-level tax lists for the 1700s were described in wiki search results as surviving for some years and wards, but were not returned as a digitized collection.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1678432 (1799 onward); earlier lists held at the New York State Archives in Albany.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for census records throughout most of the 1700s, before the first federal census of 1790.

### Other record types
- **Mayor's Court records:** The court records of the Mayor's Court of New York City are cited as a key colonial-era source at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records, covering commercial disputes, debt cases, and civil matters that name city residents not found elsewhere.
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** Held at the New York State Archives in Albany; named as the primary repository for colonial-era NYC government records by both the FamilySearch Wiki search result and the Wikipedia article on the Province of New York.
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society / New-York Historical Society:** Both hold extensive colonial-era research collections, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1469062 (Church Records 1640–1940); 2078654 (Land Records 1630–1975); 1542780 (Probate Records 1629–1971); 1678432 (Tax Assessment Rolls 1799–1804); 1 browse-only Dutch Reformed Church volume (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 1700–1776) | Church, land, probate; only online Dutch Reformed registers for 1700–1776 | Free |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Revolutionary War service records, pension files | Free / in-person |
| Fold3 | https://www.fold3.com/ | Military records not available online elsewhere | Subscription |
| Ancestry | https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ | 1790 federal census (end of period only) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | https://www.findagrave.com/ | Church burial ground transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | https://www.newspapers.com/ | Colonial newspapers from 1725 (marriage and death notices, legal notices) — gap in other vital records for this period | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 1 digitized volume for New York City in the 1700–1799 window; totalResults was 1, indicating this is the complete digitized set. A volume summary was requested but not returned by the tool; browse-only versus indexed tallies by record type are therefore not available.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives, Albany | New York Colonial Manuscripts; colonial land grants; colonial court records; militia rolls; early tax lists | In-person / written request |
| New-York Historical Society | Abstracts of Wills (Prerogative Court of New York); colonial church records; manuscript collections | In-person; published volumes in libraries |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society | Extensive colonial-era research collections | In-person; subscription online access (https://www.newyorkfamilyhistory.org/) |
| Trinity Church Archives, New York City | Anglican baptism, marriage, and burial registers ca. 1698 onward | Contact the Archives directly |
| National Archives, Northeast Region | Federal records including Revolutionary War materials | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- Ward-level tax assessment lists for the 1700s (before 1799) were not returned as any digitized FamilySearch collection.
- Colonial militia rolls for New York City are not available as a digitized online collection based on tool results.
- Mayor's Court records for the 1700s are not represented in any digitized FamilySearch collection returned.
- Anglican (Trinity Church) baptism, marriage, and burial register images for the 1700s were not returned as a digitized FamilySearch volume.
- Presbyterian and French Huguenot church registers were not returned as digitized volumes for this period.
- New York Colonial Manuscripts are held physically at the New York State Archives in Albany; no digitized collection covering this series was returned.

## Known record losses

No tool result returned during this survey states that a specific New York City record set from the 1700s was destroyed or lost. The absence of digitized online collections for many record types is a coverage gap, not a confirmed loss. The British military occupation of 1776–1783 may have disrupted or damaged some records; researchers should confirm the fate of specific series directly with the New York State Archives before concluding a record does not exist.

## Research tips

- **Church records are the vital records for this period.** No civil registration existed in New York City in the 1700s. Dutch Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian registers are the sole source for baptisms, marriages, and burials. Begin with FamilySearch collection 1469062 and the browse-only Dutch Reformed volume (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 1700–1776), then move to physical church archives, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **"New York City" in the 1700s means Manhattan only.** Ancestors in Brooklyn (Kings County), Queens, Staten Island (Richmond County), or the Bronx area (Westchester County) fall under entirely separate jurisdictions with their own record series. Do not assume a New York County search covers those areas.
- **Probate went through the Prerogative Court, not the county.** The New-York Historical Society's "Abstracts of Wills" is the primary finding aid for colonial New York City wills; county-level probate indexes will not catch them, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.
- **Tax lists and militia rolls replace the missing census.** The 1790 federal census is the only federal enumeration for this period. Ward-level tax assessment lists and militia rolls predate it and name residents who appear nowhere else. Both are at the New York State Archives in Albany, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.
- **The Dutch Reformed volume requires reading 18th-century Dutch.** FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 007733180 is 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, and entirely in Dutch. Plan for Dutch-script paleography skills or a specialist.
- **Visit the FamilySearch Wiki pages directly.** All four wiki place-specific sections returned only generic content during this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Vital_Records directly for current guidance before assuming those pages have no New York-specific information.

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |

| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Revolutionary War service records, pension files | Free / in-person |
| Fold3 | https://www.fold3.com/ | Military records not available online elsewhere | Subscription |
| Ancestry | https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ | 1790 federal census (end of period only) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 1 digitized volume for New York City in the 1700–1799 window; totalResults was 1, indicating this is the complete digitized set. A volume summary was requested but not returned by the tool; browse-only versus indexed tallies by record type are therefore not available.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives, Albany | New York Colonial Manuscripts; colonial land grants; colonial court records; militia rolls; early tax lists | In-person / written request |
| New-York Historical Society | Abstracts of Wills (Prerogative Court of New York); colonial church records; manuscript collections | In-person; published volumes in libraries |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society | Extensive colonial-era research collections | In-person; subscription online access (https://www.newyorkfamilyhistory.org/) |
| Trinity Church Archives, New York City | Anglican baptism, marriage, and burial registers ca. 1698 onward | Contact the Archives directly |
| National Archives, Northeast Region | Federal records including Revolutionary War materials | In-person |

- Ward-level tax assessment lists for the 1700s (before 1799) were not returned as any digitized FamilySearch collection.
- Colonial militia rolls for New York City are not available as a digitized online collection based on tool results.
- Mayor's Court records for the 1700s are not represented in any digitized FamilySearch collection returned.
- Anglican (Trinity Church) baptism, marriage, and burial register images for the 1700s were not returned as a digitized FamilySearch volume.
- Presbyterian and French Huguenot church registers were not returned as digitized volumes for this period.
- New York Colonial Manuscripts are held physically at the New York State Archives in Albany; no digitized collection covering this series was returned.

## Known record losses

No tool result returned during this survey states that a specific New York City record set from the 1700s was destroyed or lost. The absence of digitized online collections for many record types is a coverage gap, not a confirmed loss. The British military occupation of 1776–1783 may have disrupted or damaged some records; researchers should confirm the fate of specific series directly with the New York State Archives before concluding a record does not exist.

## Research tips

- **Church records are the vital records for this period.** No civil registration existed in New York City in the 1700s. Dutch Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian registers are the sole source for baptisms, marriages, and burials. Begin with FamilySearch collection 1469062 and the browse-only Dutch Reformed volume (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 1700–1776), then move to physical church archives, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **"New York City" in the 1700s means Manhattan only.** Ancestors in Brooklyn (Kings County), Queens, Staten Island (Richmond County), or the Bronx area (Westchester County) fall under entirely separate jurisdictions with their own record series. Do not assume a New York County search covers those areas.
- **Probate went through the Prerogative Court, not the county.** The New-York Historical Society's "Abstracts of Wills" is the primary finding aid for colonial New York City wills; county-level probate indexes will not catch them, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.
- **Tax lists and militia rolls replace the missing census.** The 1790 federal census is the only federal enumeration for this period. Ward-level tax assessment lists and militia rolls predate it and name residents who appear nowhere else. Both are at the New York State Archives in Albany, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.
- **The Dutch Reformed volume requires reading 18th-century Dutch.** FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 007733180 is 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, and entirely in Dutch. Plan for Dutch-script paleography skills or a specialist.
- **Visit the FamilySearch Wiki pages directly.** All four wiki place-specific sections returned only generic content during this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Vital_Records directly for current guidance before assuming those pages have no New York-specific information.

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced (saved as `loc_001`):

---

**Virginia, 1775–1783 — Records for Military Service & Wartime Families**

Virginia in 1775–1783 was one of the best-documented colonies, with county-level records stretching back to the 1630s, but the war years created some important gaps. Here is how to approach the research:

**Starting Point: Military Records**
- **FamilySearch — Virginia Military Records, 1775–1783** (free, indexed): The most direct route to a soldier ancestor.
- **Revolutionary War Pension Application Files (National Archives):** These often contain sworn statements of service, names of family members, and residence history — an invaluable source for both the veteran and his household.

**Substitute for the Missing 1790 Census**
Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The best substitute is the **county personal property and land tax lists beginning in 1782**, which can place a family in a specific county — the key to every other Virginia record type.

**County-Level Records (held locally and at the Library of Virginia, Richmond)**
- Church records and registers
- Marriage bonds
- Deed books
- Court order books
- Probate files (wills, inventories)

Many of these are accessible through **FamilySearch collections** and the **Library of Virginia** in Richmond.

**Bounty Land Grants**
Veterans who received bounty land grants in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** have warrant and survey records at the **Virginia State Library**, even if the family never actually relocated there.

---

**Recommended Next Step:** Identify which Virginia county your ancestor lived in during the 1780s using the tax lists, then focus the search on that county's court records, church registers, and deed books.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during period:** Colony through 1775; declared independence June 29, 1776; became the Commonwealth of Virginia; ratified U.S. Constitution in 1788
- **Administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital); Richmond became capital in 1780
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colony) → independent commonwealth from 1776
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tools for this period
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantation economy; grain farming, iron works, maritime trade
- **Ethnic composition:** English-origin majority; large enslaved African population; Scots-Irish and German settlers in western counties; Loyalist minority
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (established through 1776, reorganized as Episcopal afterward); Baptist (rapidly expanding); Methodist; Presbyterian; Lutheran and German Reformed in western counties
- **Key historical events:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Dunmore's Proclamation (1775); major battles culminating at Yorktown (1781); disestablishment of the Anglican church disrupted parish record-keeping

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's territory during this period included present-day West Virginia (separated 1863) and Kentucky (admitted as a state 1792); records for families in those regions are in Virginia-era county records
- Western frontier counties (Augusta, Botetourt, Fincastle, Montgomery, Washington, Rockbridge) were formed and reorganized during this period
- County-level record-keeping was established from the 1630s and was the primary administrative unit throughout this period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed during 1775–1783. The FamilySearch Wiki's Virginia Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and did not supply a specific registration start date or level; the wiki should be consulted directly.
- **What exists:** No civil birth or death records for this period at any level
- **Marriage records:** County-level marriage bonds and licenses survive for many Virginia counties from the colonial period onward — the primary marriage source for 1775–1783
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia, Richmond; FamilySearch collection 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900)
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials); county court marriage bonds; family Bible records; FamilySearch collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Church of England (reorganized as Episcopal after 1776); Baptist (rapidly expanding); Methodist; Presbyterian; Lutheran and German Reformed (western counties)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; vestry books (poor relief, orphan lists, pew tax rolls)
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; Virginia Theological Seminary (Episcopal); Virginia Baptist Historical Society; FamilySearch collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230)
- **Gaps:** Anglican church disestablishment after 1776 disrupted parish register-keeping in many counties; Baptist and Methodist records expanded but early survival is inconsistent
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** No federal census was taken during 1775–1783; the first federal census (1790) was taken after this period and Virginia's 1790 return was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **State enumerations:** Virginia began county tax enumerations in 1782; FamilySearch volume 005301449 holds 87 images of state enumerations/tax lists (1782–1799), full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — must be searched by text, not by name
- **Other enumerations:** County tax lists from the 1780s are the accepted substitute for the missing 1790 census; FamilySearch collection 1456723 (Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850) is indexed
- **Access:** Collection 1456723 — indexed + images; volume 005301449 — full-text searchable, not name-indexed

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship orders, county court order books
- **Date range:** Virginia county court records date from the mid-1600s; the war period is fully within the existing county record series
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collections 2134567 (Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567) and 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)
- **Digitized volumes:** Volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795), 158 images, 61% name-indexed

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Virginia Land Office administered grants after 1776; the FamilySearch Wiki's Virginia Land and Property page returned only generic content during this survey — consult that page directly for full detail on original custodians
- **Types:** Land grants/patents, deeds, deed books, bounty land warrants (post-war), mortgages, tax lists
- **Bounty land (post-war):** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to its veterans; warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to their claims (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands); FamilySearch volume 005301447 holds 341 images of Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (1779–1800), browse-only (no index, not full-text searchable)
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 1734285

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **Record types and locations:**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls: NARA, Record Group 93
  - Virginia militia records: Library of Virginia, Richmond
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files: NARA, Record Group 15
  - Virginia State Navy records: published
  - Revolutionary War land bounty warrants: FamilySearch volume 005301447 (1779–1800), 341 images, **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** Collection 1945678 (Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783), https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678 — indexed + images
- **Online access:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized NARA pension files and service records; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for original records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Colonial Anglican/Episcopal churchyard cemeteries throughout Virginia; family burying grounds (very common in Virginia's rural landscape); municipal cemeteries are later
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has Virginia coverage; headstone survival for 1775–1783 burials is inconsistent given age and weathering
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this era are rare; vestry books may note burials; family Bibles record deaths

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) was the dominant colonial paper throughout this period
- **Content value:** Estate sale notices, military appointments, legal notices, runaway servant/enslaved person notices; formal obituaries were not a regular feature in this era
- **Where held:** Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Library of Virginia; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has some Virginia holdings

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Norfolk and Hampton Roads were primary Virginia ports; transatlantic traffic was severely disrupted 1775–1783
- **Record types:** Passenger lists are sparse for this wartime period; county court records (collection 2134567) may hold naturalization entries for foreign-born veterans; Loyalist property confiscation and departure records document emigration to Canada and Britain
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); county court records (FamilySearch collection 2134567); British Audit Office papers (The National Archives, Kew) for Loyalist claims
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members. For 1775–1783, such manifests are rare; focus on county court naturalization entries for foreign-born soldiers.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property tax and land tax; state enumerations
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1456723 covers 1782–1850; volume 005301449 covers state enumerations 1782–1799
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; county courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1456723 (indexed) and volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census, providing annual lists of male heads of household and taxable property

### Other record types
- **Loyalist records:** Confiscation and sale of Loyalist property generated county court records; post-war restitution claims are in British Audit Office papers at The National Archives, Kew — not available on U.S. online platforms
- **Vestry records:** Anglican vestry books name churchwardens, overseers of the poor, and persons receiving parish relief — many survive at Library of Virginia and local churches

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1945678: Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) | Military service for the war period | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 1598230: Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230) | Vital records absent from civil registration | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 1734285: Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) | Marriage bonds, deeds, wills | Free |

Locality guide written as `loc_001`.

---

Virginia in 1775-1783 was one of the best-documented colonies, with county-level records stretching back to the 1630s, but the war years created some important gaps. The most direct route to a soldier ancestor is FamilySearch's indexed collection of Virginia Military Records, 1775-1783 (free), followed by pension application files at the National Archives which often contain sworn statements of service, family members' names, and residence history. Because Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814, the county personal property and land tax lists beginning in 1782 serve as the best substitute for placing families in a specific county, and the county is the key to every other record type. Church records, marriage bonds, deed books, court order books, and probate files are all held at county level, with many accessible through FamilySearch collections and through the Library of Virginia in Richmond. Veterans who received bounty land grants in the Virginia Military District of Ohio have warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library even if the family never moved there.

To go further with a specific ancestor, the next step is to identify which Virginia county that person lived in during the 1780s using the tax lists, then narrow the search to that county's court records, church registers, and deed books.
