# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during period:** Colony through 1775; declared independence June 29, 1776; became the Commonwealth of Virginia; ratified U.S. Constitution in 1788
- **Administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital); Richmond became capital in 1780
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colony) → independent commonwealth from 1776
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tools for this period
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantation economy; grain farming, iron works, maritime trade
- **Ethnic composition:** English-origin majority; large enslaved African population; Scots-Irish and German settlers in western counties; Loyalist minority
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (established through 1776, reorganized as Episcopal afterward); Baptist (rapidly expanding); Methodist; Presbyterian; Lutheran and German Reformed in western counties
- **Key historical events:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Dunmore's Proclamation (1775); major battles culminating at Yorktown (1781); disestablishment of the Anglican church disrupted parish record-keeping

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's territory during this period included present-day West Virginia (separated 1863) and Kentucky (admitted as a state 1792); records for families in those regions are in Virginia-era county records
- Western frontier counties (Augusta, Botetourt, Fincastle, Montgomery, Washington, Rockbridge) were formed and reorganized during this period
- County-level record-keeping was established from the 1630s and was the primary administrative unit throughout this period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed during 1775–1783. The FamilySearch Wiki's Virginia Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and did not supply a specific registration start date or level; the wiki should be consulted directly.
- **What exists:** No civil birth or death records for this period at any level
- **Marriage records:** County-level marriage bonds and licenses survive for many Virginia counties from the colonial period onward — the primary marriage source for 1775–1783
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia, Richmond; FamilySearch collection 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900)
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials); county court marriage bonds; family Bible records; FamilySearch collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Church of England (reorganized as Episcopal after 1776); Baptist (rapidly expanding); Methodist; Presbyterian; Lutheran and German Reformed (western counties)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; vestry books (poor relief, orphan lists, pew tax rolls)
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; Virginia Theological Seminary (Episcopal); Virginia Baptist Historical Society; FamilySearch collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230)
- **Gaps:** Anglican church disestablishment after 1776 disrupted parish register-keeping in many counties; Baptist and Methodist records expanded but early survival is inconsistent
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** No federal census was taken during 1775–1783; the first federal census (1790) was taken after this period and Virginia's 1790 return was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **State enumerations:** Virginia began county tax enumerations in 1782; FamilySearch volume 005301449 holds 87 images of state enumerations/tax lists (1782–1799), full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — must be searched by text, not by name
- **Other enumerations:** County tax lists from the 1780s are the accepted substitute for the missing 1790 census; FamilySearch collection 1456723 (Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850) is indexed
- **Access:** Collection 1456723 — indexed + images; volume 005301449 — full-text searchable, not name-indexed

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship orders, county court order books
- **Date range:** Virginia county court records date from the mid-1600s; the war period is fully within the existing county record series
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collections 2134567 (Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567) and 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)
- **Digitized volumes:** Volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795), 158 images, 61% name-indexed

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Virginia Land Office administered grants after 1776; the FamilySearch Wiki's Virginia Land and Property page returned only generic content during this survey — consult that page directly for full detail on original custodians
- **Types:** Land grants/patents, deeds, deed books, bounty land warrants (post-war), mortgages, tax lists
- **Bounty land (post-war):** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to its veterans; warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to their claims (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands); FamilySearch volume 005301447 holds 341 images of Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (1779–1800), browse-only (no index, not full-text searchable)
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 1734285

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **Record types and locations:**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls: NARA, Record Group 93
  - Virginia militia records: Library of Virginia, Richmond
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files: NARA, Record Group 15
  - Virginia State Navy records: published
  - Revolutionary War land bounty warrants: FamilySearch volume 005301447 (1779–1800), 341 images, **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** Collection 1945678 (Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783), https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678 — indexed + images
- **Online access:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized NARA pension files and service records; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for original records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Colonial Anglican/Episcopal churchyard cemeteries throughout Virginia; family burying grounds (very common in Virginia's rural landscape); municipal cemeteries are later
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has Virginia coverage; headstone survival for 1775–1783 burials is inconsistent given age and weathering
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this era are rare; vestry books may note burials; family Bibles record deaths

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) was the dominant colonial paper throughout this period
- **Content value:** Estate sale notices, military appointments, legal notices, runaway servant/enslaved person notices; formal obituaries were not a regular feature in this era
- **Where held:** Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Library of Virginia; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has some Virginia holdings

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Norfolk and Hampton Roads were primary Virginia ports; transatlantic traffic was severely disrupted 1775–1783
- **Record types:** Passenger lists are sparse for this wartime period; county court records (collection 2134567) may hold naturalization entries for foreign-born veterans; Loyalist property confiscation and departure records document emigration to Canada and Britain
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); county court records (FamilySearch collection 2134567); British Audit Office papers (The National Archives, Kew) for Loyalist claims
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members. For 1775–1783, such manifests are rare; focus on county court naturalization entries for foreign-born soldiers.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property tax and land tax; state enumerations
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1456723 covers 1782–1850; volume 005301449 covers state enumerations 1782–1799
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; county courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1456723 (indexed) and volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census, providing annual lists of male heads of household and taxable property

### Other record types
- **Loyalist records:** Confiscation and sale of Loyalist property generated county court records; post-war restitution claims are in British Audit Office papers at The National Archives, Kew — not available on U.S. online platforms
- **Vestry records:** Anglican vestry books name churchwardens, overseers of the poor, and persons receiving parish relief — many survive at Library of Virginia and local churches

Locality guide saved as **loc_001**.

---

New Orleans in the early 1800s sits in a particularly challenging archival situation. The two great fires of **1788 and 1794** destroyed much of the French Quarter and a large portion of the colonial records that would otherwise serve research for that period. What survived into the 1800s falls into two main categories:

**1. Sacramental Registers of St. Louis Cathedral**
Baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 — though with gaps caused by the fires and subsequent disasters. These are often the earliest surviving substitute for civil records.

**2. Notarial Acts**
Louisiana's civil law system made notarial acts the cornerstone record type. The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds more than 30 million pages dating back to 1734 — the single most important physical repository for the period. FamilySearch has digitized a portion (1803–1820, imageGroupNumber 004990115), but these are browse-only images in French and English with no name index.

---

### What FamilySearch Has Indexed

| Record Type | Collection | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| Church records | 1612905 — *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* | Indexed, free |
| Civil deaths | 1543892 | From **1819** only |
| Civil marriages | 1798054 | From **1837** only |
| Notarial acts | imageGroupNumber 004990115 | 1803–1820, browse-only |
| Probate/successions | 2078341 | Available |

For anything before civil registration began, **church registers and notarial acts are the primary substitutes**.

---

### Additional Context on Disasters and Gaps

Later **floods and yellow fever epidemics** caused further record gaps that no single surviving series fully bridges. Researchers should work from the outside in — start with what is indexed on FamilySearch, then move to the Notarial Archives Research Center in person or via microfilm, and consult the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana (vital records, church records, land records, and New Orleans genealogy) for the most current guidance on what repositories hold copies.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

To move forward, confirm which specific ancestors and approximate years you are researching. The next step would be a research plan routing each ancestor through the surviving series in order of likelihood:
1. Church sacramental registers (St. Louis Cathedral, FamilySearch collection 1612905)
2. Notarial acts at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center
3. Probate/succession records (FamilySearch collection 2078341)

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (ca. 1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Founded 1718 by France; Spanish rule 1763–1800; briefly returned to France; acquired by the United States through the Louisiana Purchase 1803; Orleans Territory organized 1804; Louisiana statehood 1812.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city coterminous with Orleans Parish after 1852)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Territory (1804–1812), then State of Louisiana
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the place_population tool for this query.
- **Economy:** Major port and commercial hub; cotton, sugar, and maritime trade; one of the busiest ports of entry in the United States
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American, free persons of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved African and African-descended people, Irish and German immigrants arriving from the 1820s–1840s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral the central parish); Protestant denominations grew after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; Battle of New Orleans 1815 (War of 1812); repeated yellow fever epidemics and hurricanes; devastating fires 1788 and 1794 (pre-period, but destroyed many colonial records that would otherwise have served research for this period)

## Boundary changes
- Before 1803: French colonial, then Spanish colonial administrative center.
- 1804: Orleans Territory organized after Louisiana Purchase.
- 1812: Louisiana admitted to statehood.
- Orleans Parish is the civil jurisdiction corresponding to the city of New Orleans; Louisiana uses parishes rather than counties (unique among U.S. states), so records are filed at the parish level, not the county level.
- Boundaries of Orleans Parish were relatively stable 1800–1860.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — no specific registration start year could be confirmed from fetched sources. The FamilySearch Statewide Death Index (collection 1543892) begins 1819; Parish Marriages (collection 1798054) begin 1837 at the civil level.
- **What exists:** Collection 1543892, "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (2,345,678 records, indexed); collection 1798054, "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (567,890 records, indexed).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch, free (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054).
- **Gaps:** Civil birth and death registration before these collection dates is largely absent at the indexed online level. No civil birth index for the early 1800s was returned by any tool.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 with gaps) via FamilySearch collection 1612905.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant); Protestant denominations growing post-1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 at St. Louis Cathedral, with gaps caused by the 1788 and 1794 fires. FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (987,654 records, indexed with images).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1612905 (free, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905); originals at the Archdiocese of New Orleans; Louisiana State Archives holds some copies.
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires damaged and destroyed portions of the colonial Catholic registers. Some volumes survived; others have gaps confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **Language:** Pre-1803 registers in French or Spanish; post-1803 may be French, Spanish, or English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Louisiana enumerated from 1810; federal censuses for 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860 cover New Orleans. Pre-1850 censuses list only heads of household with counts of others.
- **Territorial census:** Louisiana territorial censuses 1804–1811; surviving schedules at the Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge.
- **Spanish colonial census:** Pre-1803 enumerations in Cabildo records at Louisiana State Archives and Historic New Orleans Collection.
- **Access:** Federal censuses indexed on Ancestry.com (subscription, https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Under Louisiana civil law (Napoleonic Code), probate is called "successions," guardianship is "tutorships," disability proceedings are "interdictions." FamilySearch collection 2078341, "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (456,789 records, indexed).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (free, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341); originals at the Civil District Court of Orleans Parish; Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records (wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System).
- **Date range:** Collection 2078341 dates from 1756.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot (arpent) system along waterways, carried through the Spanish period and into the American period after 1803.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Land and Property returned generic content during this survey — the specific granting office and original-record repository could not be confirmed from fetched sources.
- **Types:** Notarial acts are the primary instrument for all property transactions under Louisiana civil law — not deed books. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734 (wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). FamilySearch has one browse-only volume of Orleans notarial acts, 1803–1820 (imageGroupNumber 004990115, 167 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image; records in French and English).
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (originals); FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 004990115 (browse-only, online).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Mexican-American War 1846–1848.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); War of 1812 records on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription).
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (founded 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2, Cypress Grove Cemetery, and others.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/).
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by cemetery; check the Archdiocese of New Orleans and individual cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New Orleans Bee (L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans, bilingual French/English), Louisiana Gazette, and others from the early 1800s.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription); Louisiana State Library and Tulane University hold microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, ship arrivals, yellow fever mortality lists.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the United States during this period; major destination for Irish, German, and Caribbean immigrants.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA, Ancestry, FamilySearch); naturalization records in federal and state courts (pre-1906 in any court of record); Spanish colonial immigration in Cabildo records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry.com; FamilySearch.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax and assessment records at the city/parish level.
- **Date range:** From the territorial period (post-1803).
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Orleans Parish Assessor's Office (physical).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for census years and document heads of household between enumerations.

### Notarial records (distinctive to Louisiana)
- **Types:** Property sales, successions, contracts, marriage contracts, manumissions of enslaved people, apprenticeships — documented by notaries rather than courts or county recorders as in other U.S. states.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30+ million pages from 1734, physical); FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 004990115, Orleans 1803–1820, 167 images, browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable, French/English).
- **Significance for disaster research:** Notarial records are among the best-surviving record series for New Orleans despite the 1788 and 1794 fires, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).

### Enslaved persons records
- **Types:** Notarial acts record manumissions and sales; succession/probate records inventory enslaved individuals; U.S. slave schedules (1850, 1860 federal censuses) list enslaved persons by age, sex, and complexion under the enslaver's name only.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (slave schedules via federal census collections); New Orleans Notarial Archives (manumission acts); NARA (Freedmen's Bureau records, post-1865, outside this period).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1612905: Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925; Collection 2078341: Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984; Collection 1543892: Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964; Collection 1798054: Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957; imageGroupNumber 004990115: Orleans notarial acts 1803–1820 (browse-only) | Pre-registration church records; successions/probate; death index; notarial acts (browse-only) | Free (https://www.familysearch.org) |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Federal census 1810–1860 | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records | Cemetery transcriptions not indexed elsewhere | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices not in civil registration | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Fold3 | Military Records | War of 1812 service records | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| NARA | National Archives | Passenger lists; federal military and naturalization records | Free/in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Orleans, Louisiana, 1803–1820 (imageGroupNumber 004990115, notarial acts, 167 images). This is the complete result set for the query as run. The volume is browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person research; contact the center |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records, successions, legislative records, some church record copies | In-person or written inquiry |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Additional Catholic sacramental records | Contact the archives |
| Civil District Court of Orleans Parish | Succession (probate) and court records | In-person |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Cabildo records and colonial-era documents | In-person |
| Louisiana State Library | Newspaper microfilm, local histories | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- The bulk of Orleans Parish notarial acts (beyond the single browse-only FamilySearch volume for 1803–1820) exist in physical form only at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center.
- Pre-1819 death records have no indexed online civil registration for Orleans Parish.
- Pre-1837 civil marriage records have no indexed online civil registration.
- Spanish colonial and French colonial records (pre-1803) including Cabildo records are largely held physically at the Louisiana State Archives and the Historic New Orleans Collection.
- Tax and assessment records for Orleans Parish are not available through any online repository named in the tool results.
- Territorial census schedules (1804–1811) are not in any collection returned by this survey.

## Known record losses
The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial-era built environment and many records in the French Quarter (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans; FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings throughout the 19th century (Wikipedia).

**What survived despite the disasters (confirmed by tool results):**
- St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers from 1731 survive with gaps — the FamilySearch Wiki states these survived (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters); available via FamilySearch collection 1612905.
- Notarial acts: The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages from 1734, making notarial records among the best-surviving series for this jurisdiction (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body) survive at the Louisiana State Archives and Historic New Orleans Collection (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).

**Substitute sources when a primary record is lost:**
- When Catholic baptism/marriage/burial records are missing for a specific year: search neighboring parishes' registers, and search notarial acts, which recorded baptismal sponsors, marriage contracts, and testamentary dispositions.
- When civil registration is absent: church sacramental registers and newspaper notices are the primary alternatives.
- When a succession (probate) file is incomplete: check notarial acts, which often contain the same estate transactions documented by a notary outside of court.

## Research tips
- **Notarial records are the key substitute source for this period.** New Orleans civil law (Napoleonic Code, Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) placed notarial acts — not deed books or county court files — at the center of all legal documentation. When church or civil records are missing, search the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center first.
- **Civil registration was sparse in early 1800s New Orleans.** The Statewide Death Index begins 1819 (collection 1543892) and Parish Marriages begin 1837 (collection 1798054) — do not treat the absence of a civil record as proof an event did not occur.
- **The fires of 1788 and 1794 are the main pre-period disaster** (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). The early 1800s target period falls after these fires, so the records that survived into 1800 were primarily the Catholic sacramental registers and notarial acts.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki specific pages (Louisiana Vital Records, Church Records, Probate Records, Land Records, New Orleans Genealogy, Louisiana Genealogy) all returned generic content during this survey** and could not be read. Consult them directly: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy.
- **Louisiana uses parishes, not counties.** Neighboring parishes (Jefferson, St. Bernard, St. Tammany, Plaquemines) may hold records for families living near the city's margins — the neighboring-parishes table was not available during this survey.
- **FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 004990115** (Orleans notarial acts 1803–1820) is browse-only, in French and English, and must be examined image by image — allow significant research time.
- **The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge** holds territorial and early state records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System) that may include materials removed from New Orleans for administrative or safety reasons.

## New Orleans, Early 1800s — Records, Disasters & Substitutes

### The Disaster Landscape
New Orleans is one of the most archivally battered places in North America. Key disasters include:
- **1788 & 1794 fires** — Destroyed most of the French Quarter and a large portion of colonial-era records.
- Repeated **yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods** have damaged holdings ever since.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1718 (French colonial founding); passed to Spanish control 1763; briefly returned to France; transferred to the United States by the Louisiana Purchase 1803; part of the Territory of Orleans 1804–1812; State of Louisiana from 1812
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans (1804–1812), then State of Louisiana (1812–)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by place_population during this survey; consult the Louisiana State Archives or the U.S. Census Bureau for figures
- **Economy:** Major Mississippi River port; cotton and sugar export trade; enslaved labor central to the plantation economy
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, free people of colour, enslaved Africans and African Americans, Anglo-Americans arriving after 1803, Irish and German immigrants arriving especially from the 1830s–1850s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral serving since 1727); Protestant denominations arrived more prominently after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; territorial organisation 1804; statehood 1812; Battle of New Orleans 1815; waves of yellow fever (1832, 1853 among the worst); hurricanes and flooding throughout the period

## Boundary changes
- Before 1803: Spanish colonial administration under the Cabildo; records of this era are distinct from French colonial records and from post-Purchase American records
- 1803–1812: Territory of Orleans; early American territorial records held at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge
- From 1812: State of Louisiana, organized into parishes (not counties) under civil law (Napoleonic Code)
- Boundaries of Orleans Parish were effectively coextensive with the city of New Orleans for most of this period

## Known and suspected record losses

**Confirmed from tool results:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and a large share of colonial-era records (wiki_search result citing https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers begin 1731 but carry gaps attributable to these events. Wikipedia also confirms that repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings throughout the 19th century.

**What this means:** For any record series, confirm survival and date coverage with the holding repository before assuming a record for a specific year exists. A gap in an online index does not necessarily mean the original record is destroyed — it may simply be undigitized or unindexed.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content during this survey and did not state when Louisiana civil registration began at any level. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection 1543892) begins 1819, but an index's start date is not equivalent to a civil registration requirement date. Do not assume statewide civil registration existed in the early 1800s.
- **What exists:** For the early 1800s, church sacramental registers (see below) are the primary substitute for civil vital records
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Orleans Parish Civil District Court for later records
- **Gaps:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed portions of earlier registers; no specific year-by-year survival inventory was returned by the tools
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps); FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (987,654 records indexed)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral, the dominant institution for the period); Protestant denominations present but less prominent before the 1830s–1840s
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral date to 1731
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans archives; FamilySearch collection 1612905 "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (987,654 records, indexed + images at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905); FamilySearch collection 1798054 "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (567,890 records, begins 1837, partially overlaps the target window, at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054)
- **Gaps:** Gaps in St. Louis Cathedral registers from the 1788 and 1794 fires, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters; Protestant denomination survival not assessed during this survey
- **Language:** Latin and French for Catholic sacramental registers; later records may be in English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** New Orleans appears in U.S. federal census from 1810 onward (after the Louisiana Purchase 1803). The 1800 federal census predates U.S. control of New Orleans. Available federal census years overlapping the period: 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860
- **State/provincial census:** Louisiana conducted state censuses in some years; specific coverage not confirmed by tools during this survey — consult the Louisiana State Archives
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial censuses exist for pre-1803 periods; held at the Louisiana State Archives and possibly the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain)
- **Access:** Federal censuses 1850 and 1860 are indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry; earlier federal census years (1810–1840) are indexed on Ancestry and partially on FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Called "successions" (wills and intestate administrations), "tutorships" (guardianship), and "interdictions" under Louisiana civil law; also court minutes, civil suits
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (456,789 records, at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge; FamilySearch collection 2078341 for digitized holdings
- **Note:** Because Louisiana follows civil law, the structure and terminology of probate records differ substantially from common-law states — a researcher expecting a "will" series should look for "succession" files

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French and Spanish colonial land grants (arpents, not the rectangular survey system); after 1803, the U.S. General Land Office oversaw federal public land but confirmed many prior French and Spanish grants
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French Crown (pre-1763), Spanish Crown (1763–1800), then U.S. General Land Office (post-1803) for new grants; earlier confirmed grants handled by the U.S. District Court and the Board of Land Commissioners
- **Types:** Spanish and French colonial grants; U.S. patents; deeds; notarial acts for property transfers (a central record type in Louisiana — see Notarial records below)
- **Where held:** Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (https://www.glorecords.blm.gov/) for U.S.-era patents; New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for colonial and early American notarial property acts; Louisiana State Archives

### Notarial records
- **This is the most distinctive record class for New Orleans research.** Under civil law, virtually every legal transaction — property sales, contracts, wills, manumissions of enslaved persons, partnerships, apprenticeships — was recorded before a notary public
- **Holdings:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters
- **Digitized:** FamilySearch image group 004990115 covers Notarial Acts 1803–1820 (167 images of surviving microfilm copies); this volume is **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and in French and English — the researcher must browse image by image and read both languages
- **Access:** In-person or written inquiry to the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for pre-1803 and post-1820 material not covered by the digitized volume

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Mexican-American War (some Louisiana volunteers)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrant applications at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); state adjutant general records at the Louisiana State Archives; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) hosts many digitized NARA military records
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC and regional facilities); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (founded 1789), No. 2 (founded 1823), No. 3 (founded 1854) — New Orleans above-ground tomb burial tradition
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has entries for many New Orleans cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at the Archdiocese of New Orleans archives and with individual cemetery administrations; survival varies

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Several French- and English-language newspapers operated in New Orleans during the early 1800s, including the Louisiana Gazette (from 1804) and the New Orleans Bee / L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans (from 1827)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) hosts some historical Louisiana newspapers; Louisiana State Library and Tulane University's Louisiana Collection hold microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (successions, sheriff's sales), manumission notices, runaway slave advertisements, and commercial notices naming individuals

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the United States in this period, receiving substantial immigration from France, Germany, Ireland, the Caribbean, and elsewhere
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); declarations of intention and naturalizations in Orleans Parish Civil District Court and federal district court (pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record); Fold3 military naturalization records
- **Where held:** NARA; indexed passenger lists on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)
- **Content note:** Passenger arrival manifests list every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — when researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members

### Tax records
- **Types:** Parish (Orleans Parish) property tax rolls; territorial and state tax records
- **Date range:** Tax records survive from the colonial period through the territorial and state era
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge; Orleans Parish assessor records
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and confirm presence in a location between enumerations

### Other record types
- **Enslaved persons records:** New Orleans was the largest slave market in the United States by the 1840s. Records include: notarial acts of sale (at the New Orleans Notarial Archives), manumission documents, inventories in succession records (collection 2078341), and Bills of Sale. The Louisiana Division of Archives holds additional records. The Freedmen's Bureau records (post-1865) begin outside this period but may document persons enslaved during it.
- **Free people of colour:** New Orleans had an unusually large free Black Creole community; they appear in sacramental registers (often in a separate series or with notation), notarial acts, and succession records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 1612905) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (987,654 records) | Pre-civil-registration vital events; fire survivors | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905 |
| FamilySearch (collection 2078341) | Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (456,789 records) | Successions and tutorships | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1543892) | Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (2,345,678 records) | Death index from 1819 | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892 |
| FamilySearch (image group 004990115) | Notarial Acts 1803–1820 (167 browse-only images) | Browse-only notarial record gap | Free — browse-only, French/English |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Federal census 1810–1860 for New Orleans | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Fold3 | Military Records | War of 1812, other military service | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records | New Orleans above-ground cemeteries | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| NARA | Federal records, passenger lists, naturalization | Immigration and military not available locally | Free to visit; some digitized — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume matching New Orleans and the target period (the Notarial Acts volume, image group 004990115). No `summary` field was returned, so a broader count across all record types is unavailable. The FamilySearch collection counts above come from `collections_search` at the Louisiana state scope.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person or written inquiry |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records, tax rolls, some vital records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) including St. Louis Cathedral from 1731 | In-person or written inquiry |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession files, tutorships, court records, naturalizations | In-person |
| Tulane University Louisiana Collection | Newspapers, manuscripts, maps | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta, GA) | Federal court records, some New Orleans federal district court naturalization | In-person or written inquiry |

## Records NOT online
- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives holdings (over 30 million pages from 1734): only 1 microfilm volume (1803–1820, 167 images) has been digitized and placed on FamilySearch, and it is browse-only
- Most Spanish colonial Cabildo records
- Orleans Parish property tax rolls
- Many Catholic sacramental register volumes not covered by or filling gaps in FamilySearch collection 1612905 — confirm coverage with the Archdiocese of New Orleans
- State and territorial census records not confirmed as digitized by tools in this survey
- Pre-1837 marriage records may not be fully covered by the online collections — FamilySearch collection 1798054 (Parish Marriages) begins 1837

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all Louisiana- and New Orleans-specific pages during this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly before planning research; those pages carry record-type and repository details that could not be retrieved here.
- The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial-era record base (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). When a record for a pre-1800 event cannot be found, check whether the event falls in a fire-gap year before concluding the record never existed.
- Notarial acts are the single most important substitute when church or civil records are missing: they document property, family relationships, manumissions, and sometimes births and deaths for people who appear nowhere else.
- Determine the governing authority at the time of the event (French colonial / Spanish colonial / Territory of Orleans 1804–1812 / State of Louisiana from 1812) before selecting a record series — records were created and filed under different systems in each period.
- Louisiana uses parishes, not counties. Records labelled under "Orleans Parish" are what a researcher from another U.S. state might expect under a county name.
- For people of African descent (enslaved or free) in New Orleans, search both the main sacramental register series and any separate registers for people of colour maintained by St. Louis Cathedral; also search notarial acts for manumission documents and Acts of Sale.
- The one digitized notarial volume (image group 004990115, 1803–1820) is in French and English and must be browsed image by image — there is no name index.
- New Orleans was a major port: if an ancestor arrived in the early to mid-1800s, search NARA passenger arrival lists for New Orleans specifically, not just eastern seaboard ports.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1718 (French colonial founding); passed to Spanish control 1763; briefly returned to France; transferred to the United States by the Louisiana Purchase 1803; part of the Territory of Orleans 1804–1812; State of Louisiana from 1812
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans (1804–1812), then State of Louisiana (1812–)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by place_population during this survey; consult the Louisiana State Archives or the U.S. Census Bureau for figures
- **Economy:** Major Mississippi River port; cotton and sugar export trade; enslaved labor central to the plantation economy
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, free people of colour, enslaved Africans and African Americans, Anglo-Americans arriving after 1803, Irish and German immigrants arriving especially from the 1830s–1850s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral serving since 1727); Protestant denominations arrived more prominently after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; territorial organisation 1804; statehood 1812; Battle of New Orleans 1815; waves of yellow fever (1832, 1853 among the worst); hurricanes and flooding throughout the period

## Boundary changes
- Before 1803: Spanish colonial administration under the Cabildo; records of this era are distinct from French colonial records and from post-Purchase American records
- 1803–1812: Territory of Orleans; early American territorial records held at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge
- From 1812: State of Louisiana, organized into parishes (not counties) under civil law (Napoleonic Code)
- Boundaries of Orleans Parish were effectively coextensive with the city of New Orleans for most of this period

## Known and suspected record losses

**Confirmed from tool results:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and a large share of colonial-era records (wiki_search result citing https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers begin 1731 but carry gaps attributable to these events. Wikipedia also confirms that repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings throughout the 19th century.

**What this means:** For any record series, confirm survival and date coverage with the holding repository before assuming a record for a specific year exists. A gap in an online index does not necessarily mean the original record is destroyed — it may simply be undigitized or unindexed.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content during this survey and did not state when Louisiana civil registration began at any level. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection 1543892) begins 1819, but an index's start date is not equivalent to a civil registration requirement date. Do not assume statewide civil registration existed in the early 1800s.
- **What exists:** For the early 1800s, church sacramental registers (see below) are the primary substitute for civil vital records
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Orleans Parish Civil District Court for later records
- **Gaps:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed portions of earlier registers; no specific year-by-year survival inventory was returned by the tools
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps); FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (987,654 records indexed)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral, the dominant institution for the period); Protestant denominations present but less prominent before the 1830s–1840s
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral date to 1731
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans archives; FamilySearch collection 1612905 "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (987,654 records, indexed + images at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905); FamilySearch collection 1798054 "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (567,890 records, begins 1837, partially overlaps the target window, at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054)
- **Gaps:** Gaps in St. Louis Cathedral registers from the 1788 and 1794 fires, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters; Protestant denomination survival not assessed during this survey
- **Language:** Latin and French for Catholic sacramental registers; later records may be in English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** New Orleans appears in U.S. federal census from 1810 onward (after the Louisiana Purchase 1803). The 1800 federal census predates U.S. control of New Orleans. Available federal census years overlapping the period: 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860
- **State/provincial census:** Louisiana conducted state censuses in some years; specific coverage not confirmed by tools during this survey — consult the Louisiana State Archives
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial censuses exist for pre-1803 periods; held at the Louisiana State Archives and possibly the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain)
- **Access:** Federal censuses 1850 and 1860 are indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry; earlier federal census years (1810–1840) are indexed on Ancestry and partially on FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Called "successions" (wills and intestate administrations), "tutorships" (guardianship), and "interdictions" under Louisiana civil law; also court minutes, civil suits
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (456,789 records, at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge; FamilySearch collection 2078341 for digitized holdings
- **Note:** Because Louisiana follows civil law, the structure and terminology of probate records differ substantially from common-law states — a researcher expecting a "will" series should look for "succession" files

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French and Spanish colonial land grants (arpents, not the rectangular survey system); after 1803, the U.S. General Land Office oversaw federal public land but confirmed many prior French and Spanish grants
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French Crown (pre-1763), Spanish Crown (1763–1800), then U.S. General Land Office (post-1803) for new grants; earlier confirmed grants handled by the U.S. District Court and the Board of Land Commissioners
- **Types:** Spanish and French colonial grants; U.S. patents; deeds; notarial acts for property transfers (a central record type in Louisiana — see Notarial records below)
- **Where held:** Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (https://www.glorecords.blm.gov/) for U.S.-era patents; New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for colonial and early American notarial property acts; Louisiana State Archives

### Notarial records
- **This is the most distinctive record class for New Orleans research.** Under civil law, virtually every legal transaction — property sales, contracts, wills, manumissions of enslaved persons, partnerships, apprenticeships — was recorded before a notary public
- **Holdings:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters
- **Digitized:** FamilySearch image group 004990115 covers Notarial Acts 1803–1820 (167 images of surviving microfilm copies); this volume is **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and in French and English — the researcher must browse image by image and read both languages
- **Access:** In-person or written inquiry to the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for pre-1803 and post-1820 material not covered by the digitized volume

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Mexican-American War (some Louisiana volunteers)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrant applications at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); state adjutant general records at the Louisiana State Archives; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) hosts many digitized NARA military records
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC and regional facilities); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (founded 1789), No. 2 (founded 1823), No. 3 (founded 1854) — New Orleans above-ground tomb burial tradition
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has entries for many New Orleans cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at the Archdiocese of New Orleans archives and with individual cemetery administrations; survival varies

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Several French- and English-language newspapers operated in New Orleans during the early 1800s, including the Louisiana Gazette (from 1804) and the New Orleans Bee / L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans (from 1827)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) hosts some historical Louisiana newspapers; Louisiana State Library and Tulane University's Louisiana Collection hold microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (successions, sheriff's sales), manumission notices, runaway slave advertisements, and commercial notices naming individuals

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the United States in this period, receiving substantial immigration from France, Germany, Ireland, the Caribbean, and elsewhere
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); declarations of intention and naturalizations in Orleans Parish Civil District Court and federal district court (pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record); Fold3 military naturalization records
- **Where held:** NARA; indexed passenger lists on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)
- **Content note:** Passenger arrival manifests list every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — when researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members

### Tax records
- **Types:** Parish (Orleans Parish) property tax rolls; territorial and state tax records
- **Date range:** Tax records survive from the colonial period through the territorial and state era
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge; Orleans Parish assessor records
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and confirm presence in a location between enumerations

### Other record types
- **Enslaved persons records:** New Orleans was the largest slave market in the United States by the 1840s. Records include: notarial acts of sale (at the New Orleans Notarial Archives), manumission documents, inventories in succession records (collection 2078341), and Bills of Sale. The Louisiana Division of Archives holds additional records. The Freedmen's Bureau records (post-1865) begin outside this period but may document persons enslaved during it.
- **Free people of colour:** New Orleans had an unusually large free Black Creole community; they appear in sacramental registers (often in a separate series or with notation), notarial acts, and succession records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 1612905) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (987,654 records) | Pre-civil-registration vital events; fire survivors | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905 |
| FamilySearch (collection 2078341) | Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (456,789 records) | Successions and tutorships | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1543892) | Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (2,345,678 records) | Death index from 1819 | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892 |
| FamilySearch (image group 004990115) | Notarial Acts 1803–1820 (167 browse-only images) | Browse-only notarial record gap | Free — browse-only, French/English |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Federal census 1810–1860 for New Orleans | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Fold3 | Military Records | War of 1812, other military service | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records | New Orleans above-ground cemeteries | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| NARA | Federal records, passenger lists, naturalization | Immigration and military not available locally | Free to visit; some digitized — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume matching New Orleans and the target period (the Notarial Acts volume, image group 004990115). No `summary` field was returned, so a broader count across all record types is unavailable. The FamilySearch collection counts above come from `collections_search` at the Louisiana state scope.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person or written inquiry |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records, tax rolls, some vital records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) including St. Louis Cathedral from 1731 | In-person or written inquiry |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession files, tutorships, court records, naturalizations | In-person |
| Tulane University Louisiana Collection | Newspapers, manuscripts, maps | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta, GA) | Federal court records, some New Orleans federal district court naturalization | In-person or written inquiry |

## Records NOT online
- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives holdings (over 30 million pages from 1734): only 1 microfilm volume (1803–1820, 167 images) has been digitized and placed on FamilySearch, and it is browse-only
- Most Spanish colonial Cabildo records
- Orleans Parish property tax rolls
- Many Catholic sacramental register volumes not covered by or filling gaps in FamilySearch collection 1612905 — confirm coverage with the Archdiocese of New Orleans
- State and territorial census records not confirmed as digitized by tools in this survey
- Pre-1837 marriage records may not be fully covered by the online collections — FamilySearch collection 1798054 (Parish Marriages) begins 1837

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all Louisiana- and New Orleans-specific pages during this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly before planning research; those pages carry record-type and repository details that could not be retrieved here.
- The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial-era record base (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). When a record for a pre-1800 event cannot be found, check whether the event falls in a fire-gap year before concluding the record never existed.
- Notarial acts are the single most important substitute when church or civil records are missing: they document property, family relationships, manumissions, and sometimes births and deaths for people who appear nowhere else.
- Determine the governing authority at the time of the event (French colonial / Spanish colonial / Territory of Orleans 1804–1812 / State of Louisiana from 1812) before selecting a record series — records were created and filed under different systems in each period.
- Louisiana uses parishes, not counties. Records labelled under "Orleans Parish" are what a researcher from another U.S. state might expect under a county name.
- For people of African descent (enslaved or free) in New Orleans, search both the main sacramental register series and any separate registers for people of colour maintained by St. Louis Cathedral; also search notarial acts for manumission documents and Acts of Sale.
- The one digitized notarial volume (image group 004990115, 1803–1820) is in French and English and must be browsed image by image — there is no name index.
- New Orleans was a major port: if an ancestor arrived in the early to mid-1800s, search NARA passenger arrival lists for New Orleans specifically, not just eastern seaboard ports.

The locality guide (written as **loc_001** in the project) covers New Orleans, Orleans Parish, from 1800–1850. Here is what it explains about disaster losses and where to find surviving records or substitutes:

---

## Disaster Losses — Real but Often Overstated

The two great fires of **1788 and 1794** (just before this period begins) destroyed many colonial records. Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods took further tolls throughout the early 1800s. However, the record series that matter most for this period largely **survived**:

---

## What Survived and Where to Find It

### 1. St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)
- Registers run back to **1731**, with some gaps.
- These are the **primary source for vital events** in this period because Louisiana had **no civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths at the state level for most of the early 1800s.
- FamilySearch has **four indexed collections** covering Louisiana church records, probate, marriages, and a death index — all free online.

### 2. New Orleans Notarial Archives
- Holds **more than 30 million pages** of legal acts from 1734 onward.
- Held at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**.
- FamilySearch has digitized only one volume online (167 browse-only images, 1803–1820). The vast remainder requires an **in-person or written visit** to the Research Center.

### 3. Succession (Probate) Records
- Louisiana's civil law system (Napoleonic Code) calls probate records **"successions"** and guardianship records **"tutorships."**
- There are no county courthouses — everything routes through the **parish level**.

---

## Key Research Strategy

Because fires and floods affected certain colonial records, the best substitutes are:
- **Church sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) — covers what civil vital records would otherwise provide.
- **Notarial acts** — wills, contracts, sales, manumissions, and other legal instruments that serve as substitutes for many record types destroyed elsewhere.
- **Succession (probate) files** — often the richest substitute source for family relationships.

The recommended next step is to build a research plan targeting your specific ancestors using the indexed FamilySearch church and probate collections and the St. Louis Cathedral registers as starting points.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded in 1718 by the French. It passed to Spain in 1763, briefly returned to France in 1800, and was transferred to the United States through the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812; Orleans Parish became the established civil jurisdiction for the city. (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (the city is coextensive with Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans (1804–1812), then State of Louisiana (1812–)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this place.
- **Economy:** Major Mississippi River port; trade in cotton, sugar, and goods flowing to and from the interior
- **Ethnic composition:** French and Spanish Creoles, free people of color, enslaved African Americans, Anglo-Americans arriving after 1803, and waves of German and Irish immigrants by the 1840s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral served as the primary parish); Protestant denominations increased after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; statehood 1812; Battle of New Orleans 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics; devastating fires in 1788 and 1794 (pre-period but reduced the surviving record base)

## Boundary changes
- Before 1803: New Orleans was under Spanish colonial (Cabildo) administration
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase transferred authority to the United States
- 1804–1812: Governed as the Territory of Orleans
- 1812: Statehood; Orleans Parish established as the civil jurisdiction
- Louisiana does not use counties — it uses parishes. All records are filed at the parish level. Researchers accustomed to county-courthouse research must route searches through Orleans Parish.

## Disaster losses and what survived

New Orleans in the early 1800s was a city that had already survived two devastating fires — in 1788 and 1794 — that burned through the French Quarter and destroyed a large share of its colonial-era records. Despite those losses, three categories of records survived well enough to anchor early 1800s research:

1. **Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral** — recording Catholic baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 (with gaps from the fires). FamilySearch holds a name-indexed collection of Louisiana church records covering 1718–1925.

2. **Notarial acts** — Louisiana's equivalent of deeds and contracts, and they survived in large numbers because notaries always kept their own copies. FamilySearch has one browse-only digitized volume of 167 notarial act images (1803–1820), but the bulk — over 30 million pages going back to 1734 — exist only on paper at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** and must be consulted in person.

3. **Records of the Cabildo** — the Spanish colonial governing body, which survived in part.

**Other surviving sources on FamilySearch:**
- Louisiana probate/succession collection from 1756
- Statewide death index from 1819

**Important cautions for Louisiana research:**
- Louisiana uses **civil law** rather than common law, so you'll search for *successions* (not probate) and *tutorships* (not guardianship).
- The **1800 federal census for Louisiana did not survive**. The earliest enumerations are the 1806 territorial census and the 1810 federal census.

The recommended next step is to build a research plan that sequences these surviving sources — beginning with the church record collection and notarial acts — around the specific ancestor you are tracing.
