# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800-1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded in 1718 by the French. It passed to Spanish control in 1763, returned briefly to France in 1800, and was transferred to the United States through the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. The Territory of Orleans was established in 1804; Louisiana was admitted as a state in 1812.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans serves as the seat of Orleans Parish. Louisiana uses civil parishes — not counties — as its primary administrative division.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish, Louisiana (state since 1812); previously Territory of Orleans (1804-1812).
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by tool query for this place.
- **Economy:** Major port city; principal trade, cotton, and sugar commerce in the early American South.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish colonial, African (free and enslaved), Caribbean immigrants, and Anglo-American settlers arriving in increasing numbers after 1803.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic predominant, centered on St. Louis Cathedral (established 1720s). Protestant denominations arrived in larger numbers after the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Key historical events:** Fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. Louisiana Purchase 1803. Recurring yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods throughout the period. Source: Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans).

## Boundary changes
- **1763:** New Orleans passed from French to Spanish control; records continued under Spanish colonial governance (the Cabildo).
- **1800-1803:** Briefly returned to France before the Louisiana Purchase transferred the territory to the United States.
- **1804:** Territory of Orleans established; US civil and territorial courts began generating records alongside the continuing civil-law notarial system.
- **1812:** Louisiana admitted as a state; the existing civil-law (Napoleonic Code) framework was retained and remains unique among US states.
- Records created before 1803 are under French or Spanish colonial authority. Early vital events may appear in records of the Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body) or in sacramental registers maintained by St. Louis Cathedral.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana_Vital_Records page did not return place-specific content during this survey, so no confirmed civil registration start date at any level can be stated from tool results. FamilySearch collection 1543892 ("Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964") begins in 1819, indicating some death registration existed from that year.
- **What exists:** During the early 1800s, civil vital registration in New Orleans was irregular. Sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) at St. Louis Cathedral are the primary pre-civil-registration vital-event source.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (987,654 records, ~493,827 images, free, indexed); FamilySearch collection 1543892, "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964" (2,345,678 records; index only, no images, free).
- **Gaps:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed many colonial-era records. St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survive from 1731 but with gaps caused by the fires. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Notarial acts often recorded marriage contracts and settlement of estates. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic is the dominant denomination. St. Louis Cathedral has maintained sacramental registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731. Protestant congregations became more established after 1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (free, indexed, ~493,827 images) is the main online source. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905.
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed a portion of the colonial sacramental registers; the surviving registers have gaps attributable to these fires. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **Language:** Records from before 1803 are in French or Spanish; after 1803, a mix of French and English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Available federal censuses within the period: 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850. The 1800 Louisiana census did not survive.
- **State/provincial census:** Louisiana conducted a territorial census in 1806 and a state census in 1850.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and available online through FamilySearch and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana uses "successions" rather than traditional probate. Succession records include wills, inventories of estates, administrator appointments, and creditor proceedings. Tutorships (guardianship) and interdictions are civil-law proceedings unique to Louisiana.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341, "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (456,789 records, ~228,394 images, free, indexed), covers the target period. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 is the primary online source. Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French long-lot/arpent survey system (civil law), not the rectangular survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana_Land_and_Property page did not return place-specific content during this survey; the specific land-grant office cannot be confirmed from tool results. Federal land grants after 1803 are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office.
- **Types:** Notarial acts include property sales, transfers, and mortgages — the functional equivalent of common-law deeds.
- **Date range:** Notarial acts available from 1734. FamilySearch image group 004990115 covers 1803-1820 (167 images, browse-only, French and English).
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (originals). FamilySearch image group 004990115 is a browse-only microfilm copy.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); territorial militia service.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) is the primary online access point.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (opened 1789) is the oldest surviving cemetery in New Orleans.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes burials.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers; survivorship of pre-1800 records is affected by the fire disasters.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Louisiana Gazette and New Orleans Advertiser (from 1804) and other early papers published legal notices, death notices, and marriage announcements.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); the Louisiana State Archives and New Orleans Public Library hold microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate notices, and legal advertising (successions, public sales) supplement lost vital records.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the antebellum United States.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests), declarations of intention, naturalizations. Under Louisiana's civil-law system, naturalizations were processed through the territorial and state courts.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds passenger lists and naturalization records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax and personal property tax.
- **Date range:** Territorial and early state tax records from the early 1800s.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge.
- **Substitute value:** Tax records can substitute for missing census years and establish arrival/departure from the jurisdiction.

### Notarial records (Louisiana-specific)
- **Types:** Notarial acts documented property sales, marriage contracts, successions, mortgages, manumission papers, and commercial agreements — replacing most functions served by common-law deeds and contracts in other states.
- **Date range:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds 30+ million pages from 1734. FamilySearch image group 004990115 covers 1803-1820 (167 images, browse-only, French and English).
- **Where held:** Originals at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center. FamilySearch image group 004990115 is a browse-only digitized microfilm copy.
- **Significance for disaster research:** Notaries retained copies of every act they drew. This redundancy meant that many notarial acts survived the 1788 and 1794 fires even when other record types were destroyed. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1612905: Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 records, ~493,827 images) | Church vital events covering pre-civil-registration period; fills gap left by destroyed civil records | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 1798054: Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (567,890 records) | Marriage records from 1837 onward | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 2078341: Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 records, ~228,394 images) | Successions naming family members; fills gap where vital records were destroyed | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 1543892: Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (2,345,678 records; index only, no images) | Death registration from 1819 | Free |
| FamilySearch | Image group 004990115: Notarial Acts 1803-1820, 167 images (browse-only, French/English) | Notarial property and succession records; fills gap left by destroyed deed-equivalent records | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Federal census 1810-1850; fills gap in years missing from civil registration | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | War of 1812 service, pension, and bounty land records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Burial records; fills gap where burial registers were destroyed | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituaries, marriage and estate notices substituting for destroyed vital records | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists, naturalization records, federal military records | Free/Fee |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (image group 004990115) covering New Orleans/Orleans 1803-1820. The tool did not return a volume_summary despite the request, so record-type group counts are unavailable. The single volume above is the complete digitized result for this place and period in FamilySearch.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30 million+ pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person at New Orleans |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records, tax records, court records | In-person / mail request |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | Local history, early newspapers, city directories | In-person |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers not yet digitized | Contact the Archives directly |

## Records NOT online
- The vast majority of the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center's holdings (30 million+ pages from 1734) are not online; only 167 images covering 1803-1820 are digitized on FamilySearch (browse-only, image group 004990115).
- Pre-1803 sacramental registers that survived the fires are partially represented in FamilySearch collection 1612905 but many volumes remain unindexed or physical-only.
- Early territorial court records from 1804-1812 are largely physical-only at the Louisiana State Archives.
- Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body) records are physical; online availability was not confirmed by tool results.
- The FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana_Land_and_Property page was unavailable during this survey; specific land record online coverage cannot be confirmed.

## Known record losses
- The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial-era built environment of New Orleans and many records. Source: Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) and FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy," section "Records Surviving Disasters" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- Despite the fires, significant records survived: sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) and notarial acts (redundant copies retained by notaries helped many survive). Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- The 1800 federal census for Louisiana did not survive.
- Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods caused further archival damage across the period. Source: Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans).
- **Substitute sources for destroyed records:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (FamilySearch collection 1612905); notarial acts at the Notarial Archives Research Center and FamilySearch image group 004990115; Cabildo records (Spanish colonial); newspaper legal notices (Newspapers.com); federal census enumerations (1810-1850); succession records (FamilySearch collection 2078341); tax records at the Louisiana State Archives.

## Research tips
- **Notarial acts are the foundation of early New Orleans research.** Under Louisiana's civil-law (Napoleonic Code) system, notarial acts documented property transfers, marriage contracts, successions, and many other transactions. Many survived the 1788 and 1794 fires because notaries retained duplicate copies. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages from 1734. FamilySearch image group 004990115 (167 browse-only images, French and English) covers 1803-1820 and must be browsed image-by-image with no name index. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers are the primary vital-event source before civil registration.** They record baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731, with gaps where the fires destroyed pages. FamilySearch collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925," free, indexed, ~493,827 images) is the main online access point. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **Use Louisiana civil-law terminology when searching.** Search for "successions" (not probate/wills), "tutorships" (not guardianships), and "notarial acts" (not deeds). FamilySearch collection 2078341 covers successions. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System).
- **Records before 1803 may be in French or Spanish.** Prepare to read records in both languages. The FamilySearch notarial acts volume (image group 004990115) is in both French and English; pre-1803 sacramental and Cabildo records are in French or Spanish.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana and New Orleans returned only generic content** through the wiki-query-api during this survey. Consult them directly before relying on their absence: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy.
- **Search neighboring parishes.** New Orleans sits in Orleans Parish; a family near parish boundaries may have generated records in Jefferson, St. Bernard, or St. Tammany parishes. The neighboring parishes were not returned in tool results; verify boundary locations before limiting the search to Orleans Parish alone.

- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge.
- **Substitute value:** Tax records can substitute for missing census years and establish arrival/departure from the jurisdiction.

### Notarial records (Louisiana-specific)
- **Types:** Notarial acts documented property sales, marriage contracts, successions, mortgages, manumission papers, and commercial agreements — replacing most functions served by common-law deeds and contracts in other states.
- **Date range:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds 30+ million pages from 1734. FamilySearch image group 004990115 covers 1803-1820 (167 images, browse-only, French and English).
- **Where held:** Originals at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center. FamilySearch image group 004990115 is a browse-only digitized microfilm copy.
- **Significance for disaster research:** Notaries retained copies of every act they drew. This redundancy meant that many notarial acts survived the 1788 and 1794 fires even when other record types were destroyed. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1612905: Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 records, ~493,827 images) | Church vital events covering pre-civil-registration period; fills gap left by destroyed civil records | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 1798054: Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (567,890 records) | Marriage records from 1837 onward | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 2078341: Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 records, ~228,394 images) | Successions naming family members; fills gap where vital records were destroyed | Free |
| FamilySearch | Collection 1543892: Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (2,345,678 records; index only, no images) | Death registration from 1819 | Free |
| FamilySearch | Image group 004990115: Notarial Acts 1803-1820, 167 images (browse-only, French/English) | Notarial property and succession records; fills gap left by destroyed deed-equivalent records | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Federal census 1810-1850; fills gap in years missing from civil registration | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | War of 1812 service, pension, and bounty land records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Burial records; fills gap where burial registers were destroyed | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituaries, marriage and estate notices substituting for destroyed vital records | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists, naturalization records, federal military records | Free/Fee |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (image group 004990115) covering New Orleans/Orleans 1803-1820. The tool did not return a volume_summary despite the request, so record-type group counts are unavailable. The single volume above is the complete digitized result for this place and period in FamilySearch.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30 million+ pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person at New Orleans |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records, tax records, court records | In-person / mail request |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | Local history, early newspapers, city directories | In-person |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers not yet digitized | Contact the Archives directly |

## Records NOT online
- The vast majority of the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center's holdings (30 million+ pages from 1734) are not online; only 167 images covering 1803-1820 are digitized on FamilySearch (browse-only, image group 004990115).
- Pre-1803 sacramental registers that survived the fires are partially represented in FamilySearch collection 1612905 but many volumes remain unindexed or physical-only.
- Early territorial court records from 1804-1812 are largely physical-only at the Louisiana State Archives.
- Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body) records are physical; online availability was not confirmed by tool results.
- The FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana_Land_and_Property page was unavailable during this survey; specific land record online coverage cannot be confirmed.

## Known record losses
- The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial-era built environment of New Orleans and many records. Source: Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) and FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy," section "Records Surviving Disasters" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- Despite the fires, significant records survived: sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) and notarial acts (redundant copies retained by notaries helped many survive). Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- The 1800 federal census for Louisiana did not survive.
- Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods caused further archival damage across the period. Source: Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans).
- **Substitute sources for destroyed records:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (FamilySearch collection 1612905); notarial acts at the Notarial Archives Research Center and FamilySearch image group 004990115; Cabildo records (Spanish colonial); newspaper legal notices (Newspapers.com); federal census enumerations (1810-1850); succession records (FamilySearch collection 2078341); tax records at the Louisiana State Archives.

## Research tips
- **Notarial acts are the foundation of early New Orleans research.** Under Louisiana's civil-law (Napoleonic Code) system, notarial acts documented property transfers, marriage contracts, successions, and many other transactions. Many survived the 1788 and 1794 fires because notaries retained duplicate copies. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages from 1734. FamilySearch image group 004990115 (167 browse-only images, French and English) covers 1803-1820 and must be browsed image-by-image with no name index. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers are the primary vital-event source before civil registration.** They record baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731, with gaps where the fires destroyed pages. FamilySearch collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925," free, indexed, ~493,827 images) is the main online access point. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "New Orleans Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **Use Louisiana civil-law terminology when searching.** Search for "successions" (not probate/wills), "tutorships" (not guardianships), and "notarial acts" (not deeds). FamilySearch collection 2078341 covers successions. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System).
- **Records before 1803 may be in French or Spanish.** Prepare to read records in both languages. The FamilySearch notarial acts volume (image group 004990115) is in both French and English; pre-1803 sacramental and Cabildo records are in French or Spanish.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana and New Orleans returned only generic content** through the wiki-query-api during this survey. Consult them directly before relying on their absence: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy.
- **Search neighboring parishes.** New Orleans sits in Orleans Parish; a family near parish boundaries may have generated records in Jefferson, St. Bernard, or St. Tammany parishes. The neighboring parishes were not returned in tool results; verify boundary locations before limiting the search to Orleans Parish alone.

Here is what the locality guide found:

---

**Boston Port of Entry — 1840s Immigration Records**

Boston in the 1840s was one of the five principal American ports of entry, and the decade was its peak wave of Irish Famine immigration. Here are the key records and repositories to consult:

**Primary Arrival Records**
- **Customs Passenger Lists, Port of Boston** (National Archives Record Group 36) — held in original at the National Archives facility in Waltham, Massachusetts. Note: 1840s manifests record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — they will *not* give you an Irish county or parish.
- **FamilySearch** carries an indexed collection of Massachusetts passenger lists, 1820–1891 (collection 1784312), including a digitized volume covering 1840–1850. That volume is only 3% name-indexed but is **full-text searchable**, so a text search can surface entries that a name search misses.
- **Ancestry** carries a parallel indexed version of the same series.

**Finding Specific Origins**
- ***The Pilot* newspaper's missing-persons column**, indexed by Boston College — relatives placed notices that routinely name the specific origin townland or parish in Ireland. This is often the single best tool for getting past "Ireland" to a specific locality.

**Post-Arrival Records**
- **Naturalization Records** — FamilySearch collection 1459213 (Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906, ~345,678 records). Before 1906, any court of record could naturalize an immigrant, so search federal, state district, and city court records alike.
- **Catholic Parish Registers** — Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and others, held at the **Archdiocese of Boston Archives**. FamilySearch collection 1921657 is a starting point, but verify which parishes it covers.

**Census Anchor**
- The **1850 federal census** is a valuable anchor: it was the first to name every household member (not just the head), so an ancestor who arrived in the 1840s and remained in Boston will appear by name, age, and stated birthplace.

---

**Suggested next step:** Open a research question tied to your specific ancestor, then use the research-plan tool, which will draw on this locality survey to build a prioritized search sequence.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1630; incorporated as a city 1822
- **County:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** No figures were returned by the place_population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic seaport; one of the five principal US ports of entry in the 1840s. Commerce, trade, and textile manufacturing dominated.
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive Irish immigration during the 1840s — especially those fleeing the Great Famine (1845–1852). By 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston). German and other Northern European immigrants also arrived.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish arrivals), Congregationalist, Unitarian, Episcopal, Baptist, Methodist.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine (1845–1852) drove the peak decade of pre-Civil War Irish immigration through Boston; the port's customs infrastructure produced the primary documentary record for these arrivals.

## Boundary changes
- place_search_all returned no boundary-change data for Boston. Boston remained within Suffolk County throughout the 1840s. No boundary changes during the target period are indicated by tool results.

## Available record types

### Immigration and naturalization records (primary focus)
- **Customs passenger lists (1820–1891):** In National Archives Record Group 36; originals held at the National Archives at Boston, Waltham, Massachusetts, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston. Indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1784312, Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891, 1,234,567 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) and on Ancestry.
- **Content of 1840s lists:** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only — no specific parish or townland, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston. This is far less detail than post-1890s Ellis Island manifests.
- **Digitized volume:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume (image group 003345210) covering Port of Boston Passenger Lists, 1840–1850: 389 images, 3% name-indexed, full-text searchable. This is a full-text-searchable but not name-indexed volume — browse or full-text search it on FamilySearch.
- **Naturalization records:** FamilySearch collection 1459213, Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (345,678 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213). Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record (federal, state, or local), so search all court levels.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content; no specific civil registration start year at the statewide or town level was confirmed by a tool result. The FamilySearch Wiki does not state one per tool results returned.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 2061550, Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (3,456,789 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) covers Boston at the town level throughout the 1840s.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collection 2061550); originals at the Massachusetts State Archives and the City of Boston Archives.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below) and The Pilot newspaper missing-persons notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (primary for Irish immigrants), Congregationalist, Unitarian, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Catholic parish registers (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and others) from the 1840s onward are held at the Archdiocese of Boston Archives, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston. FamilySearch collection 1921657, Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (987,654 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) covers this period — verify which parishes are included.
- **Language:** Latin for Catholic sacramental registers; English for most Protestant records.
- **Gaps:** Coverage of individual 1840s Catholic parishes within collection 1921657 is unconfirmed from tool results.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 (head of household named only) and 1850 (all members named) cover Boston. The 1850 census is the first to list immigrants individually by name, age, and birthplace — critical for confirming arrival decade.
- **State census:** No Massachusetts state census for this period was confirmed by tool results.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules began with the 1850 census.
- **Access:** 1840 and 1850 federal censuses are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories; also naturalizations (any court pre-1906).
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1678901, Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (567,890 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collection 1678901); originals at Suffolk County Probate Court and Massachusetts State Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for Massachusetts land and property pages; the specific granting office is not confirmed from tool results.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages.
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds; not identified as an online FamilySearch collection in tool results.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) per curated external links.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) per curated external links.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at individual cemeteries and the City of Boston Archives; not identified as online collections in tool results.

### Newspaper records
- **Key resource — The Pilot:** This Irish Catholic newspaper published arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements for immigrants in Boston during the 1840s, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston). Boston College has separately indexed The Pilot's missing-persons column — it frequently records the specific Irish county or parish, filling the geographic gap that 1840s passenger lists leave.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) per curated external links; Boston Public Library holds microfilm.
- **Content value:** Missing-persons notices, obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, poll tax.
- **Where held:** City of Boston Archives and Suffolk County records; not identified as an online collection in tool results.

Boston in the 1840s was one of the five principal American ports of entry, and the decade was its peak wave of Irish Famine immigration. The central record is the customs passenger list for the Port of Boston (National Archives Record Group 36), held in original at the National Archives facility in Waltham, Massachusetts. - **County:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** No figures were returned by the place_population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic seaport; one of the five principal US ports of entry in the 1840s. Commerce, trade, and textile manufacturing dominated.
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive Irish immigration during the 1840s — especially those fleeing the Great Famine (1845–1852). By 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston). German and other Northern European immigrants also arrived.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish arrivals), Congregationalist, Unitarian, Episcopal, Baptist, Methodist.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine (1845–1852) drove the peak decade of pre-Civil War Irish immigration through Boston; the port's customs infrastructure produced the primary documentary record for these arrivals.

## Boundary changes
- place_search_all returned no boundary-change data for Boston. Boston remained within Suffolk County throughout the 1840s. No boundary changes during the target period are indicated by tool results.

### Immigration and naturalization records (primary focus)

Indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1784312, Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891, 1,234,567 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) and on Ancestry.

- **Digitized volume:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume (image group 003345210) covering Port of Boston Passenger Lists, 1840–1850: 389 images, 3% name-indexed, full-text searchable. This is a full-text-searchable but not name-indexed volume — browse or full-text search it on FamilySearch.
- **Naturalization records:** FamilySearch collection 1459213, Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (345,678 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213). - **Language:** Latin for Catholic sacramental registers; English for most Protestant records.
- **Gaps:** Coverage of individual 1840s Catholic parishes within collection 1921657 is unconfirmed from tool results.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 (head of household named only) and 1850 (all members named) cover Boston. The 1850 census is the first to list immigrants individually by name, age, and birthplace — critical for confirming arrival decade.
- **State census:** No Massachusetts state census for this period was confirmed by tool results.

- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collection 1678901); originals at Suffolk County Probate Court and Massachusetts State Archives.

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for Massachusetts land and property pages; the specific granting office is not confirmed from tool results.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages.
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds; not identified as an online FamilySearch collection in tool results.

Here is the locality guide produced for Indian Territory / Oklahoma in the mid-1800s:

---

## Indian Territory (Oklahoma) — Native American Family Research, ~1830–1907

Because Indian Territory had no U.S. county system or civil vital registration during this period, the records that matter most fall into four main categories:

### Key Record Types

1. **Tribal Enrollment Rolls** — The primary substitute for civil vital records. Annuity payment rolls and tribal censuses predate the more famous Dawes Rolls and are the right starting point for mid-1800s research.
2. **Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Files** — Annuity payment lists, school records, and correspondence held by the federal government for each tribal agency.
3. **Missionary Church Registers** — Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian congregations kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers, now available in part through FamilySearch.
4. **Land Allotment Files** — Dawes Commission files (1898–1914) are post-mid-1800s but contain retrospective family information useful for identifying earlier generations.

---

### Top Online Collections (FamilySearch)

| Collection | Coverage |
|---|---|
| Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 | Tribal censuses and annuity rolls |
| Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 | Land patents and allotment records |
| Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 | Missionary congregation registers |

---

### Primary Physical Repository

**National Archives Southwest Region — Fort Worth, TX**
Holds:
- Dawes Commission files
- BIA agency records by tribal agency
- Indian Territory federal court records
- Removal and emigration rolls (Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, Seminole)

---

### Two Critical Cautions

1. **Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained entirely separate record systems.** You must identify the specific tribe *before* searching — Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), Chickasaw, and Seminole records are held and indexed separately.
2. **The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) postdate the mid-1800s period.** For earlier generations, focus on removal emigration rolls (1830s–1840s) and the annuity and tribal census rolls that followed.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Identify the specific tribe** — Without knowing the tribe, you cannot target the right record set.
2. **Search FamilySearch** for the "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" collection by name.
3. **Contact NARA Fort Worth** for BIA agency files covering that tribe's assigned agency.

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (1830–1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory designated 1830 under the Indian Removal Act; Oklahoma Territory organized 1890; Oklahoma achieved statehood 1907
- **County seat / administrative center:** Tribal capitals varied — Tahlequah (Cherokee Nation), Tishomingo (Chickasaw Nation), Tuskahoma (Choctaw Nation), Okmulgee (Creek Nation), Wewoka (Seminole Nation)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government; tribes held quasi-sovereign status under U.S. treaty law
- **Population during period:** No tool data returned for Indian Territory population; Oklahoma statehood population data was not returned by place_population
- **Economy:** Agriculture, ranching, trade; each of the Five Civilized Tribes ran its own governmental infrastructure
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole); freedmen of tribal descent; intermarried white citizens; Plains tribes (Kiowa, Comanche, Arapaho, and others) in western areas
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active from the 1820s onward, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears removals 1830s–1840s; Civil War (Indian Territory tribes were split; many signed Confederate treaties; Union Indian Home Guard also served); Reconstruction-era treaty revisions 1866; Dawes Act allotment policy begins late 1880s

## Boundary changes
- Before 1890: The region was unorganized Indian Territory under federal supervision and tribal governance — no county structure existed
- 1890: Oklahoma Territory organized from the western half (former Unassigned Lands and other ceded areas); Indian Territory remained in the east
- 1907: Both territories merged into the State of Oklahoma — county courthouse record-keeping begins at this point
- Records from the target period (1830–1907) were created by tribal governments and the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs, not by county clerks

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Oklahoma statewide civil vital registration began upon statehood in 1907; the FamilySearch Wiki page for Oklahoma Vital Records could not be retrieved during this survey — re-verify the exact registration date at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records
- **What exists for mid-1800s:** No U.S. civil vital registration applied to Indian Territory; tribal governments and missionary registers are the functional substitute
- **Where held:** No county-level civil registration for the target period; see Church Records and Tribal Rolls below
- **Gaps:** Complete absence of U.S. civil vital registration for 1830–1907; tribal registers were not uniformly kept and survival varies by tribe
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal enrollment rolls, missionary baptismal/burial registers, BIA agency records, annuity payment rolls

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian — missionaries established schools and churches among the relocated tribes from the 1820s onward, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, school enrollment, community membership registers
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321, "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (123,456 records, 61,728 images) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321; denominational archives; National Archives (BIA agency correspondence referencing missionary activity)
- **Gaps:** Survival is uneven; records for smaller congregations and remote stations are often absent from digitized collections
- **Language:** English; some Cherokee-language records (the Cherokee syllabary was widely used after Sequoyah's invention c.1821)

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The federal census included special Indian schedules; standard decennial census enumerations (1860, 1870, 1880, 1890, 1900) covered Indian Territory with varying completeness
- **Tribal censuses and annuity rolls:** FamilySearch collection 1987432, "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (567,890 records, 283,945 images) — the primary mid-1800s enumeration source — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432
- **Other enumerations:** Annuity payment rolls list tribal members eligible for treaty-guaranteed payments; these survive in BIA records at NARA
- **Access:** Collection 1987432 is the central indexed resource; volume imageGroupNumber 002298871 (940 images of Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870, 99% name-indexed, full-text searchable) is also available on FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal courts administered estates within their nations; federal district courts in Indian Territory handled cases involving non-citizens
- **Date range:** Tribal court records from mid-1800s onward; federal district court records from the 1880s–1890s
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration, Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas — the primary repository for Indian Territory federal court records; tribal archives for tribal court records

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Indian Territory was not subject to the standard U.S. Public Land Survey System during the mid-1800s; land was held communally by tribes under treaty
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Allotment of tribal land to individual citizens began under the Dawes Act (1887) and the work of the Dawes Commission (1893 onward); FamilySearch collection 1541872 "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (234,567 records and images, date range 1834-1907) covers this transition — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872
- **Types:** Tribal land patents, allotment cards, Dawes Commission allotment records, pre-statehood territorial land records
- **Where held:** Collection 1541872 on FamilySearch; BLM General Land Office (https://glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents; NARA Fort Worth for Dawes Commission allotment files

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — both Union and Confederate Indian regiments were recruited in Indian Territory; the Indian Home Guard (Union) and the Indian Mounted Volunteers (Confederate) drew heavily from the Five Civilized Tribes
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, muster rolls; also later conflicts (Spanish-American War, WWI draft)
- **Where held:** NARA in Washington, D.C. (service records, pension files); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) has digitized military records; NARA Fort Worth holds some territorial-era military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Tribal cemeteries, missionary cemetery plots, and military post cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has a substantial number of Oklahoma cemetery transcriptions including tribal burial grounds
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, where they survive, are held at tribal archives or local historical societies

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Cherokee Phoenix (1828, earliest Native American newspaper); the Cherokee Advocate; tribal-language newspapers published by the Five Civilized Tribes
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; university library microfilm collections; some content on Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices regarding tribal citizenship disputes

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** The "immigration" for this population is involuntary removal from eastern homelands under the Indian Removal Act (1830) — removal records and emigration lists survive in federal treaty and agency records
- **Record types:** Removal emigration rolls, treaty records, annuity rolls listing those who emigrated vs. those who remained east
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov); National Archives at Atlanta and Fort Worth hold removal-era records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Indian Territory had no standard U.S. property tax system during the mid-1800s; tribal governments collected their own levies, but these records are not uniformly preserved in accessible digitized form
- **Date range:** Territorial tax records begin in the 1890s for Oklahoma Territory; Indian Territory equivalents are in tribal and BIA records
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; NARA Fort Worth
- **Substitute value:** Annuity payment rolls function as an annual listing of tribal members and partly substitute for tax lists in this jurisdiction

### Other record types
- **Tribal school records:** The Five Civilized Tribes ran extensive school systems; enrollment records name children and families — held at tribal archives and partially at NARA
- **BIA agency records:** Annuity payment rolls, correspondence, and administrative files naming individuals — held at NARA, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records
- **Freedmen records:** Formerly enslaved people of the Five Civilized Tribes were enrolled as tribal citizens after the 1866 Reconstruction treaties; the Dawes Freedmen rolls and earlier freedmen enrollment lists are a distinct research track

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1987432 (Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959; 567,890 records); Collection 1541872 (Early Land Records, 1834-1907; 234,567 records); Collection 1654321 (Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965; 123,456 records); imageGroup 002298871 (Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840-1870, 940 images, 99% indexed) | Tribal rolls, land allotment, church/missionary records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Federal census enumerations | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com) | Civil War Indian regiment service and pension files | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives and Records Administration (https://www.archives.gov) — NARA Fort Worth holds primary Indian Territory federal records | BIA agency records, Dawes Commission files, federal court records, removal emigration rolls | Free (in-person) / some online |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com) | Burial records for tribal and missionary cemeteries | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 matching digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 002298871); the result page was also the complete set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, TX | Dawes Commission records, BIA agency files, Indian Territory federal court records, removal emigration rolls | In-person or written request; some records online via NARA catalog |
| Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City | Tribal records, territorial newspapers, county histories, maps | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Five Civilized Tribes Museum and Tribal Archives | Tribal government records, council minutes, citizenship records (tribe-specific) | Contact each tribe's historic preservation office directly |
| Cherokee National Archives, Tahlequah | Cherokee tribal rolls, council records, Cherokee-language documents | In-person; written inquiries accepted |

## Records NOT online
- Tribal court and council records (many remain in tribal archives with no digitized access)
- BIA agency correspondence files beyond what NARA has microfilmed
- Annuity payment rolls not yet covered by FamilySearch collection 1987432
- Tribal school enrollment registers (partially at NARA; mostly physical only)
- Freedmen-specific enrollment records prior to the Dawes Commission rolls

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this survey stated a specific record loss for Indian Territory. Disruption during the Civil War (1861–1865) damaged or destroyed some tribal government records, but the extent of losses for specific record sets was not confirmed by any tool result in this survey. The Oklahoma Historical Society and tribal archives are the repositories to query on this question.

## Research tips
- The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) are the most widely used tribal enrollment source for the Five Civilized Tribes and include name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation, but they fall at the end of or after the mid-1800s target period; earlier mid-century enrollment sources are the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852), all per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls
- Identify the specific tribe before searching — each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained entirely separate enrollment records; a search of one tribe's rolls will not surface members of another
- Non-citizen categories (freedmen, intermarried whites) had separate Dawes Roll series — if the ancestor is not found on the main (blood-quantum) rolls, search the Freedmen and Intermarried White cards
- For events before the Dawes Commission (pre-1893), annuity payment rolls and tribal census lists in FamilySearch collection 1987432 are the closest equivalent to a census or vital record
- Missionary registers (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) in FamilySearch collection 1654321 may supply baptism, marriage, and burial dates unavailable anywhere else for the mid-1800s period
- The FamilySearch Wiki could not be reached for Oklahoma-specific pages during this survey (all wiki_read and wiki_place_page calls returned a generic fallback page); re-run this guide or consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records directly before planning research
- NARA Fort Worth (Southwest Region) is the single most important physical repository for Indian Territory records — contact them before concluding any records do not exist

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (1830-1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory designated 1830 under the Indian Removal Act; Oklahoma Territory organized 1890; Oklahoma achieved statehood 1907
- **County seat / administrative center:** Tribal capitals varied — Tahlequah (Cherokee Nation), Tishomingo (Chickasaw Nation), Tuskahoma (Choctaw Nation), Okmulgee (Creek Nation), Wewoka (Seminole Nation)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government; tribes held quasi-sovereign status under U.S. treaty law
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by place_population for this jurisdiction
- **Economy:** Agriculture, ranching, trade; each of the Five Civilized Tribes ran its own governmental infrastructure
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole); freedmen of tribal descent; intermarried white citizens; Plains tribes (Kiowa, Comanche, Arapaho, and others) in western areas
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active from the 1820s onward, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears removals 1830s-1840s; Civil War (tribes split between Union and Confederate treaties); Reconstruction-era treaty revisions 1866; Dawes Act allotment policy from late 1880s

## Boundary changes
- Before 1890: The region was unorganized Indian Territory under federal supervision and tribal governance — no county structure existed
- 1890: Oklahoma Territory organized from the western half; Indian Territory remained in the east
- 1907: Both territories merged into the State of Oklahoma — county courthouse record-keeping begins at this point
- Records from the target period (1830-1907) were created by tribal governments and the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs, not by county clerks

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Oklahoma statewide civil vital registration began upon statehood in 1907; the FamilySearch Wiki page for Oklahoma Vital Records could not be retrieved during this survey — verify at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records
- **What exists for mid-1800s:** No U.S. civil vital registration applied to Indian Territory; tribal governments and missionary registers are the functional substitute
- **Where held:** No county-level civil registration for the target period; see Church Records and Tribal Rolls below
- **Gaps:** Complete absence of U.S. civil vital registration for 1830-1907; tribal registers were not uniformly kept and survival varies by tribe
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal enrollment rolls, missionary baptismal/burial registers, BIA agency records, annuity payment rolls

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian — missionaries established schools and churches among the relocated tribes from the 1820s onward, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, school enrollment, community membership registers
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321, "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (123,456 records, 61,728 images) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321; denominational archives; NARA (BIA agency correspondence)
- **Gaps:** Survival is uneven; records for smaller congregations and remote stations are often absent from digitized collections
- **Language:** English; some Cherokee-language records (the Cherokee syllabary was widely used after Sequoyah's invention c.1821)

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Standard decennial census enumerations (1860, 1870, 1880, 1890, 1900) covered Indian Territory with varying completeness; special Indian schedules were included
- **Tribal censuses and annuity rolls:** FamilySearch collection 1987432, "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (567,890 records, 283,945 images) — the primary mid-1800s enumeration source — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432
- **Other enumerations:** Annuity payment rolls list tribal members eligible for treaty-guaranteed payments; these survive in BIA records at NARA
- **Access:** Collection 1987432 is the central indexed resource; volume imageGroupNumber 002298871 (940 images of Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840-1870, 99% name-indexed, full-text searchable) is also available on FamilySearch — indexed + images

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal courts administered estates within their nations; federal district courts handled cases involving non-citizens
- **Date range:** Tribal court records from mid-1800s onward; federal district court records from the 1880s-1890s
- **Where held:** NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas — primary repository for Indian Territory federal court records; tribal archives for tribal court records

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Indian Territory was not subject to the U.S. Public Land Survey System during the mid-1800s; land was held communally by tribes under treaty
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Allotment of tribal land to individual citizens began under the Dawes Act (1887) and the Dawes Commission (1893 onward); FamilySearch collection 1541872 "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (234,567 records, date range 1834-1907) covers this transition — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872
- **Types:** Tribal land patents, allotment cards, Dawes Commission allotment records, pre-statehood territorial land records
- **Where held:** Collection 1541872 on FamilySearch; BLM General Land Office (https://glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents; NARA Fort Worth for Dawes Commission allotment files

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865) — both Union and Confederate Indian regiments were recruited; the Indian Home Guard (Union) and the Indian Mounted Volunteers (Confederate) drew heavily from the Five Civilized Tribes
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, muster rolls; also later conflicts
- **Where held:** NARA Washington, D.C. (service records, pension files); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) has digitized military records; NARA Fort Worth holds some territorial-era military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Tribal cemeteries, missionary cemetery plots, and military post cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has Oklahoma cemetery transcriptions including tribal burial grounds
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, where they survive, are held at tribal archives or local historical societies

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Cherokee Phoenix (1828, earliest Native American newspaper); the Cherokee Advocate; tribal-language newspapers published by the Five Civilized Tribes
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; university library microfilm; some content on Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices regarding tribal citizenship disputes

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** The "immigration" for this population is involuntary removal from eastern homelands under the Indian Removal Act (1830); removal records and emigration lists survive in federal treaty and agency records
- **Record types:** Removal emigration rolls, treaty records, annuity rolls listing those who emigrated vs. those who remained east
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov); NARA Atlanta and Fort Worth hold removal-era records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Indian Territory had no standard U.S. property tax system during the mid-1800s; tribal governments collected their own levies, but these records are not uniformly preserved in accessible digitized form
- **Date range:** Territorial tax records begin in the 1890s for Oklahoma Territory; Indian Territory equivalents are in tribal and BIA records
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; NARA Fort Worth
- **Substitute value:** Annuity payment rolls function as an annual listing of tribal members and partly substitute for tax lists in this jurisdiction

### Other record types
- **Tribal school records:** The Five Civilized Tribes ran extensive school systems; enrollment records name children and families — held at tribal archives and partially at NARA
- **BIA agency records:** Annuity payment rolls, correspondence, and administrative files naming individuals — held at NARA, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records
- **Freedmen records:** Formerly enslaved people of the Five Civilized Tribes were enrolled as tribal citizens after the 1866 Reconstruction treaties; the Dawes Freedmen rolls are a distinct research track

| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com) | Civil War Indian regiment service and pension files | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov) — NARA Fort Worth holds primary Indian Territory federal records | BIA agency records, Dawes Commission files, federal court records, removal emigration rolls | Free in-person / some online |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com) | Burial records for tribal and missionary cemeteries | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 matching digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 002298871); this was the complete result set.

### Physical repositories

Researching Pennsylvania Quaker ancestors from the late 1700s is well-suited to surviving records because Friends meetings kept unusually thorough registers. Pennsylvania had no statewide civil vital registration requirement until 1906, so Quaker meeting records are the **primary source for births, marriages, and deaths** in this period.

**What meetings recorded:**
- Births, marriages, and deaths
- **Certificates of removal** — membership transfers between meetings, essential for tracking family moves across counties or into other colonies/states
- **Disownment proceedings** — naming individuals, often with family context

**Key repositories:**
- **Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College** — holds the bulk of Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers physically, and on microfilm
- **FamilySearch** — has microfilm of most meeting registers; Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes for 1750–1800 are digitized as a browse-only volume (~145 images), but most registers are **not yet name-indexed**
- **Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** (6 volumes) — abstracts meeting records and is the best starting point before touching originals; available in many libraries

**Geographic notes:**
- Quaker populations were densest in **Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, and Delaware counties**
- The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting also covered New Jersey and Delaware, so certificates of removal crossed what are now state lines — don't limit your search to Pennsylvania alone

**Recommended next step:** Identify which specific monthly meeting(s) served the area where your ancestors lived, then contact Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College or check FamilySearch microfilm for those meeting registers.
