# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States — Quaker Communities (1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pennsylvania was founded as a proprietary colony in 1681 under William Penn's Charter of Privileges. It became the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (second state to ratify the U.S. Constitution) in 1787. The target period 1750–1800 thus spans both the colonial era and the early national period.
- **Administrative centers:** Philadelphia (dominant colonial capital and Quaker center); Lancaster and other interior towns
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colony, to 1776); United States (1776/1787 onward)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Primarily agricultural (grain, livestock); Philadelphia was a major Atlantic commercial port
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers (dominant in southeastern counties), Welsh Quakers, Germans (Lutheran, Reformed, Mennonite, Amish), Scots-Irish (Presbyterian)
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Baptist, Mennonite/Amish
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783) disrupted record-keeping in some areas and triggered Quaker disownment proceedings against members who bore arms

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's external boundaries were largely stable 1750–1800
- County boundaries changed frequently as new counties were carved from older ones; Chester County (formed 1682) and Bucks County (formed 1682) are parents to many southeastern Pennsylvania counties created during this period — records for those areas before county formation are filed under the parent county
- The same family may appear in predecessor county deed books, probate records, and tax lists under an earlier county name before a successor county was created

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil vital registration until 1906 (state level), per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records). The Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content during this survey and gave no county-level dates.
- **What exists for 1750–1800:** No statewide civil registration existed during this period. Quaker meeting registers and other church records are the principal substitutes for vital events.
- **Where held:** Vital events are documented almost entirely in religious records for this period (see Church Records below).
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania Vital Records page could not be loaded during this survey; consult it directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records.

### Church records — Quaker (Society of Friends) [PRIMARY SOURCE]
- **Meeting structure and records kept:** The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting organized monthly meetings throughout Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware. Monthly meetings are the level at which individual vital-event records were created. Each monthly meeting kept: (1) birth and death registers; (2) marriage records — a couple announced their intention, were approved by a clearness committee, then married at a subsequent meeting with all attendees signing the marriage certificate as witnesses, making these certificates exceptionally well-documented; (3) certificates of removal, issued when a member transferred to another monthly meeting, documenting migration between counties, colonies, and states — one of the most powerful tools for tracing Quaker family movement; (4) disownment (disciplinary) minutes naming individuals read out of meeting for military service, marrying outside the faith, or other offenses; (5) general monthly and quarterly meeting minutes recording community business.
- **Densest Quaker populations 1750–1800:** Chester County, Bucks County, Philadelphia, and Delaware County, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records) and Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania).
- **Where held:** The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College holds the largest collection of American Quaker records, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records). The Quaker and Special Collections at Haverford College is a second primary repository, per Wikipedia. FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).
- **Digitized at FamilySearch:** 1 digitized volume was found for Pennsylvania 1750–1800: imageGroupNumber 001188322, "Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes," 145 images, covering Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, 1750–1800. This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be read image by image.
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts Pennsylvania and other states' meeting records and is the standard indexed starting point for Quaker genealogy, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).
- **Language:** English.
- **The 1827 schism note:** The Hicksite-Orthodox split of 1827–1828 postdates this period; 1750–1800 records are unified under one meeting structure.

### Church records — other denominations
- **Denominations present:** Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican (Episcopal after the Revolution), Baptist, Mennonite/Amish, each keeping its own registers
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Denominational archives, local congregations, FamilySearch microfilm, Pennsylvania State Archives, and Historical Society of Pennsylvania
- **Language:** German-language records common for Lutheran, Reformed, Mennonite, and Amish communities

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available from 1790 (first federal enumeration); heads of household listed with counts of free persons, not all names. No federal enumeration exists before 1790.
- **Pre-1790 substitutes:** Provincial and county tax assessment lists (see Tax Records) serve as the primary census substitutes for 1750–1789
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed and available free at FamilySearch and on Ancestry

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1999196, "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196), covers this period. It holds 3,200,560 images but 0 indexed records — **browse-only** images, navigated by county and date range without a name search.
- **Where held:** County courthouses hold originals; browse-only digitized images on FamilySearch (collection 1999196)
- **Note:** Probate records frequently document family relationships and can confirm or supplement meeting register evidence

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds; colonial Pennsylvania used a warrant-and-survey system under the Penn Proprietors, continued by the Commonwealth after 1776
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Penn family proprietary Land Office issued warrants and patents (colonial); the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania Land Office continued after 1776. The FamilySearch Wiki Land and Property page for Pennsylvania was not retrievable during this survey.
- **Types:** Land warrants, surveys, patents, county deed books, mortgage books
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Land Office warrants and surveys); county recorder of deeds (county deed books)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783)
- **Quaker note:** Many Quakers were disowned by their monthly meetings for military service during the Revolution; disownment proceedings in meeting minutes are as important a record as the military service record itself. An ancestor may appear in both NARA military records and meeting disownment minutes.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files at NARA; Pennsylvania militia records at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal service records, pensions, and bounty land; Pennsylvania State Archives for state militia

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Plain, often unmarked graves were Quaker practice; burial grounds were attached to meeting houses. Sexton records at Friends Historical Library may record burials not otherwise documented.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes some Quaker burial grounds, but 18th-century grave coverage is uneven
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pennsylvania Gazette (Philadelphia, founded 1728) and other colonial-era papers published marriage notices, death notices, and legal notices during this period
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Library of Congress Chronicling America hold digitized Pennsylvania newspapers; Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds additional microfilm
- **Content value:** Marriage and death notices supplement meeting records; legal notices name individuals in property transactions and disputes

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the dominant port of entry for 18th-century Pennsylvania immigrants
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (Philadelphia arrivals), county court naturalization papers (pre-1906), Quaker certificates of removal from England, Ireland, and Wales to Pennsylvania meetings
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds federal-era passenger lists; Friends Historical Library holds Quaker certificates of removal from British meetings; pre-federal arrival lists are in Pennsylvania colonial records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members. Certificates of removal from British meetings are essential for tracing Quaker families to their English, Welsh, or Irish origins.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Provincial and county tax assessment lists; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax (Valuation of 1798) enumerates heads of household with property descriptions
- **Date range:** Colonial assessment lists from the mid-1700s; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax covers the close of this period
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; many transcribed or microfilmed at FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists before 1790 are the primary census substitute; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax is particularly valuable as a near-1800 enumeration

### Other record types
- Meeting house account books, Quaker school records, and records of the poor (Friends receiving meeting relief) are held at Friends Historical Library and at the originating meetings
- 19th-century published county histories (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware counties) frequently abstract earlier Quaker family records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, browse-only, 3.2M images); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 indexed records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (volume 001188322, browse-only, 145 images) | Probate and marriage records overlapping the period; one Quaker yearly meeting volume | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1790 federal census | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Quaker burial ground indexes | Free |
| NARA | Military and immigration records (https://www.archives.gov/) | Revolutionary War service, pensions, Philadelphia passenger lists | Free / fee for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** Only 1 digitized volume was returned for Pennsylvania 1750–1800 across all record-type groupings searched; this is the complete result set for those parameters.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College, Swarthmore PA | Largest collection of American Quaker records: Pennsylvania monthly meeting minutes, birth/death registers, marriage certificates, certificates of removal | In-person; contact library for microfilm and finding aids |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College, Haverford PA | Quaker records including Pennsylvania meeting materials | In-person; contact library |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg PA | Land Office warrants/surveys, provincial tax lists, militia records, court records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia PA | County histories, deeds, colonial newspapers | In-person; some digitized collections |
| County courthouses (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware, etc.) | County deed books, probate records, court minutes | In-person or mail request |

## Records NOT online
- Monthly meeting birth/death registers and minutes for most Pennsylvania meetings (other than the one Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume, imageGroupNumber 001188322): held physically at Friends Historical Library and on FamilySearch microfilm, not fully digitized or name-indexed
- Certificates of removal: physical originals at Friends Historical Library; not systematically indexed online
- Colonial Pennsylvania Land Office warrants and surveys: Pennsylvania State Archives; not fully digitized
- Pre-1790 provincial and county tax assessment lists: partially microfilmed at FamilySearch; physical originals at Pennsylvania State Archives
- County deed books for most Pennsylvania counties, 1750–1800: physical at county courthouses; some browse-only images may be available at FamilySearch for certain counties

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this survey identified specific record losses for Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records or Pennsylvania county records in the 1750–1800 period. Contact Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) or the Pennsylvania State Archives to confirm whether specific meeting registers survive.

## Research tips
1. **Start with the Hinshaw abstracts.** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) provides indexed abstracts of Pennsylvania monthly meeting records. It is the standard first-pass tool before accessing original registers. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)
2. **Trace certificates of removal to follow migration.** When a Quaker family moved, the originating meeting issued a certificate of removal to the receiving meeting, naming the individual, family members, and both meetings. Follow certificates forward to trace movement to new Pennsylvania counties or other states, and backward to trace origins in England, Ireland, or Wales. Originals are at Friends Historical Library.
3. **Search across the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting's full geographic scope.** The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting covered Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware. A family disappearing from a Pennsylvania county may have moved to a New Jersey or Delaware meeting. Do not stop the search at the Pennsylvania border.
4. **Use disownment proceedings as evidence, not dead ends.** Members read out of meeting — especially for Revolutionary War service — are named and dated in monthly meeting minute books. These entries are valuable records even when the individual left the meeting permanently.
5. **Use tax lists as pre-1790 census substitutes.** No federal census exists before 1790; provincial and county tax assessment lists from the 1750s–1780s are the primary substitutes. The 1798 Federal Direct Tax provides near-1800 coverage.
6. **The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania-specific pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic content during this survey** — re-run this locality guide or check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly before finalizing any research plan, as Pennsylvania-specific guidance was not available here.

- **Date range:** Colonial assessment lists from the mid-1700s; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax covers the close of this period
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; many transcribed or microfilmed at FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists before 1790 are the primary census substitute; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax is particularly valuable as a near-1800 enumeration

### Other record types
- Meeting house account books, Quaker school records, and records of the poor (Friends receiving meeting relief) are held at Friends Historical Library and at the originating meetings
- 19th-century published county histories (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware counties) frequently abstract earlier Quaker family records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, browse-only, 3.2M images); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 indexed records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (volume 001188322, browse-only, 145 images) | Probate and marriage records overlapping the period; one Quaker yearly meeting volume | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1790 federal census | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Quaker burial ground indexes | Free |
| NARA | Military and immigration records (https://www.archives.gov/) | Revolutionary War service, pensions, Philadelphia passenger lists | Free / fee for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** Only 1 digitized volume was returned for Pennsylvania 1750–1800 across all record-type groupings searched; this is the complete result set for those parameters.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College, Swarthmore PA | Largest collection of American Quaker records: Pennsylvania monthly meeting minutes, birth/death registers, marriage certificates, certificates of removal | In-person; contact library for microfilm and finding aids |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College, Haverford PA | Quaker records including Pennsylvania meeting materials | In-person; contact library |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg PA | Land Office warrants/surveys, provincial tax lists, militia records, court records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia PA | County histories, deeds, colonial newspapers | In-person; some digitized collections |
| County courthouses (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware, etc.) | County deed books, probate records, court minutes | In-person or mail request |

## Records NOT online
- Monthly meeting birth/death registers and minutes for most Pennsylvania meetings (other than the one Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume, imageGroupNumber 001188322): held physically at Friends Historical Library and on FamilySearch microfilm, not fully digitized or name-indexed
- Certificates of removal: physical originals at Friends Historical Library; not systematically indexed online
- Colonial Pennsylvania Land Office warrants and surveys: Pennsylvania State Archives; not fully digitized
- Pre-1790 provincial and county tax assessment lists: partially microfilmed at FamilySearch; physical originals at Pennsylvania State Archives
- County deed books for most Pennsylvania counties, 1750–1800: physical at county courthouses; some browse-only images may be available at FamilySearch for certain counties

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this survey identified specific record losses for Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records or Pennsylvania county records in the 1750–1800 period. Contact Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) or the Pennsylvania State Archives to confirm whether specific meeting registers survive.

## Research tips
1. **Start with the Hinshaw abstracts.** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) provides indexed abstracts of Pennsylvania monthly meeting records. It is the standard first-pass tool before accessing original registers. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)
2. **Trace certificates of removal to follow migration.** When a Quaker family moved, the originating meeting issued a certificate of removal to the receiving meeting, naming the individual, family members, and both meetings. Follow certificates forward to trace movement to new Pennsylvania counties or other states, and backward to trace origins in England, Ireland, or Wales. Originals are at Friends Historical Library.
3. **Search across the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting's full geographic scope.** The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting covered Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware. A family disappearing from a Pennsylvania county may have moved to a New Jersey or Delaware meeting. Do not stop the search at the Pennsylvania border.
4. **Use disownment proceedings as evidence, not dead ends.** Members read out of meeting — especially for Revolutionary War service — are named and dated in monthly meeting minute books. These entries are valuable records even when the individual left the meeting permanently.
5. **Use tax lists as pre-1790 census substitutes.** No federal census exists before 1790; provincial and county tax assessment lists from the 1750s–1780s are the primary substitutes. The 1798 Federal Direct Tax provides near-1800 coverage.
6. **The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania-specific pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic content during this survey** — re-run this locality guide or check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly before finalizing any research plan, as Pennsylvania-specific guidance was not available here.

---

**Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1900)**

Pennsylvania had **no statewide birth or death registration** during this period, making church and civil alternatives essential. Here are the key record types and repositories:

### Most Valuable Record Sources

1. **Federal Censuses (1870, 1880, 1900)** — List every person's occupation and can pinpoint specific trades within a mill. Note: the 1890 census was destroyed by fire, leaving a critical ten-year gap.

2. **Church Baptism & Burial Registers** — Especially ethnic Catholic *national parishes* (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) serving mill workers. Contact the **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** for access.

3. **Pittsburgh City Directories** — Held at the **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh**; track address and occupation year by year between censuses, helping bridge the 1890 gap.

4. **Company Employment Records** — Scattered survivors are held at:
   - **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh)
   - **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area Archives**
   *(Neither collection is online — a visit or written request is needed.)*

5. **Naturalization Records** — Before 1906, these could be filed in any Pennsylvania court. Search both:
   - **Allegheny County Courthouse**
   - **National Archives at Philadelphia**
   - FamilySearch has a partially indexed digitized series covering Pennsylvania naturalizations through 1915.

### Recommended Next Steps

- Identify which **specific mill** your ancestor worked in and which **ethnic parish** served his neighborhood.
- Contact the **Heinz History Center** and the **Diocese of Pittsburgh archives** directly.
- Run the **1880 and 1900 federal census schedules** to establish occupation, neighbors, and household structure — these anchor everything else.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland counties; Pittsburgh incorporated as a city in 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Pittsburgh became the center of America's steel industry in the late 1800s; the city and surrounding mill towns attracted massive waves of immigrant labor. The `place_population` tool returned no data for this survey period — consult the published decennial census volumes.
- **Economy:** Iron and steel manufacturing dominated; Carnegie's steel empire and other firms drove rapid industrial growth throughout the 1870s-1890s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers migrated to the mills in large numbers (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple national parishes by ethnicity), Protestant denominations (Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal), and smaller congregations.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Railroad Strike of 1877, the Homestead Steel Strike of 1892, and rapid annexation of surrounding mill boroughs into Pittsburgh during the 1870-1907 period directly affected where records were created and which jurisdiction holds them.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries were stable throughout 1870-1900, having been formed in 1788.
- The independent City of Allegheny (across the Ohio River from Pittsburgh) was not annexed into Pittsburgh until 1907 — records from that city for the 1870-1900 period are held separately from Pittsburgh's records. If your ancestor lived in Allegheny City, search under the City of Allegheny, not the City of Pittsburgh.
- Many surrounding mill boroughs (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport) were separate municipalities with their own record-keeping during this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did NOT have statewide civil registration during 1870-1900. The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection (FamilySearch collection 2255317) begins in 1906, confirming statewide death registration did not exist earlier. County-level marriage recording is evidenced from 1885 (FamilySearch collection 1921317). No statewide birth registration exists for this period.
- **What exists:** County marriage records from approximately 1885; no civil birth or death records for 1870-1900 at any level confirmed by tool results.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (Register of Wills / Office of the Prothonotary) for marriage licenses; FamilySearch collections 1921317 (County Marriages 1885-1950, 524,189 records, indexed) and 1571957 (Civil Marriages 1677-1950, 312,045 records, indexed).
- **Gaps:** No civil birth records during this period; no civil death records during this period — church registers and mortality schedules are essential substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Federal census mortality schedules (appended to the 1870 and 1880 censuses) list individuals who died in the year preceding the enumeration. Church baptism and burial registers are the primary birth and death evidence for 1870-1900.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (with distinct national parishes for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian communities), Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal, and others.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, first communions.
- **Where held:** Individual parishes retain their registers; some have been deposited with the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives. The FamilySearch Wiki wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records) specifically notes that Catholic parishes served specific ethnic communities and their registers are often the best source for family data.
- **Gaps:** No comprehensive index of Pittsburgh-area Catholic parish registers was confirmed by any tool result. National parishes are indexed separately from territorial parishes and may be overlooked in a geographic search.
- **Language:** Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, and German registers will be in those languages — the researcher must read the original language or obtain a translation.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available for 1870, 1880, 1900 (the 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire). Each schedule lists occupation, which is the core industrial identifier for mill workers.
- **Mortality schedules:** Appended to the 1870 and 1880 federal censuses; list deaths in the prior year with cause, birthplace, and occupation — a critical substitute for absent civil death records.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses are indexed and available free at FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) and by subscription at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions.
- **Date range:** From county formation 1788 onward.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (Register of Wills). FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994) holds 3,200,560 browse-only images — no name index; must be browsed image by image.
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images (volume 008120441, 1,180 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a public-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki land and property page returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property directly for Pennsylvania-specific guidance on land grants and warrantee maps.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records.
- **Date range:** From county formation 1788.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (county courthouse) for deeds and mortgages; county tax records at the Allegheny County Archives.

### Industrial and occupational records (primary focus)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary — some survive at the Senator John Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives (https://www.riversofsteel.com). These are NOT digitized online; in-person visits or written requests are required. The FamilySearch Wiki search result specifically names both repositories (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records).
- **Union membership lists:** Available for some unions; the records of steelworkers' unions of this era may be held by the United Steelworkers union archives or at labor history collections at the University of Pittsburgh.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from the 1810s; these list residents by name, address, and occupation annually — invaluable when census years are missing. FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual reports listing factories, their locations, and workforce statistics — useful for confirming which mill a worker was attached to.
- **Federal census occupation column:** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal census schedules all include an occupation column; for mill workers, this often identifies the specific trade (puddler, roller, heater, laborer).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865; veterans common in 1870-1900 household), Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Civil War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Spanish-American War service records at NARA.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has indexed Civil War pension and service records by subscription.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh), Calvary Catholic Cemetery, and numerous ethnic Catholic and Protestant cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many Pittsburgh-area cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries; contact each cemetery directly.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh had major newspapers throughout this period (Pittsburgh Post, Pittsburgh Gazette, Pittsburgh Press); these carried obituaries, marriage notices, and industrial accident reports.
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) by subscription; Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh microfilm holdings.
- **Content value:** Industrial accident reports from the steel mills are particularly valuable for identifying a worker's employer, neighborhood, and surviving family.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most European immigrants arrived through New York (Castle Garden/Ellis Island) or Baltimore.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry), naturalization petitions and declarations of intention.
- **Naturalization:** FamilySearch volume 008120443 (Naturalization Records 1790-1915, 351 images, 15% name-indexed) covers Pennsylvania. Pre-1906 naturalizations at Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia (https://www.archives.gov/) — the FamilySearch Wiki search specifically names both repositories (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County real estate and personal property tax records.
- **Date range:** From county formation.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Archives; some years digitized, but no specific digitized collection was confirmed by tool results.
- **Substitute value:** Annual tax records can substitute for missing census years and confirm residence year by year.

### Other record types
- **Labor/union records:** See Industrial and Occupational Records above.
- **School records:** Pittsburgh public school records may be held by the Pittsburgh Public Schools administrative archives.
- **Institutional records:** Allegheny County poorhouse and hospital records may document workers injured or impoverished by industrial accidents.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Collection 1921317 (PA County Marriages 1885-1950, 524,189 records); Collection 1571957 (PA Civil Marriages 1677-1950, 312,045 records); Collection 1502909 (PA Compiled Marriages 1700-1900, 198,765 records); Collection 1999196 (PA Probate Records browse-only); Naturalization Records 1790-1915 (15% indexed) | Marriage and probate records; naturalization records partially indexed | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census collection | 1870, 1880, 1900 census with occupation data | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records | Burial evidence when death records absent | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical newspapers | Obituaries, accident reports, marriage notices | Subscription |

---

Pittsburgh and Allegheny County, Pennsylvania were surveyed for the 1870-1900 steel boom period. Pennsylvania had no statewide birth or death registration during those thirty years, so the records that matter most are church baptism and burial registers (especially those of ethnic Catholic national parishes serving Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian mill workers), the federal censuses for 1870, 1880, and 1900 (which list every person's occupation and can identify the specific trade within the mill), and Pittsburgh city directories held at the Carnegie Library, which track address and occupation year by year between census dates. Company employment records from the steel mills survive only in scattered form at the Senator John Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives — neither collection is online, so a visit or written request is required. Naturalization records before 1906 could be filed in any Pennsylvania court, so both the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia need to be searched; FamilySearch has a partially indexed digitized volume covering Pennsylvania naturalizations through 1915. The 1890 federal census was destroyed in a fire, leaving a ten-year gap that city directories and any surviving mill records are the best way to bridge.

The most productive next step is to identify which specific mill or mills your ancestor worked in and which ethnic parish served his neighborhood, then contact the Heinz History Center and the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives directly, while simultaneously running the 1880 and 1900 federal census schedules to establish occupation, neighbors, and household structure.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland counties; Pittsburgh incorporated as a city in 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Pittsburgh became the center of America's steel industry in the late 1800s; the city and surrounding mill towns attracted massive waves of immigrant labor. The `place_population` tool returned no data for this survey period — consult the published decennial census volumes.
- **Economy:** Iron and steel manufacturing dominated; Carnegie's steel empire and other firms drove rapid industrial growth throughout the 1870s-1890s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers migrated to the mills in large numbers (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple national parishes by ethnicity), Protestant denominations (Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal), and smaller congregations.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Railroad Strike of 1877, the Homestead Steel Strike of 1892, and rapid annexation of surrounding mill boroughs into Pittsburgh during the 1870-1907 period directly affected where records were created and which jurisdiction holds them.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries were stable throughout 1870-1900, having been formed in 1788.
- The independent City of Allegheny (across the Ohio River from Pittsburgh) was not annexed into Pittsburgh until 1907 — records from that city for the 1870-1900 period are held separately from Pittsburgh's records. If your ancestor lived in Allegheny City, search under the City of Allegheny, not the City of Pittsburgh.
- Many surrounding mill boroughs (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport) were separate municipalities with their own record-keeping during this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did NOT have statewide civil registration during 1870-1900. The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection (FamilySearch collection 2255317) begins in 1906, confirming statewide death registration did not exist earlier. County-level marriage recording is evidenced from 1885 (FamilySearch collection 1921317). No statewide birth registration exists for this period.
- **What exists:** County marriage records from approximately 1885; no civil birth or death records for 1870-1900 at any level confirmed by tool results.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (Register of Wills / Office of the Prothonotary) for marriage licenses; FamilySearch collections 1921317 (County Marriages 1885-1950, 524,189 records, indexed) and 1571957 (Civil Marriages 1677-1950, 312,045 records, indexed).
- **Gaps:** No civil birth records during this period; no civil death records during this period — church registers and mortality schedules are essential substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Federal census mortality schedules (appended to the 1870 and 1880 censuses) list individuals who died in the year preceding the enumeration. Church baptism and burial registers are the primary birth and death evidence for 1870-1900.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (with distinct national parishes for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian communities), Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal, and others.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, first communions.
- **Where held:** Individual parishes retain their registers; some have been deposited with the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives. The FamilySearch Wiki wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records) specifically notes that Catholic parishes served specific ethnic communities and their registers are often the best source for family data.
- **Gaps:** No comprehensive index of Pittsburgh-area Catholic parish registers was confirmed by any tool result. National parishes are indexed separately from territorial parishes and may be overlooked in a geographic search.
- **Language:** Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, and German registers will be in those languages — the researcher must read the original language or obtain a translation.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available for 1870, 1880, 1900 (the 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire). Each schedule lists occupation, which is the core industrial identifier for mill workers.
- **Mortality schedules:** Appended to the 1870 and 1880 federal censuses; list deaths in the prior year with cause, birthplace, and occupation — a critical substitute for absent civil death records.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses are indexed and available free at FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) and by subscription at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions.
- **Date range:** From county formation 1788 onward.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (Register of Wills). FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994) holds 3,200,560 browse-only images — no name index; must be browsed image by image.
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images (volume 008120441, 1,180 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a public-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki land and property page returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property directly for Pennsylvania-specific guidance on land grants and warrantee maps.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records.
- **Date range:** From county formation 1788.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (county courthouse) for deeds and mortgages; county tax records at the Allegheny County Archives.

### Industrial and occupational records (primary focus)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary — some survive at the Senator John Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives (https://www.riversofsteel.com). These are NOT digitized online; in-person visits or written requests are required. The FamilySearch Wiki search result specifically names both repositories (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records).
- **Union membership lists:** Available for some unions; the records of steelworkers' unions of this era may be held by the United Steelworkers union archives or at labor history collections at the University of Pittsburgh.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from the 1810s; these list residents by name, address, and occupation annually — invaluable when census years are missing. FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual reports listing factories, their locations, and workforce statistics — useful for confirming which mill a worker was attached to.
- **Federal census occupation column:** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal census schedules all include an occupation column; for mill workers, this often identifies the specific trade (puddler, roller, heater, laborer).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865; veterans common in 1870-1900 household), Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Civil War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Spanish-American War service records at NARA.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has indexed Civil War pension and service records by subscription.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh), Calvary Catholic Cemetery, and numerous ethnic Catholic and Protestant cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many Pittsburgh-area cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries; contact each cemetery directly.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh had major newspapers throughout this period (Pittsburgh Post, Pittsburgh Gazette, Pittsburgh Press); these carried obituaries, marriage notices, and industrial accident reports.
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) by subscription; Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh microfilm holdings.
- **Content value:** Industrial accident reports from the steel mills are particularly valuable for identifying a worker's employer, neighborhood, and surviving family.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most European immigrants arrived through New York (Castle Garden/Ellis Island) or Baltimore.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry), naturalization petitions and declarations of intention.
- **Naturalization:** FamilySearch volume 008120443 (Naturalization Records 1790-1915, 351 images, 15% name-indexed) covers Pennsylvania. Pre-1906 naturalizations at Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia (https://www.archives.gov/) — the FamilySearch Wiki search specifically names both repositories (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County real estate and personal property tax records.
- **Date range:** From county formation.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Archives; some years digitized, but no specific digitized collection was confirmed by tool results.
- **Substitute value:** Annual tax records can substitute for missing census years and confirm residence year by year.

### Other record types
- **Labor/union records:** See Industrial and Occupational Records above.
- **School records:** Pittsburgh public school records may be held by the Pittsburgh Public Schools administrative archives.
- **Institutional records:** Allegheny County poorhouse and hospital records may document workers injured or impoverished by industrial accidents.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (Yellow Fever Epidemic Context, ca. 1780–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County formed 1682 from the original Penn grant; Philadelphia chartered as a city in 1701.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 at the time of the 1793 epidemic — the largest U.S. city and the national capital (1790–1800). The epidemic killed approximately 5,000 residents (roughly one-tenth of the population) between August and November 1793. Place_population tool returned no data for this query.
- **Economy:** Port trade, commerce, and manufacturing; national capital status drew government workers and merchants.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quaker founders, German immigrants, Scots-Irish, a free Black community, and recent immigrants from Ireland and other European nations.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Quaker (Friends meetings), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Catholic (St. Mary's), and Jewish (Mikveh Israel).
- **Key historical events:** The 1793 yellow fever epidemic killed approximately 5,000 residents between August and November 1793 (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793), generating a concentrated surge of burial, probate, and orphans' court records. The Revolutionary War ended in 1783, a decade prior; many men in the city in 1793 had Revolutionary War service records.

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia City (incorporated 1701) and Philadelphia County coexisted as separate but overlapping jurisdictions until 1854 consolidation. In 1793, both existed; the city occupied the central portion of the county, with surrounding townships also within the county. Records were generated at both city and county levels.
- No major boundary changes within the 1780–1810 target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania statewide civil registration did not exist in 1793. The FamilySearch Wiki's Philadelphia Genealogy article on church records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) states that Pennsylvania's statewide registration began in 1906. There were no statewide-mandated civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for any event in 1793.
- **What exists:** No civil vital certificates for 1793. FamilySearch collection 1571957 (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950; 312,045 records, indexed) and collection 1502909 (Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900; 198,765 records, indexed) cover the period but represent locally filed documents and compiled entries, not a statewide system.
- **Where held:** County courthouse for locally filed marriage bonds/licenses; FamilySearch online for the digitized collections.
- **Gaps:** Comprehensive — civil vital registration simply did not exist in 1793. Church records and epidemic-specific published lists are the primary substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers, Mathew Carey's published list of the dead, Committee relief records.

### Epidemic-specific records (1793 yellow fever)
- **Mathew Carey's published list:** 'A Short Account of the Malignant Fever Lately Prevalent in Philadelphia' (1793) includes names of persons who died during the epidemic. This is a key compiled secondary source, identified by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) as a primary genealogical source for the epidemic.
- **Committee records:** Minutes and reports of the Committee Appointed by the Citizens — the civic relief body chaired by Mayor Matthew Clarkson — documented relief efforts, identifying recipients and the dead. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives, per the FamilySearch Wiki and Wikipedia.
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Records of the epidemic hospital at Bush Hill. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives, per the same sources.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, founded 1695), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting, from 1681), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Catholic (St. Mary's, founded 1763), Jewish (Mikveh Israel, 1740).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Burial registers are especially dense in late 1793 due to the epidemic.
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) names Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') as key burial record holders for the epidemic. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records. FamilySearch has 1 digitized Quaker volume: Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (volume 001188322, 145 images) — browse-only; 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable, must be browsed image by image.
- **Gaps:** Non-Episcopal, non-Quaker registers are less thoroughly digitized. German Lutheran and Reformed registers require reading in German.
- **Language:** English for most records; German for Lutheran and Reformed congregations.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 census (three years before the epidemic) and 1800 census (seven years after) are the bracketing enumerations. The 1790 census captures Philadelphia household structure just before the epidemic; the 1800 census may reflect family changes caused by deaths.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a regular state census; tax assessments serve a similar function for intercensal years.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and imaged online at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, Orphans' Court petitions. Expect a surge of intestate administrations in late 1793 and 1794 due to sudden epidemic deaths.
- **Testate or intestate:** Many epidemic deaths were sudden; persons who died intestate generated administrations, not wills. Search both series.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1682) onward.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) holds 3,200,560 browse-only images; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image. Originals held at the Philadelphia Register of Wills (Philadelphia City Hall Annex) and the Philadelphia City Archives. Orphans' Court records for children orphaned by the epidemic are also at the Philadelphia City Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a federal land-grant state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Proprietary grants under William Penn's charter; the Pennsylvania Land Office administered grants. Records at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, ground rents (a distinctive Philadelphia tenure form), tax assessments.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives holds deed books and ground rent ledgers. Tax assessment records are at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783), ended a decade before the epidemic. Men living in Philadelphia in 1793 may have Revolutionary War service records and pension files.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/). Pennsylvania State Archives holds state-level muster rolls.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church burial ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, St. Mary's Catholic churchyard, Mikveh Israel cemetery.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for major Philadelphia churchyards, though coverage of 1793 inscriptions varies.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at individual church archives. 1793 burial registers are especially dense due to the epidemic.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Multiple newspapers were published in Philadelphia in 1793, including the Pennsylvania Gazette, Federal Gazette, and Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser. They published lists of the dead, estate administration notices, and public health committee announcements.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and the Library Company of Philadelphia.
- **Content value:** Death notices, estate executor announcements, epidemic victim lists. August–November 1793 issues are the most directly relevant.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major Atlantic port and the primary port for German, Scots-Irish, and other immigrant streams.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists, naturalization petitions (in any court of record, pre-1906), Orphans' Court naturalization records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/). Published abstracts include Strassburger and Hinke's 'Pennsylvania German Pioneers' (1934) for German arrivals.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County taxable inhabitants lists, ward-level property tax assessments.
- **Date range:** Available from the late 18th century through the target period.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists for 1789, 1791, 1793, 1794, and 1798 can document presence in Philadelphia before and after the epidemic, substitute for missing census years, and show property changes consistent with estate settlement.

### Other record types
- **Orphans' Court guardianship records:** Children orphaned by the 1793 epidemic entered Orphans' Court proceedings; these name surviving parents, guardians, and children with approximate ages.
- **City directories:** Philadelphia city directories were published from 1785. The 1793 and 1795 editions bracket the epidemic and show who was present and then absent.
- **Published compiled works:** The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania hold published transcriptions and indexes of church records and colonial-era vital events.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, 3.2M browse-only images); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, indexed); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, indexed); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (volume 001188322, 145 browse-only images) | Probate surge from epidemic; marriage records; Quaker records | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census collection including 1790 and 1800 Philadelphia enumerations | Census coverage bracketing the epidemic | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records for major Philadelphia churchyards | Burial documentation for epidemic dead | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Philadelphia newspapers including 1793 issues | Death notices and epidemic lists not in church registers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War pension and service records for men living in Philadelphia in 1793 | Military records for the pre-epidemic generation | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger arrival lists for Philadelphia port; early naturalization records | Immigration and naturalization documentation | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for this place and period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800, volume 001188322). This is the complete result set (totalResults: 1). Church and epidemic-specific manuscript holdings at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives are not digitized on FamilySearch.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | City and county government records: tax assessments, deed books, Orphans' Court, Committee relief records, Bush Hill hospital records | In-person (appointments recommended) |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Manuscript collections: Committee minutes, church records, newspapers, diaries, personal papers from the epidemic period | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records; published abstracts | In-person; some materials published |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | 18th-century Philadelphia newspaper runs, published histories | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Pennsylvania Land Office records, provincial and state records | In-person; some records online |
| Philadelphia Register of Wills | Original wills and administrations | In-person |
| Individual church archives | Original baptism, marriage, and burial registers | Contact each church or diocese |

## Records NOT online
- Philadelphia Committee relief records and Bush Hill hospital records (at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives)
- Most 1793-era church burial registers for individual congregations other than the Quaker meeting
- Philadelphia city directories for 1793 and 1795 (some may be available via HathiTrust or Google Books as digitized books)
- Ward-level tax assessment lists for 1793–1794

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that specific Philadelphia records for the 1793 period were destroyed or lost. The Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania are the repositories identified by tool results as holding the primary epidemic-related manuscript sources. An empty online search result reflects digitization gaps, not necessarily record loss.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all Philadelphia- and Pennsylvania-specific pages during this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki article at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793 identifies key epidemic records; consult it directly before beginning research.
- Begin with Mathew Carey's 'Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793), which names individuals who died. It is the most direct compiled list of epidemic dead named by any tool result in this survey (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).
- Compare the 1790 and 1800 federal census household compositions: individuals present in 1790 but absent in 1800 (with no migration evidence) may be epidemic victims; new household members in 1800 may be surviving children, a remarried spouse, or boarders taken in by a reduced household.
- Probate collection 1999196 (browse-only, 3.2M images) must be navigated directly to the Philadelphia County volumes for late 1793–1795 to find epidemic-era administrations; name-searching is not possible.
- Philadelphia ground rent records at the Philadelphia City Archives name heirs who assumed rent obligations after an ancestor's death, providing succession evidence not available from burial registers.
- Orphans' Court records at the Philadelphia City Archives document children left without parents by the epidemic and name guardians — a source of relationship evidence unavailable from church registers alone.

- **Orphans' Court guardianship records:** Children orphaned by the 1793 epidemic entered Orphans' Court proceedings; these name surviving parents, guardians, and children with approximate ages.
- **City directories:** Philadelphia city directories were published from 1785. The 1793 and 1795 editions bracket the epidemic and show who was present and then absent.
- **Published compiled works:** The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania hold published transcriptions and indexes of church records and colonial-era vital events.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, 3.2M browse-only images); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, indexed); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, indexed); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (volume 001188322, 145 browse-only images) | Probate surge from epidemic; marriage records; Quaker records | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census collection including 1790 and 1800 Philadelphia enumerations | Census coverage bracketing the epidemic | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records for major Philadelphia churchyards | Burial documentation for epidemic dead | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Philadelphia newspapers including 1793 issues | Death notices and epidemic lists not in church registers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War pension and service records for men living in Philadelphia in 1793 | Military records for the pre-epidemic generation | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger arrival lists for Philadelphia port; early naturalization records | Immigration and naturalization documentation | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for this place and period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800, volume 001188322). This is the complete result set (totalResults: 1). Church and epidemic-specific manuscript holdings at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives are not digitized on FamilySearch.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | City and county government records: tax assessments, deed books, Orphans' Court, Committee relief records, Bush Hill hospital records | In-person (appointments recommended) |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Manuscript collections: Committee minutes, church records, newspapers, diaries, personal papers from the epidemic period | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records; published abstracts | In-person; some materials published |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | 18th-century Philadelphia newspaper runs, published histories | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Pennsylvania Land Office records, provincial and state records | In-person; some records online |
| Philadelphia Register of Wills | Original wills and administrations | In-person |
| Individual church archives | Original baptism, marriage, and burial registers | Contact each church or diocese |

## Records NOT online
- Philadelphia Committee relief records and Bush Hill hospital records (at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives)
- Most 1793-era church burial registers for individual congregations other than the Quaker meeting
- Philadelphia city directories for 1793 and 1795 (some may be available via HathiTrust or Google Books as digitized books)
- Ward-level tax assessment lists for 1793–1794

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that specific Philadelphia records for the 1793 period were destroyed or lost. The Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania are the repositories identified by tool results as holding the primary epidemic-related manuscript sources. An empty online search result reflects digitization gaps, not necessarily record loss.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all Philadelphia- and Pennsylvania-specific pages during this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki article at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793 identifies key epidemic records; consult it directly before beginning research.
- Begin with Mathew Carey's 'Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793), which names individuals who died. It is the most direct compiled list of epidemic dead named by any tool result in this survey (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).
- Compare the 1790 and 1800 federal census household compositions: individuals present in 1790 but absent in 1800 (with no migration evidence) may be epidemic victims; new household members in 1800 may be surviving children, a remarried spouse, or boarders taken in by a reduced household.
- Probate collection 1999196 (browse-only, 3.2M images) must be navigated directly to the Philadelphia County volumes for late 1793–1795 to find epidemic-era administrations; name-searching is not possible.
- Philadelphia ground rent records at the Philadelphia City Archives name heirs who assumed rent obligations after an ancestor's death, providing succession evidence not available from burial registers.
- Orphans' Court records at the Philadelphia City Archives document children left without parents by the epidemic and name guardians — a source of relationship evidence unavailable from church registers alone.

Researching Chicago families around the Great Fire of 1871 is one of the most record-loss-heavy problems in American genealogy. Here's a comprehensive overview of what survived and where to find it:

---

## The Core Challenge

The fire of **October 8–10, 1871** burned the Cook County Courthouse and destroyed most pre-fire civil vital records, deeds, probate files, tax rolls, and many church registers. This means your research strategy must rely heavily on records held *outside* Chicago at the time of the fire, or records created *after* the fire.

---

## Key Surviving & Replacement Sources

### Federal Census (Pre-Fire)
- **1870 U.S. Federal Census** — Survived because originals were held in Washington, D.C. This is your most important pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families.

### Church Records (FamilySearch)
- **FamilySearch Collection 1803978** — Chicago-area church records, 1833–1925, name-indexed and free. Many parishes kept their registers offsite or in fireproof safes, making this a critical source.

### Land & Property Records
- **Burnt Record Act of 1872** — Illinois law allowing property owners to re-record pre-fire deeds. These post-fire re-recordings are on FamilySearch (partially indexed, 1871–1880, ~41% name-indexed; the rest must be browsed image by image).
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records** — Held at the **Chicago History Museum**; document pre-fire property ownership.

### City Directories
- Directories from the 1840s onward survived. Held at the **Newberry Library** (Chicago). These can place a family at a specific address before and after the fire.

### Post-Fire Civil Registration
- **Cook County Clerk's office** and **FamilySearch** hold indexed birth, death, and marriage records beginning in 1871 (conveniently, the fire itself marks the practical start of surviving civil registration).

### Reconstructed Court Records
- A browse-only digitized set of **reconstructed pre-fire court records (1865–1871)** exists on FamilySearch — must be examined image by image, as it is not name-indexed.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** (Chicago) | City directories, maps, Illinois genealogy collections |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance records, photographs, newspapers |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (many survived the fire) |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University** | Post-fire Cook County records |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Church records, census, post-fire property re-recordings |

---

## Research Strategy

1. **Start with the 1870 census** to document the family before the fire.
2. **Search FamilySearch church records** (Collection 1803978) — many parishes preserved their registers.
3. **Check city directories** at the Newberry Library to track movement before and after October 1871.
4. **Search post-fire property re-recordings** for land-owning families.
5. **Contact the Bernardin Archives** directly if the family was Catholic.

---

The natural next step is building a sequenced research plan based on what you already know about your specific ancestor. Would you like help with that?
