entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1840–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Incorporated:** Chicago incorporated as a city in 1837 within Cook County, Illinois.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago (also the county seat of Cook County).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Cook County, Illinois; Illinois is a federal public-land state.
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by the place_population tool for this query.
- **Economy:** Major railroad hub, meatpacking, lumber trade, and manufacturing — industries that drew large immigrant waves.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large German, Irish, Scandinavian, Polish, and Bohemian immigrant communities, especially after 1850; each community maintained separate church records.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish and Polish immigrants), Lutheran (German and Scandinavian), Methodist, Episcopal, Baptist, Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical event:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and the bulk of the city's pre-fire records. This is the central fact shaping every research strategy for this place and period.

## Boundary changes
- Chicago's city limits expanded significantly through annexation during the 19th century, particularly in 1889 when large surrounding townships (including Hyde Park and Lake View) were annexed.
- Cook County boundaries were stable during the target period. Illinois is a federal public-land state, so land grants originate with the federal government.
- No predecessor county holds the Chicago records — Cook County was the jurisdiction from incorporation.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Illinois Vital Records page did not return place-specific content during this survey; a statewide registration start date cannot be stated from tool results. The four FamilySearch collections all begin at 1871, consistent with post-fire county-level recording.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 2024189, "Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940" (1,450,000 records); collection 1913456, "Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947" (980,000 records); collection 1756321, "Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920" (620,000 records). All start in 1871 — county-level registration that survived the fire or was re-established immediately after.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (indexed, free); originals at the Cook County Clerk's office per the FamilySearch Wiki result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories.
- **Gaps:** Pre-fire civil vital records (before October 1871) were destroyed when the Cook County Courthouse burned. There are no FamilySearch-indexed civil registration records for Chicago before 1871.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (collection 1803978, covering 1833–1925) are the primary substitute for pre-fire births, marriages, and burials.

### Church records
- **Collections:** FamilySearch collection 1803978, "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" (285,000 records, indexed) — covers multiple denominations and spans the pre-fire period.
- **Catholic records:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. Per the FamilySearch Wiki result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories, this is the repository for Catholic baptism, marriage, and burial registers.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collection 1803978, free, indexed); Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (originals and some registers).
- **Gaps:** Many individual parish registers were destroyed in the fire; surviving registers vary by congregation. The church records collection covers 1833 onward, but gaps by parish are unknown without examining individual volumes.
- **Language:** German-language registers for German Lutheran and Catholic parishes; Polish, Bohemian, and Scandinavian-language registers for those congregations.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, and 1870 schedules for Chicago survived the fire because originals were held in Washington, D.C. — per the Wikipedia article on the Great Chicago Fire (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire). The 1870 census is the best pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families. The 1880, 1900 censuses also cover this period. The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed nationally (not a Chicago-specific loss).
- **State census:** Illinois did not conduct a statewide census in this period; no state enumeration fills the 1890 gap.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules for 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 record deaths in the year preceding each census — useful as a substitute for missing death records.
- **Access:** Federal census schedules are indexed on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, estate inventories — filed at the county level (Cook County Circuit Court).
- **Record loss:** Pre-fire probate and court records were held in the Cook County Courthouse and were destroyed in October 1871. Two digitized volumes of reconstructed records are available on FamilySearch: volume 009982110 (38 images, 1865–1871, labeled "Pre-fire County Court Records, reconstructed copies") is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) — it must be examined image by image.
- **Post-fire records:** Post-1871 probate records were re-established; contact the Cook County Circuit Court or the Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University.
- **Where held:** IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University for post-fire Cook County records, per the FamilySearch Wiki result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Illinois is a federal public-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Original federal land grants and patents are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website. County-level deeds are at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds.
- **Record loss and reconstruction:** Pre-fire Cook County deed books were destroyed. The Illinois Burnt Record Act (1872) required property owners to re-register their deeds. FamilySearch volume 009982111 (112 images, 1871–1880, 41% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) contains post-fire property re-recordings and is partially searchable by name.
- **Insurance records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum contains insurance and abstract records that document pre-fire property ownership — per the Wikipedia article on the Great Chicago Fire (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire).
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (federal patents, free online); Chicago History Museum (insurance/abstract records); Cook County Recorder of Deeds (post-1872 deed books).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA; Civil War draft registrations; Illinois adjutant general records at the Illinois State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) holds federal records for this area; Illinois State Archives (Springfield) holds state military records; Fold3 (subscription) provides online access to many service and pension records.

### Cemetery records

Researching Chicago families around the Great Fire of 1871 is one of the most record-loss-heavy problems in American genealogy. The fire of October 8-10, 1871 burned the Cook County Courthouse and destroyed most pre-fire civil vital records, deeds, probate files, tax rolls, and many church registers. For land and property, the Chicago History Museum holds Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records that document pre-fire ownership. City directories from the 1840s onward survived and are at the Newberry Library. The Cook County Clerk's office and FamilySearch hold indexed birth, death, and marriage records beginning in 1871. Two digitized volumes exist on FamilySearch for the fire era: a browse-only set of reconstructed pre-fire court records (1865-1871, must be examined image by image) and a partially indexed set of post-fire property re-recordings (1871-1880, 41% name-indexed). Physical repositories that hold the most for this period are the Newberry Library, the Chicago History Museum, the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (Catholic parish registers), and the Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (post-fire county records). Here is the locality guide for Louisiana in the French colonial period (1700s):

---

**Louisiana French Colonial Period (1700s) — Records & Repositories**

Louisiana was governed first by **France (1699–1762)** and then by **Spain (1769–1803)**, with no U.S.-style civil vital registration during either period. Surviving records fall into two main streams:

---

### 1. Catholic Sacramental Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)
- These were the **only legally recognized vital records** under French law.
- Held by the **Archdiocese of New Orleans**.
- Partially available **free on FamilySearch** in collection **1612905**, starting from 1718.
- Two additional browse-only volumes on FamilySearch (image groups **004330991** and **004330992**) cover Archdiocesan sacramental registers — both are **entirely unindexed** and must be read page by page in 18th-century French or Spanish.

---

### 2. Colonial Civil Records (Superior Council)
- Includes **land grants, notarial contracts, and estate inventories**.
- Held physically at the **Louisiana Historical Center** in New Orleans.
- Partially digitized, but much requires on-site research.

---

### 3. Spanish Colonial Records (1769–1803)
- Held at the **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain.
- Not broadly searchable online.

---

### 4. French Colonial Records & Census Rolls
- Held at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France.
- Not broadly searchable online in the same way as domestic collections.

---

**Key Takeaway:** The best starting point for online research is the FamilySearch sacramental register collection (1612905). The unindexed volumes must be browsed image by image. For deeper colonial research — land, probate, and notarial records — the Louisiana Historical Center and European archives are essential. Research in this period requires reading 18th-century French or Spanish handwriting.

If you'd like to move forward with a specific research plan targeting particular families or questions, let me know and we can map out the next steps.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700s / ca. 1699-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Colonial power(s):** French (1699-1762), Spanish (1762-1800), briefly French again (1800-1803); transferred to the United States by the Louisiana Purchase in 1803
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville)
- **Parent jurisdiction (French period):** New France / Ministry of the Marine (Paris); records held locally and in France
- **Population during period:** No FamilySearch population data was returned for this colonial period. Census rolls taken by the colonial administration exist but are scattered between Louisiana and French archives.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, later sugar), fur trade, Mississippi River commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers, Africans (enslaved under the Code Noir), Native Americans, German and Swiss colonists, Canary Islanders (under Spanish rule), Acadian exiles (Cajuns, arriving from 1755 onward)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively under French rule (the only legally recognized church); Catholicism remained dominant under Spain
- **Key historical events:** Foundation of New Orleans 1718; Code Noir enforced from early colonial period; Acadian expulsion and migration to Louisiana from 1755; French cession to Spain 1762 (effective 1769); Louisiana Purchase 1803

## Boundary changes
- French Louisiana (1699-1762) encompassed a vast territory along the Mississippi River basin — far larger than modern Louisiana.
- Spain took nominal control in 1762 by the Treaty of Fontainebleau but did not assume effective governance until 1769; records from the intervening years (1762-1769) may follow French administrative conventions despite Spanish sovereignty.
- Under Spain, the colony was divided into administrative districts (posts) rather than parishes.
- The modern state of Louisiana was carved from a much larger territory after the Louisiana Purchase (1803). Records created in the colonial period cover a geographic area that does not align with present-day state boundaries.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil (government) vital registration existed during the French or Spanish colonial periods. The FamilySearch Vital Records page returned only generic content and did not supply a Louisiana-specific civil registration start date.
- **What exists:** Vital events in the 1700s are recorded exclusively in Catholic church registers — not in any civil government series. See Church Records below.
- **Pre-registration sources:** Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the sole vital record for this era.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively (the only legally recognized church under French colonial law)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons), marriages (including marriage contracts in notarial records), and burials
- **What FamilySearch holds:**
  - FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (date range 1718-1925; 987,654 records; free, name-indexed with images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905 — this is the primary online entry point for colonial-era Catholic registers.
  - FamilySearch digitized volume 004330991: Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, covering Orleans, Louisiana, 1720-1803, 264 images — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; in French and Spanish. Must be read image by image.**
- **Original registers:** St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans holds registers from 1720, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records). The Archdiocese of New Orleans archives holds additional records.
- **Gaps:** Registers before 1718 are sparse or unlocated online. Records from outpost parishes (Natchitoches, Mobile, Illinois Country) are held separately and may not be in the main FamilySearch collection.
- **Language:** French (1699-1769), then Spanish (1769-1803), with some French persisting under Spanish rule. Researchers must read the original language.

### Census records
- **Colonial enumerations:** The French and Spanish colonial administrations conducted periodic census rolls of the settler population. These are not federal census records. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records), colonial census rolls are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France.
- **U.S. federal census:** Louisiana was not part of the United States during the 1700s; the first federal census of Louisiana occurred in 1810 after the Purchase. No U.S. federal census covers the colonial period.
- **Access:** ANOM holdings are physical/on-site in France; some have been microfilmed or partially digitized through French archival initiatives.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, succession proceedings, guardianships, civil suits — all handled by the Superior Council (Conseil Superieur) under France, and by the Cabildo under Spain
- **Date range:** The FamilySearch collection 2078341, "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (date range 1756-1984; 456,789 records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341 — this overlaps the later colonial period.
- **Original custody:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records), Superior Council records are held at the Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans, and have been partially digitized.
- **Testate / intestate:** Both wills (testate) and intestate estate administrations appear in the Superior Council series; the same body handled all civil proceedings.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French civil law (not English common law metes-and-bounds or U.S. rectangular survey). French concessions used the long-lot system; Spanish grants continued similar practices.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** France through the Superior Council; Spain through the Spanish colonial government (Cabildo and Governor)
- **Types:** French land concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, marriage settlements, property transfers
- **What exists:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants): notarial archives in New Orleans hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward. Colonial land grants also appear in the American State Papers: Public Lands series. The Louisiana State Land Office holds relevant records.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Volume 004330992 covers French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), Louisiana, 1699-1769, 149 images — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; in French and Spanish.**
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center:** The oldest continuously operating notarial office in North America; provides public access to notarial records from the 1730s.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The 1700s saw French-Native American conflicts (Natchez War 1729-1731), French and Indian War (1754-1763), and various border actions under Spanish rule.
- **Record types:** Colonial military muster rolls and service records are in French and Spanish colonial archives.
- **Where held:** French military records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France. Spanish military records are in Spanish colonial archives (Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain). Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) is listed as a curated external resource and may hold some derivative material.
- **U.S. records:** Not applicable — Louisiana was not under U.S. authority during the 1700s.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial burials:** Formal cemetery records for the 1700s do not exist as a distinct series; burial information is recorded in Catholic parish registers.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds some entries, but colonial-era grave markers are rare and survival is uneven.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries in the sacramental registers (see Church Records above) are the primary source.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Formal colonial-era newspapers in Louisiana were extremely limited in the 1700s and did not function as genealogical sources. The Moniteur de la Louisiane began publication only in 1794.
- **Where held:** Historical Newspapers via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is listed as a curated external resource but coverage of 1700s Louisiana papers is sparse.
- **Content value:** Minimal for the colonial period; legal notices and property transactions in the notarial records serve this function instead.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Settlers arrived from France, French Canada, the Caribbean (Saint-Domingue), and West Africa (enslaved). Acadian exiles from British Canada arrived from 1755. Canary Island settlers (Islenhos) arrived under Spanish rule in the 1770s.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists and immigration manifests for colonial Louisiana are not held in U.S. repositories in the same way as later immigration records. Embarkation records, if they survive, are in French and Spanish archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds some derivative material. For colonial-period arrivals, the ANOM in France and the Archivo General de Indias in Spain are the primary custodians of embarkation and administrative records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists for this era, where they survive, are in French or Spanish and record colonists, soldiers, engages (indentured workers), and enslaved Africans separately.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax and tribute records exist but are not a distinct genealogical series comparable to U.S. state tax lists.
- **Substitute value:** Notarial property records and census rolls (held at ANOM) function as the nearest substitutes for census and tax coverage in this period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1612905 (Church Records 1718-1925); Collection 2078341 (Probate Records 1756-1984); Volumes 004330991 and 004330992 (browse-only colonial registers) | Primary Catholic vital events and colonial notarial/probate records | Free |
| NARA | General holdings (https://www.archives.gov/) | Some derivative colonial material | Free / in-person |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Colonial-era military service | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Grave inscription searches | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a complete result set of 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana 1700-1803; both are detailed above. Both are browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records (French colonial civil records, notarial acts, court proceedings, estate inventories); partially digitized | In-person; inquire about digital access |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial records from the 1730s onward (contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions) | In-person public access |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original Catholic sacramental registers; some records also on FamilySearch | In-person / written inquiry |
| Louisiana State Land Office | Colonial land grants and concessions | In-person / online inquiry |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Colonial census rolls, administrative correspondence, official records of French Louisiana | In-person in France; some holdings partially digitized via French national archives portals |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana 1769-1800 | In-person in Spain; some holdings accessible via Portal de Archivos Espanoles (PARES) |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial census rolls (held at ANOM, France) — not in any U.S. online database
- Spanish colonial administrative records (Archivo General de Indias, Spain)
- Most French and Spanish military muster rolls
- Outpost parish registers outside New Orleans (e.g., Natchitoches, Pointe Coupee) — coverage in FamilySearch collection 1612905 may be partial
- Marriage contracts from the notarial archives prior to digitization of the New Orleans Notarial Archives

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this survey identified specific known losses for Louisiana colonial records. The two FamilySearch wiki results (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants) do not name destroyed record sets. Gaps are more likely a digitization and access issue than destruction — consult the Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM directly before concluding records do not survive.

## Research tips
- The Catholic parish register is the single most important source for colonial Louisiana family research. Catholic Church records are the only vital records for this period; begin there before any civil series. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925," is the first online stop — it is indexed and free. Search it for baptisms, marriages, and burials before browsing the unindexed volumes. (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)
- The two browse-only FamilySearch volumes (004330991 and 004330992) are in French and Spanish and require the researcher to read page by page with no name index. If you cannot read 18th-century French or Spanish script, consider engaging a professional translator or paleographer.
- The transition from French to Spanish administration (de facto 1769) splits the record trail. French-era records run to roughly 1769; Spanish-era records from 1769 to 1803. Search both series — a family active across that boundary will appear in both French and Spanish record types.
- For enslaved ancestors, the Code Noir mandated Catholic baptism, so enslaved persons appear by name (usually given name only) in the same sacramental registers as free persons. This is one of the earliest documentary sources for African-descended families in Louisiana.
- The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the oldest continuously operating notarial office in North America; marriage contracts, property sales, and estate settlements for colonial families are there. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- For ancestors who arrived as Acadian exiles after 1755, trace the family in Nova Scotia / Acadia records first, then pick up the trail in Louisiana Catholic registers upon their arrival.

- **What exists:** Vital events in the 1700s are recorded exclusively in Catholic church registers — not in any civil government series. See Church Records below.
- **Pre-registration sources:** Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the sole vital record for this era.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively (the only legally recognized church under French colonial law)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons), marriages (including marriage contracts in notarial records), and burials
- **What FamilySearch holds:**
  - FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (date range 1718-1925; 987,654 records; free, name-indexed with images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905 — this is the primary online entry point for colonial-era Catholic registers.
  - FamilySearch digitized volume 004330991: Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, covering Orleans, Louisiana, 1720-1803, 264 images — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; in French and Spanish. Must be read image by image.**
- **Original registers:** St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans holds registers from 1720, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records). The Archdiocese of New Orleans archives holds additional records.
- **Gaps:** Registers before 1718 are sparse or unlocated online. Records from outpost parishes (Natchitoches, Mobile, Illinois Country) are held separately and may not be in the main FamilySearch collection.
- **Language:** French (1699-1769), then Spanish (1769-1803), with some French persisting under Spanish rule. Researchers must read the original language.

### Census records
- **Colonial enumerations:** The French and Spanish colonial administrations conducted periodic census rolls of the settler population. These are not federal census records. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records), colonial census rolls are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France.
- **U.S. federal census:** Louisiana was not part of the United States during the 1700s; the first federal census of Louisiana occurred in 1810 after the Purchase. No U.S. federal census covers the colonial period.
- **Access:** ANOM holdings are physical/on-site in France; some have been microfilmed or partially digitized through French archival initiatives.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, succession proceedings, guardianships, civil suits — all handled by the Superior Council (Conseil Superieur) under France, and by the Cabildo under Spain
- **Date range:** The FamilySearch collection 2078341, "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (date range 1756-1984; 456,789 records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341 — this overlaps the later colonial period.
- **Original custody:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records), Superior Council records are held at the Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans, and have been partially digitized.
- **Testate / intestate:** Both wills (testate) and intestate estate administrations appear in the Superior Council series; the same body handled all civil proceedings.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French civil law (not English common law metes-and-bounds or U.S. rectangular survey). French concessions used the long-lot system; Spanish grants continued similar practices.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** France through the Superior Council; Spain through the Spanish colonial government (Cabildo and Governor)
- **Types:** French land concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, marriage settlements, property transfers
- **What exists:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants): notarial archives in New Orleans hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward. Colonial land grants also appear in the American State Papers: Public Lands series. The Louisiana State Land Office holds relevant records.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Volume 004330992 covers French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), Louisiana, 1699-1769, 149 images — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; in French and Spanish.**
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center:** The oldest continuously operating notarial office in North America; provides public access to notarial records from the 1730s.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The 1700s saw French-Native American conflicts (Natchez War 1729-1731), French and Indian War (1754-1763), and various border actions under Spanish rule.
- **Record types:** Colonial military muster rolls and service records are in French and Spanish colonial archives.
- **Where held:** French military records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France. Spanish military records are in Spanish colonial archives (Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain). Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) is listed as a curated external resource and may hold some derivative material.
- **U.S. records:** Not applicable — Louisiana was not under U.S. authority during the 1700s.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial burials:** Formal cemetery records for the 1700s do not exist as a distinct series; burial information is recorded in Catholic parish registers.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds some entries, but colonial-era grave markers are rare and survival is uneven.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries in the sacramental registers (see Church Records above) are the primary source.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Formal colonial-era newspapers in Louisiana were extremely limited in the 1700s and did not function as genealogical sources. The Moniteur de la Louisiane began publication only in 1794.
- **Where held:** Historical Newspapers via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is listed as a curated external resource but coverage of 1700s Louisiana papers is sparse.
- **Content value:** Minimal for the colonial period; legal notices and property transactions in the notarial records serve this function instead.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Settlers arrived from France, French Canada, the Caribbean (Saint-Domingue), and West Africa (enslaved). Acadian exiles from British Canada arrived from 1755. Canary Island settlers (Islenhos) arrived under Spanish rule in the 1770s.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists and immigration manifests for colonial Louisiana are not held in U.S. repositories in the same way as later immigration records. Embarkation records, if they survive, are in French and Spanish archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds some derivative material. For colonial-period arrivals, the ANOM in France and the Archivo General de Indias in Spain are the primary custodians of embarkation and administrative records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists for this era, where they survive, are in French or Spanish and record colonists, soldiers, engages (indentured workers), and enslaved Africans separately.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax and tribute records exist but are not a distinct genealogical series comparable to U.S. state tax lists.
- **Substitute value:** Notarial property records and census rolls (held at ANOM) function as the nearest substitutes for census and tax coverage in this period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1612905 (Church Records 1718-1925); Collection 2078341 (Probate Records 1756-1984); Volumes 004330991 and 004330992 (browse-only colonial registers) | Primary Catholic vital events and colonial notarial/probate records | Free |
| NARA | General holdings (https://www.archives.gov/) | Some derivative colonial material | Free / in-person |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Colonial-era military service | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Grave inscription searches | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a complete result set of 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana 1700-1803; both are detailed above. Both are browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records (French colonial civil records, notarial acts, court proceedings, estate inventories); partially digitized | In-person; inquire about digital access |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial records from the 1730s onward (contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions) | In-person public access |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original Catholic sacramental registers; some records also on FamilySearch | In-person / written inquiry |
| Louisiana State Land Office | Colonial land grants and concessions | In-person / online inquiry |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Colonial census rolls, administrative correspondence, official records of French Louisiana | In-person in France; some holdings partially digitized via French national archives portals |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana 1769-1800 | In-person in Spain; some holdings accessible via Portal de Archivos Espanoles (PARES) |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial census rolls (held at ANOM, France) — not in any U.S. online database
- Spanish colonial administrative records (Archivo General de Indias, Spain)
- Most French and Spanish military muster rolls
- Outpost parish registers outside New Orleans (e.g., Natchitoches, Pointe Coupee) — coverage in FamilySearch collection 1612905 may be partial
- Marriage contracts from the notarial archives prior to digitization of the New Orleans Notarial Archives

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this survey identified specific known losses for Louisiana colonial records. The two FamilySearch wiki results (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants) do not name destroyed record sets. Gaps are more likely a digitization and access issue than destruction — consult the Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM directly before concluding records do not survive.

## Research tips
- The Catholic parish register is the single most important source for colonial Louisiana family research. Catholic Church records are the only vital records for this period; begin there before any civil series. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925," is the first online stop — it is indexed and free. Search it for baptisms, marriages, and burials before browsing the unindexed volumes. (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)
- The two browse-only FamilySearch volumes (004330991 and 004330992) are in French and Spanish and require the researcher to read page by page with no name index. If you cannot read 18th-century French or Spanish script, consider engaging a professional translator or paleographer.
- The transition from French to Spanish administration (de facto 1769) splits the record trail. French-era records run to roughly 1769; Spanish-era records from 1769 to 1803. Search both series — a family active across that boundary will appear in both French and Spanish record types.
- For enslaved ancestors, the Code Noir mandated Catholic baptism, so enslaved persons appear by name (usually given name only) in the same sacramental registers as free persons. This is one of the earliest documentary sources for African-descended families in Louisiana.
- The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the oldest continuously operating notarial office in North America; marriage contracts, property sales, and estate settlements for colonial families are there. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- For ancestors who arrived as Acadian exiles after 1755, trace the family in Nova Scotia / Acadia records first, then pick up the trail in Louisiana Catholic registers upon their arrival.

---

**Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Late 1800s Locality Guide**

The survey focused on **Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania** (formed 1811, county seat Pottsville) from roughly **1850–1910**, the heart of the anthracite coal region. A locality guide has been saved as **loc_001** in the project.

---

### Key Record Types & Repositories

| Record | Coverage | Repository / Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Marriage records** (indexed) | 1885 onward | FamilySearch collection 1921317 |
| **Compiled marriages** | Back to 1677 | FamilySearch collection 1502909 |
| **Probate records** (browse-only images) | 1683–1994 | FamilySearch collection 1999196 |
| **Death certificates** (indexed) | 1906 onward | FamilySearch collection 2255317 |
| **Mine worker employment cards** | 1870–1900 | FamilySearch volume 002240015 (~95% name-indexed) |
| **PA State Mine Inspector annual reports** | From 1870 | Pennsylvania State Archives — names fatal accident victims by name & nationality |
| **Naturalization records** | Pre-1906 | Pennsylvania State Archives (not online) |
| **Ethnic parish registers** | Varies | Individual parishes & Diocese of Allentown archives |
| **Federal census mortality schedules** | 1850–1885 | Critical substitute for pre-1906 death records |

---

### Important Jurisdictional Notes

- **Statewide death registration** did not begin until **1906** — for earlier deaths, parish registers and mine inspector reports are the primary substitutes.
- **Lackawanna County** split off from **Luzerne County in 1878** — records for Scranton-area coal towns before that date are filed under Luzerne.
- The other main coal counties — **Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland** — each need their own separate locality survey.

---

### Suggested Next Step

Build a **research plan** using this locality guide as the foundation, targeting your specific research questions (for example, identifying the parents of a miner born ca. 1845 Pennsylvania, died ca. 1908 Schuylkill County). The mine worker employment cards and State Mine Inspector annual reports are especially valuable for the coal region and often record a worker's nationality — a crucial clue for tracing immigrant miners back to their home country.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns (1850–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from parts of Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tool for this place and period; consult published census volumes or the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining, dominant from the 1820s onward; also iron and textile industries. The coal industry shaped nearly every other record type.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large immigrant waves from Ireland and Wales in the mid-1800s, followed by Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Italy, and Ukraine in the 1880s–1900s (per Wikipedia, "Coal Region"). Ethnic origin strongly predicts which church a family used.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian parishes), Welsh Congregational, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal, and various Reformed congregations. Ethnic parishes often kept the most detailed family records.
- **Key historical events:** 1869 Avondale Mine Disaster; 1875 Long Strike; rise of the United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) after 1890. Mine disasters generated inquest and accident records.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 and its boundaries were stable through the late 1800s.
- **Lackawanna County** (covering Scranton, Carbondale) was carved from Luzerne County in **1878**. Records for events in that territory before 1878 are filed under Luzerne County — search Luzerne first for pre-1878 events in the northern coal district.
- The broader coal region spans Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties. A family near any county border likely generated records in more than one jurisdiction.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania statewide death registration began in 1906, as indicated by FamilySearch collection 2255317 (Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968). The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey, so no statewide birth or marriage registration start date could be confirmed from tool results — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records exist from at least 1885 (FamilySearch collection 1921317, Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950; 524,189 records, indexed + images). Earlier compiled marriages 1677–1900 are in collection 1502909 (198,765 records, indexed, no images). Death certificates from 1906 onward are in collection 2255317 (4,218,763 records, indexed + images).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online, free). Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds originals.
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil death registration before 1906. No indexed birth certificate collection for the late 1800s was returned by the tools.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; state Mine Inspector annual reports (from 1870) for fatalities; newspaper death notices.

### Church records

Locality guide written as **loc_001** in research.json.

---

Early Massachusetts (1620–1700) is one of the best-documented places in colonial North America. Here is a summary of the key records and repositories to help trace Puritan families:

---

## Civil Vital Records

Massachusetts Bay Colony required towns to record births, marriages, and deaths starting in **1639**, and those town clerk registers survive for most communities. The published **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series abstracts town records for over 200 towns and is an essential first stop.

---

## Published Compiled Research

The **NEHGS "Great Migration" study series** is a documented reconstruction of every known settler arriving 1620–1643 — ideal for identifying early colonists and their families with full source citations.

---

## Church Records

**Congregational church records** capture baptisms, marriages, disciplinary proceedings, and membership not found in civil records. These are often the only source for children's births and family connections.

---

## FamilySearch Indexed Collections (Free)

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 | 2061550 | Indexed, searchable by name |
| Massachusetts Church Records, 1630–1920 | 1921657 | Indexed |
| Massachusetts Probate Records, 1635–1991 | 1678901 | Indexed |

Two additional digitized collections require extra effort:
- **Town meeting and proprietors' records (1620–1698):** Browse image-by-image only; no name search available.
- **Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms (1630–1700):** Full-text searchable but not findable by standard name search — use full-text search (FTS) with Lucene queries.

---

## Census Substitutes

No federal census exists for this period. Use instead:
- **Tax lists**
- **Militia muster rolls**
- **Town meeting minutes**

---

## Critical Jurisdictional Warning — Plymouth Colony

**Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) is a separate jurisdiction.** Its records are published and indexed independently. Any ancestor in Plymouth before 1692 will **not** appear in the Massachusetts Bay Colony series. Always check which colony your ancestor lived in.

---

## Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Original colonial records, court files, province laws |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | Originals, published compilations, manuscript collections far beyond what is online |

---

If you'd like a research plan for a specific Puritan-era family, share the name and town and that next step can follow from here.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628; Plymouth Colony established 1620; Province of Massachusetts Bay formed 1692 when Plymouth Colony was absorbed into Massachusetts Bay Colony
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (seat of Massachusetts Bay Colony throughout the period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts Bay Colony (from 1628); Plymouth Colony (separate, 1620-1691); Province of Massachusetts Bay (from 1692 onward)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived during the Great Migration of 1630-1640, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony); no population data returned by the place_population tool for this jurisdiction and period
- **Economy:** Fishing, farming, fur trading, and timber; maritime and land transactions shaped the documentary record
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; small Indigenous populations; no substantial non-English European immigration in this period
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (Puritan) was the established church of the colony; no other denominations had significant institutional presence in most towns during 1620-1700
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration (1630-1640) — approximately 20,000 settlers; King Philip's War (1675-1678) — disrupted some towns and records; Salem Witch Trials (1692) — generated substantial court records; absorption of Plymouth Colony into Province of Massachusetts Bay (1692)

## Boundary changes
- **Plymouth Colony (1620-1691)** was a wholly separate colonial jurisdiction. Records for settlers within Plymouth Colony are published and indexed independently from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. A researcher must check both series for any ancestor in the region before 1692.
- **Province of Massachusetts Bay (1692):** Plymouth Colony was formally merged into Massachusetts Bay Colony under a new royal charter in 1692. After that year, all records fall under one provincial jurisdiction.
- Within Massachusetts Bay Colony, counties were established from 1643 onward (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and later others). County-level probate and deed records begin from the formation date of each county.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated from 1639 within Massachusetts Bay Colony, making Massachusetts among the earliest jurisdictions in North America to require civil registration, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). Plymouth Colony maintained similar records from the early 1620s. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey — no statewide registration date could be confirmed from that page.
- **What exists:** Town clerk records of births, marriages, and deaths from 1639 onward surviving in most towns; the Tanner-Corbin published series ("Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850") abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. FamilySearch collection 2061550, "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890," contains 3,456,789 indexed records (free) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550.
- **Where held:** Original records at town clerk offices; Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colony-level records.
- **Gaps:** Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691) are not included in the Massachusetts Bay Colony series and must be searched separately. Early 1620s-1630s town records are sparse in many towns.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church records (baptisms, marriages); colony court records; probate records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (Puritan) — established church of the colony throughout 1620-1700; no other denominations had significant institutional presence in most towns during this period
- **Record types:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, disciplinary actions (excommunications, admonishments). Church records are NOT duplicates of town vital records — they capture events and individuals not recorded civilly.
- **Where held:** Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). FamilySearch collection 1921657, "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920," contains 987,654 records (free, indexed with images) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657. FamilySearch volume 007612045 (Congregational church admissions and baptisms, Suffolk County, 1630-1700, 121 images) is full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — must be searched via the full-text search interface, not by name.
- **Gaps:** Volume 007612045 covers Suffolk County only; church records for other Massachusetts counties in the 1600s were not returned in the FamilySearch volume search for this period.
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census begins in 1790 — no federal census records exist for the 1620-1700 period.
- **State/provincial census:** No colonial-era enumeration returned by tool.
- **Other enumerations:** Town meeting minutes and proprietors' records serve as the primary substitute. FamilySearch volume 007612044 (Town meeting and proprietors' records, Massachusetts, 1620-1698, 188 images) is browse-only — must be read image by image with no name search capability.
- **Access:** No census records for this period; town meeting records, tax lists, and militia muster rolls are the closest available substitutes.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, inventories, guardianships
- **Date range:** County probate courts began operating from the 1630s per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). FamilySearch collection 1678901, "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991," contains 567,890 indexed records (free) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives (Boston); FamilySearch collection 1678901 (indexed + images)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New England standard)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town proprietors granted land within each town; the Massachusetts Archives holds colony grants and patents. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Land and Property page returned only generic content during this survey — the specific granting office was not confirmed from that page.
- **Types:** Town proprietors' records, deeds, colony grants; land allotments in town meeting records
- **Date range:** County deed books survive from county formation (1640s) onward in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). Town proprietors' records from the 1620s-1630s are among the earliest. FamilySearch volume 007612044 includes proprietors' records (browse-only) for 1620-1698.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk); Massachusetts Archives (colony grants); town clerk offices (proprietors' records)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War (1675-1678); colonial militia enrolled all able-bodied men throughout the period
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls; King Philip's War service records; early war records
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colonial militia and war records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) carries some military records, though coverage of 1600s colonial militia is limited.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burial grounds adjoining Congregational meeting houses are the primary burial record for the period
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many colonial New England gravestones; survival of 1600s stone inscriptions is variable
- **Physical records:** Sexton records from the 1600s are rare; published gravestone transcriptions and cemetery surveys by local historical societies are more common

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Massachusetts newspaper (Publick Occurrences) appeared briefly in 1690. No sustained newspaper publication existed before 1700.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for this period
- **Content value:** Minimal for 1620-1700; obituaries and marriage notices in newspapers are an 18th-century and later phenomenon

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston and Salem were the primary arrival ports for the Great Migration (1630-1640); Plymouth was the 1620 arrival point
- **Record types:** Ship manifests for the 1620s-1640s Great Migration are largely reconstructed from published works rather than surviving original port manifests. The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1784312 ("Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891") does NOT cover the colonial period (begins 1820) and is outside the target window. Colonial-era ship lists are available in published form at NEHGS and through the Great Migration series.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town rates (property and poll levies); colony tax lists
- **Date range:** Town rates survive from the 1630s in many towns
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives and town clerk offices
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name adult male householders and are valuable substitutes for the missing census in this period

### Other record types
- **Colony and county court records:** The Massachusetts General Court and county courts heard civil, criminal, and probate matters. The Massachusetts Archives holds these from the 1620s onward.
- **Town meeting minutes:** Document land allotments, officer appointments, and can name inhabitants who appear in no other record. FamilySearch volume 007612044 (browse-only, 188 images, 1620-1698).
- **Published genealogies and compiled works:** The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series, the Tanner-Corbin published vital records series ("Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"), and Colonial Society of Massachusetts church record publications are essential finding aids and may be the only surviving transcriptions of some records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 2061550 — Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (3,456,789 records); Collection 1921657 — Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (987,654 records); Collection 1678901 — Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (567,890 records); Vol. 007612044 — Town meeting & proprietors' records 1620-1698 (browse-only); Vol. 007612045 — Congregational church admissions & baptisms, Suffolk Co., 1630-1700 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed) | Primary indexed colonial vital, church, and probate records | Free — https://www.familysearch.org |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records | Gravestone inscriptions | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military Records | Colonial and later military service | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA | Federal records | Later federal records | Free to visit/request — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch volume search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts for 1620-1700; this represents the complete set (totalResults: 2, no further pages). The FamilySearch Wiki specific pages for Massachusetts (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census) all returned generic content rather than Massachusetts-specific pages during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy directly for the latest Massachusetts-specific guidance.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from 1620s; colonial militia and war records | In-person; catalog at https://www.sec.state.ma.us/arc/ |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration study series; manuscript collections; published genealogies | In-person; some holdings digitized at AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |
| County registries of deeds (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and others) | Deed books from county formation in 1640s onward | In-person; some digitized at county or state level |
| Town clerk offices | Original town vital records from 1639 | In-person or mail request |

## Records NOT online

- Full run of town meeting minutes across all Massachusetts towns (beyond FamilySearch volume 007612044, which covers one set of records browse-only): originals held in town clerk offices and the Massachusetts Archives
- County registry of deeds volumes from the 1640s-1700s: held physically at county registries; no indexed FamilySearch collection was returned for deeds in this period
- Militia muster rolls and King Philip's War service records: held at Massachusetts Archives; not returned as a digitized FamilySearch collection for 1620-1700
- Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691): published in print volumes; available at NEHGS; not returned as a dedicated FamilySearch online collection for this period
- Colonial Society of Massachusetts published church record series: print only at research libraries

## Known record losses

No tool result returned during this survey identified a specific record set as destroyed or lost for Massachusetts in the 1620-1700 period. All gaps noted above represent digitization or indexing absences, not confirmed losses. For the status of any specific town's records, contact the Massachusetts Archives (Boston) or the relevant town clerk.

## Research tips
- **Plymouth Colony is a separate research jurisdiction.** Any ancestor in Plymouth Colony before 1692 has records under that colony's separate system, published and indexed independently. Search Plymouth Colony records alongside — not as part of — Massachusetts Bay Colony records. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Start with the published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series** (Tanner-Corbin series): the standard entry point for colonial vital research, abstracting town clerk records for over 200 towns. Available at NEHGS, many research libraries, and partially online. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Use the NEHGS "Great Migration" study series** for any ancestor arriving 1620-1643: it documents every known settler with sources and family reconstruction. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Congregational church records are essential and are not duplicates of town vital records.** They record members, baptisms, disciplinary proceedings, and admissions not found in civil registration. FamilySearch collection 1921657 is indexed; FamilySearch volume 007612045 (Suffolk County, 1630-1700) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **County probate records from 1635 are essential for family reconstruction.** Wills and inventories name children, spouses, and sometimes grandchildren. FamilySearch collection 1678901 is indexed and free. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **No federal census exists for 1620-1700.** Use town meeting minutes, tax lists, proprietors' records, and militia muster rolls as substitutes. FamilySearch volume 007612044 (town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698, 188 images) must be browsed image by image with no name or text search available.

The most powerful tools for tracing Puritan families are: the published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (which abstracts town records for over 200 towns), the NEHGS "Great Migration" study series (a documented reconstruction of every known settler arriving 1620-1643), and Congregational church records — which capture baptisms, marriages, disciplinary proceedings, and membership not found in civil records. FamilySearch has three indexed collections covering this era: Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (collection 2061550, free), Church Records 1630-1920 (collection 1921657, free), and Probate Records 1635-1991 (collection 1678901, free). Two additional digitized volumes exist but require extra effort: one set of town meeting and proprietors' records (1620-1698) must be browsed image by image with no search at all, and a set of Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms (1630-1700) is full-text searchable but cannot be found by name search. The most important warning: Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) is a separate jurisdiction whose records are published and indexed independently — any ancestor in Plymouth before 1692 will not appear in the Massachusetts Bay Colony series. No federal census exists for this period, so tax lists, militia muster rolls, and town meeting minutes are the census substitutes. Physical repositories — the Massachusetts Archives in Boston and the New England Historic Genealogical Society — hold originals and published compilations that go well beyond what is online.
