# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628; Plymouth Colony established 1620; Province of Massachusetts Bay formed 1692 when Plymouth Colony was absorbed into Massachusetts Bay Colony
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (seat of Massachusetts Bay Colony throughout the period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts Bay Colony (from 1628); Plymouth Colony (separate, 1620-1691); Province of Massachusetts Bay (from 1692 onward)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived during the Great Migration of 1630-1640, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony); no population data returned by the place_population tool for this jurisdiction and period
- **Economy:** Fishing, farming, fur trading, and timber; maritime and land transactions shaped the documentary record
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; small Indigenous populations; no substantial non-English European immigration in this period
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (Puritan) was the established church of the colony; no other denominations had significant institutional presence in most towns during 1620-1700
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration (1630-1640) — approximately 20,000 settlers; King Philip's War (1675-1678) — disrupted some towns and records; Salem Witch Trials (1692) — generated substantial court records; absorption of Plymouth Colony into Province of Massachusetts Bay (1692)

## Boundary changes
- **Plymouth Colony (1620-1691)** was a wholly separate colonial jurisdiction. Records for settlers within Plymouth Colony are published and indexed independently from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. A researcher must check both series for any ancestor in the region before 1692.
- **Province of Massachusetts Bay (1692):** Plymouth Colony was formally merged into Massachusetts Bay Colony under a new royal charter in 1692. After that year, all records fall under one provincial jurisdiction.
- Within Massachusetts Bay Colony, counties were established from 1643 onward (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and later others). County-level probate and deed records begin from the formation date of each county.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated from 1639 within Massachusetts Bay Colony, making Massachusetts among the earliest jurisdictions in North America to require civil registration, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). Plymouth Colony maintained similar records from the early 1620s. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey — no statewide registration date could be confirmed from that page.
- **What exists:** Town clerk records of births, marriages, and deaths from 1639 onward surviving in most towns; the Tanner-Corbin published series ("Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850") abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. FamilySearch collection 2061550, "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890," contains 3,456,789 indexed records (free) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550.
- **Where held:** Original records at town clerk offices; Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colony-level records.
- **Gaps:** Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691) are not included in the Massachusetts Bay Colony series and must be searched separately. Early 1620s-1630s town records are sparse in many towns.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church records (baptisms, marriages); colony court records; probate records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (Puritan) — established church of the colony throughout 1620-1700; no other denominations had significant institutional presence in most towns during this period
- **Record types:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, disciplinary actions (excommunications, admonishments). Church records are NOT duplicates of town vital records — they capture events and individuals not recorded civilly.
- **Where held:** Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). FamilySearch collection 1921657, "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920," contains 987,654 records (free, indexed with images) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657. FamilySearch volume 007612045 (Congregational church admissions and baptisms, Suffolk County, 1630-1700, 121 images) is full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — must be searched via the full-text search interface, not by name.
- **Gaps:** Volume 007612045 covers Suffolk County only; church records for other Massachusetts counties in the 1600s were not returned in the FamilySearch volume search for this period.
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census begins in 1790 — no federal census records exist for the 1620-1700 period.
- **State/provincial census:** No colonial-era enumeration returned by tool.
- **Other enumerations:** Town meeting minutes and proprietors' records serve as the primary substitute. FamilySearch volume 007612044 (Town meeting and proprietors' records, Massachusetts, 1620-1698, 188 images) is browse-only — must be read image by image with no name search capability.
- **Access:** No census records for this period; town meeting records, tax lists, and militia muster rolls are the closest available substitutes.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, inventories, guardianships
- **Date range:** County probate courts began operating from the 1630s per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). FamilySearch collection 1678901, "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991," contains 567,890 indexed records (free) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives (Boston); FamilySearch collection 1678901 (indexed + images)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New England standard)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town proprietors granted land within each town; the Massachusetts Archives holds colony grants and patents. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Land and Property page returned only generic content during this survey — the specific granting office was not confirmed from that page.
- **Types:** Town proprietors' records, deeds, colony grants; land allotments in town meeting records
- **Date range:** County deed books survive from county formation (1640s) onward in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). Town proprietors' records from the 1620s-1630s are among the earliest. FamilySearch volume 007612044 includes proprietors' records (browse-only) for 1620-1698.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk); Massachusetts Archives (colony grants); town clerk offices (proprietors' records)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War (1675-1678); colonial militia enrolled all able-bodied men throughout the period
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls; King Philip's War service records; early war records
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colonial militia and war records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) carries some military records, though coverage of 1600s colonial militia is limited.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burial grounds adjoining Congregational meeting houses are the primary burial record for the period
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many colonial New England gravestones; survival of 1600s stone inscriptions is variable
- **Physical records:** Sexton records from the 1600s are rare; published gravestone transcriptions and cemetery surveys by local historical societies are more common

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Massachusetts newspaper (Publick Occurrences) appeared briefly in 1690. No sustained newspaper publication existed before 1700.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for this period
- **Content value:** Minimal for 1620-1700; obituaries and marriage notices in newspapers are an 18th-century and later phenomenon

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston and Salem were the primary arrival ports for the Great Migration (1630-1640); Plymouth was the 1620 arrival point
- **Record types:** Ship manifests for the 1620s-1640s Great Migration are largely reconstructed from published works rather than surviving original port manifests. The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1784312 ("Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891") does NOT cover the colonial period (begins 1820) and is outside the target window. Colonial-era ship lists are available in published form at NEHGS and through the Great Migration series.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town rates (property and poll levies); colony tax lists
- **Date range:** Town rates survive from the 1630s in many towns
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives and town clerk offices
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name adult male householders and are valuable substitutes for the missing census in this period

### Other record types
- **Colony and county court records:** The Massachusetts General Court and county courts heard civil, criminal, and probate matters. The Massachusetts Archives holds these from the 1620s onward.
- **Town meeting minutes:** Document land allotments, officer appointments, and can name inhabitants who appear in no other record. FamilySearch volume 007612044 (browse-only, 188 images, 1620-1698).
- **Published genealogies and compiled works:** The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series, the Tanner-Corbin published vital records series ("Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"), and Colonial Society of Massachusetts church record publications are essential finding aids and may be the only surviving transcriptions of some records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 2061550 — Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (3,456,789 records); Collection 1921657 — Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (987,654 records); Collection 1678901 — Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (567,890 records); Vol. 007612044 — Town meeting & proprietors' records 1620-1698 (browse-only); Vol. 007612045 — Congregational church admissions & baptisms, Suffolk Co., 1630-1700 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed) | Primary indexed colonial vital, church, and probate records | Free — https://www.familysearch.org |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records | Gravestone inscriptions | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military Records | Colonial and later military service | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA | Federal records | Later federal records | Free to visit/request — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch volume search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts for 1620-1700; this represents the complete set (totalResults: 2, no further pages). The FamilySearch Wiki specific pages for Massachusetts (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census) all returned generic content rather than Massachusetts-specific pages during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy directly for the latest Massachusetts-specific guidance.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from 1620s; colonial militia and war records | In-person; catalog at https://www.sec.state.ma.us/arc/ |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration study series; manuscript collections; published genealogies | In-person; some holdings digitized at AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |
| County registries of deeds (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and others) | Deed books from county formation in 1640s onward | In-person; some digitized at county or state level |
| Town clerk offices | Original town vital records from 1639 | In-person or mail request |

## Records NOT online

- Full run of town meeting minutes across all Massachusetts towns (beyond FamilySearch volume 007612044, which covers one set of records browse-only): originals held in town clerk offices and the Massachusetts Archives
- County registry of deeds volumes from the 1640s-1700s: held physically at county registries; no indexed FamilySearch collection was returned for deeds in this period
- Militia muster rolls and King Philip's War service records: held at Massachusetts Archives; not returned as a digitized FamilySearch collection for 1620-1700
- Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691): published in print volumes; available at NEHGS; not returned as a dedicated FamilySearch online collection for this period
- Colonial Society of Massachusetts published church record series: print only at research libraries

## Known record losses

No tool result returned during this survey identified a specific record set as destroyed or lost for Massachusetts in the 1620-1700 period. All gaps noted above represent digitization or indexing absences, not confirmed losses. For the status of any specific town's records, contact the Massachusetts Archives (Boston) or the relevant town clerk.

## Research tips
- **Plymouth Colony is a separate research jurisdiction.** Any ancestor in Plymouth Colony before 1692 has records under that colony's separate system, published and indexed independently. Search Plymouth Colony records alongside — not as part of — Massachusetts Bay Colony records. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Start with the published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series** (Tanner-Corbin series): the standard entry point for colonial vital research, abstracting town clerk records for over 200 towns. Available at NEHGS, many research libraries, and partially online. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Use the NEHGS "Great Migration" study series** for any ancestor arriving 1620-1643: it documents every known settler with sources and family reconstruction. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Congregational church records are essential and are not duplicates of town vital records.** They record members, baptisms, disciplinary proceedings, and admissions not found in civil registration. FamilySearch collection 1921657 is indexed; FamilySearch volume 007612045 (Suffolk County, 1630-1700) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **County probate records from 1635 are essential for family reconstruction.** Wills and inventories name children, spouses, and sometimes grandchildren. FamilySearch collection 1678901 is indexed and free. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **No federal census exists for 1620-1700.** Use town meeting minutes, tax lists, proprietors' records, and militia muster rolls as substitutes. FamilySearch volume 007612044 (town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698, 188 images) must be browsed image by image with no name or text search available.

Locality guide written as **loc_001** in the project.

---

Oklahoma during the Land Run era (1880–1910) presents a layered record landscape, because the territory had no organized civil government at all before May 1890, operated as a federal territory from 1890 to 1907, and existed alongside the entirely separate Indian Territory for that entire period.

**Key Record Types and Repositories**

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run Era, 1880–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Unassigned Lands were opened to settlement on April 22, 1889 (Land Run of 1889). Oklahoma Territory was formally organized by the Organic Act on May 2, 1890. Oklahoma became the 46th state on November 16, 1907.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Guthrie served as the territorial capital (1890–1907); Oklahoma City became the state capital at statehood.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (federal territory, 1890–1907); adjacent Indian Territory (the Five Civilized Tribes' lands) was a separate jurisdiction until both merged at statehood.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place-population tool for this jurisdiction.
- **Economy:** Homesteading, farming, and cattle ranching; the 1889 and subsequent land runs (1891, 1892, 1893, 1895) drove explosive agricultural settlement.
- **Ethnic composition:** Settlers arrived predominantly from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other Midwestern and Southern states; the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole) occupied adjacent Indian Territory; freedmen on tribal rolls also claimed land.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Catholic congregations established from 1889 onward; mission churches for Native American congregations predate the Land Run.
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of 1889 (April 22, 1889); Organic Act creating Oklahoma Territory (May 2, 1890); subsequent land runs 1891–1895; 1890 federal census largely destroyed in 1921 fire (but territorial census survives); statehood November 16, 1907.

## Boundary changes
- Before April 22, 1889: Unassigned Lands had no organized civil government; no local records were generated.
- May 2, 1890: Oklahoma Territory organized; county governments and civil record-keeping begin.
- November 16, 1907: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged at statehood. Records from Indian Territory follow a separate administrative lineage — search both territorial record sets.
- Many Land Run settlers originated in Kansas, Texas, and Missouri; trace the family in those departure-state records before 1889.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Oklahoma Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey, so no jurisdiction-specific registration start year can be confirmed here. Oklahoma became a state in 1907; most late-organized U.S. territories did not mandate statewide vital registration until the early 1900s.
- **What exists:** County marriages beginning in 1890 — FamilySearch collection 2134789, "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (456,789 records, 913,578 persons, 228,394 images; indexed + images). No statewide birth or death collection for the territorial period was returned by the tools.
- **Where held:** County courthouses for marriage records; Oklahoma State Archives for later statewide registration.
- **Gaps:** Statewide birth and death registration postdates most of the 1889–1907 territorial period. County records are the primary marriage source for that window.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, homestead proof-of-settlement documents (which establish family relationships through witness statements), territorial court records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Catholic, and Native American mission churches active from 1889 onward; mission churches predate the Land Run.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321, "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (123,456 records, 61,728 images; indexed + images). Original registers held by individual denominations and diocesan archives.
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that church records begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established congregations in the new towns — early territorial coverage is thin and uneven. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Language:** English; some Native American mission records may be in tribal languages.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1900 and 1910 federal censuses cover both Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory (indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry). The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed in a 1921 fire.
- **Territorial census:** The Oklahoma Territory Special Census of 1890 survived and is held at the Oklahoma Historical Society — one of the very few surviving 1890 census records in the nation, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run. This is an essential substitute for the destroyed federal census.
- **Other enumerations:** FamilySearch collection 1987432, "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (567,890 records, 283,945 images; indexed + images) — covers the Five Civilized Tribes and is essential for families with Native American heritage or who settled on allotted lands.
- **Access:** 1900 and 1910 federal censuses indexed online (Ancestry, FamilySearch). The 1890 territorial census is physical-only at the Oklahoma Historical Society.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, civil and criminal cases.
- **Date range:** Oklahoma Territory district court records cover 1890–1907; county-level probate begins with county organization from 1890.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth (territorial district court records, 1890–1907, including probate and naturalization); Oklahoma State Archives. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts, these include civil and criminal cases, probate, and naturalization records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (Public Land Survey System) — Oklahoma is a federal land state.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. General Land Office; initial homestead applications were filed at the Guthrie and Kingfisher land offices (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Run_of_1889).

(Record Group 49, General Land Office); FamilySearch collection 1541872, "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (234,567 records, 117,283 images; indexed + images); BLM General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov, free, name-searchable). Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run, each homestead file typically includes the original application, proof of settlement, and the final patent; rejected applications also survive.

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War veterans were among Land Run participants; Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations — held at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov); Fold3 (fold3.com) carries military records per the curated external links survey.

### Cemetery records

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Territorial newspapers (e.g., the Oklahoma Gazette, Guthrie Daily Leader) began publishing in 1889 immediately after the Land Run.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) is listed as a curated external link. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds an extensive territorial newspaper archive. The Library of Congress Chronicling America database (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) includes many Oklahoma territorial titles and is free.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, homestead-contest legal notices, marriage announcements, court notices.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Land Run settlers were domestic migrants, but many had immigrant parents or were themselves naturalized citizens; naturalization records are directly relevant.
- **Record types:** Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in any court of record, including Oklahoma Territory district courts; post-1906 naturalizations in U.S. District Court records.
- **Where held:** NARA at Fort Worth (territorial naturalizations, 1890–1907); Ancestry (later naturalizations). Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts, territorial court naturalization records are at NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Content note:** For families who immigrated before the Land Run, passenger lists record every person aboard including infants and children. Examine the full manifest for all family members when tracing an immigrant family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property and real property tax rolls.
- **Date range:** Begin with county organization from 1890.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma State Archives; county clerks.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls are one of the primary substitutes for the missing 1890 federal census. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts, county-level tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers.

- **Digitization:** FamilySearch volume 005221389: 176 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only images (must be examined page by page with no search capability).
- **Where held:** Originals at NARA; also partially covered in FamilySearch collection 1987432, "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959."

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Collection 1541872: Early Land Records (234,567 records); Collection 1987432: Indian Censuses and Rolls (567,890 records); Collection 2134789: County Marriages, 1890–1995 (456,789 records); Collection 1654321: Mission and Church Records (123,456 records) | Land claims, Indian rolls, county marriages, church records | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Homestead applications and land patents, name-searchable | Homestead filing confirmation; patent text | Free |
| Ancestry.com (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1900 and 1910 census records | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Service records, pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Burial and memorial information | Free |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Historical newspapers | Territorial-era newspapers, obituaries | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Territorial court records (RG 21), homestead case files (RG 49), Dawes Commission records | Probate, naturalizations, land-entry case files | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume search returned 2 digitized volumes matching this place and period; both are detailed above and represent the complete result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Oklahoma Historical Society (okhistory.org) | 1890 Oklahoma Territorial Census; territorial and early state records | In-person / online finding aids |
| National Archives at Fort Worth — NARA Southwest Region | Oklahoma Territory district court records 1890–1907 (civil, criminal, probate, naturalization); Dawes Commission original files | In-person / written request |
| Oklahoma State Archives (archives.ok.gov) | Territorial court records; county records; state agency records post-1907 | In-person / contact the archives |
| County courthouses | Deed records, marriage records, probate records from 1890 | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- The 1890 Oklahoma Territorial Census — physical-only at the Oklahoma Historical Society.
- County-level personal property and real property tax rolls from the 1890s — held at the Oklahoma State Archives and county clerks; not indexed or browsable online per this survey's results.
- Many early church registers from congregations established 1889–1895 beyond what is in FamilySearch collection 1654321.
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (FamilySearch volume 005221389): present on FamilySearch but browse-only (0% indexed) — effectively no name-search capability online.

- Start with the homestead file. The application and proof of settlement in FamilySearch collection 1541872 and at glorecords.blm.gov names the claimant, two to three witnesses (often neighbors or relatives), the quarter-section claimed, and proof of residence. The application and proof of settlement in FamilySearch collection 1541872 and at glorecords.blm.gov names the claimant, two to three witnesses (often neighbors or relatives), the quarter-section claimed, and proof of residence. Rejected applications survived alongside approved ones and can be equally rich in family detail. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- Search both Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory records. The two territories were administered separately until 1907. Families living near the boundary, or with members who intermarried with tribal citizens, will have records under both systems. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- Use the 1890 Territorial Census, not just the federal census. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds one of the very few surviving 1890 census records in the nation. It documents the first wave of Land Run settlers directly. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- Trace the family in its origin state before 1889. Many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts, researching them requires searching departure-state records — the 1880 federal census is the key starting point.
- Use county tax rolls in place of the missing 1890 federal census. Personal and real property tax rolls begin from 1890 and name heads of household, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations are in territorial courts at NARA Fort Worth, not in USCIS records. Oklahoma Territory district court records (1890–1907) include naturalization proceedings. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

Here is the locality research guide the subagent produced:

---

## Alabama / Mississippi Territory — Pre-Statehood, c. 1800

**Jurisdictional Context**
Around 1800, what is now Alabama was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (created 1798). That is the governing jurisdiction to search first. Alabama did not achieve statehood until 1819, and the territory itself was split in 1817 — everything south became the Alabama Territory, and then the state.

---

### Available Records (Online, Name-Indexed with Images)

| Collection | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Mississippi Territorial & State Land Records** | From 1798 | FamilySearch; name-searchable with images |
| **Mississippi County Court Records** | From 1799 | FamilySearch; name-searchable with images |
| **Alabama Church Records** | From 1803 | FamilySearch; name-searchable with images |
| **Alabama County Marriages** | From 1809 | FamilySearch; name-searchable with images |
| **BLM General Land Office Patents** | Early 1800s+ | Online at glorecords.blm.gov |
| **Census Substitute Indexes** (both territorial sides) | 1798–1817 | Index only — **no images attached** |

---

### Browsable / Unindexed Image Volumes

> **None found online.** A search of FamilySearch's image-volume layer for both Mississippi Territory and Alabama across 1790–1820 returned zero results. There are no unindexed, page-by-page browsable volumes for this region and period available through FamilySearch.

---

### Territorial Censuses (Not Online)

Territorial censuses were taken in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** and cover the Alabama region. These are **physical records held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery — not digitized or available online.

---

### Mobile / Coastal Alabama — Spanish Records

Before the U.S. took control of Mobile in 1813, the coastal area was under **Spanish authority**. Those registers and land grants are in Spanish and are held primarily at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain), with copies at the **Library of Congress**. These require physical or specialized archival access.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. Search the BLM GLO patents for land entries in the Alabama region (early land claims are a key anchor record).
2. Work through the Mississippi territorial land and court collections on FamilySearch.
3. Check the Alabama church records and county marriage collections for your families.
4. Plan a visit (or request copies) from ADAH for the territorial census manuscripts.
5. For Mobile-area families, consult the Library of Congress copies of the Spanish colonial records.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood) (1790–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory established 1817 from Mississippi Territory; Alabama statehood 14 December 1819. Mississippi Territory was itself established in 1798 from land ceded by Georgia and Spain.
- **Administrative center:** Territorial capital was Washington, Mississippi (then St. Stephens for Alabama Territory; Montgomery became state capital later)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) → Alabama Territory (1817–1819) → State of Alabama (1819–)
- **Population during period:** Sparse and rapidly growing after the Creek War of 1813–1814. The 1810 federal census recorded the Territory of Mississippi; the 1820 census is the first to enumerate Alabama as a state.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton planting, fur trade; Mobile a port hub under successive colonial regimes
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations throughout the interior; Anglo-American settlers arriving primarily from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia (especially after 1814); French and Spanish Creole communities at Mobile
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders and Baptist congregations followed the frontier settlements; Catholic parishes at Mobile (French and Spanish legacy)
- **Key historical events:** Creek War 1813–1814 (opened interior Alabama to American settlement); transfer of Mobile from Spain to the U.S. in 1813; Mississippi Territory divided 1817 to create Alabama Territory

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: Present-day Alabama was disputed territory. The northern interior was claimed by Georgia (ceded 1802). The Mobile District was Spanish West Florida.
- 1798: Mississippi Territory created, covering roughly present-day Mississippi and Alabama south of Tennessee.
- 1804: Territory enlarged to include the old District of Washington (present-day southwest Alabama).
- 1813: United States seized Mobile from Spain; Mobile District incorporated into Mississippi Territory.
- 1817: Mississippi Territory divided along roughly the present Mississippi–Alabama state line. Mississippi became the 20th state; Alabama Territory created from the eastern half.
- 1819: Alabama achieved statehood. County formation within Alabama was rapid during 1818–1820; early records are often under the first county organized in a district, not the county that later contained the place.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed in Alabama during the territorial period. Alabama's statewide birth and death registration system was not in place during 1790–1819. Marriage records were kept by county courts from each county's formation (the earliest Alabama county marriages in FamilySearch collection 1598408 begin 1809). The FamilySearch Wiki page for Alabama Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and gives no specific registration start date that can be cited.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage bonds and licenses from the formation of each county (Baldwin County from 1809 is the earliest in the FamilySearch collection). No civil birth or death records from the territorial period are known.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (originals); FamilySearch collection 1598408, Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950, has 612,345 records with images (indexed + images).
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths entirely absent from civil registration for this period. Pre-1809 marriages not found in FamilySearch collections.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary vital record source for this period. Spanish Catholic registers at Mobile cover the 1780–1813 period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile); Methodist (circuit riders); Baptist (frontier congregations from ca. 1808)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; Methodist conference minutes; Baptist church minute books
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1986396, Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (156,789 records, 78,394 images — indexed + images). For the Mobile Catholic registers specifically (Spanish-era), records are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville and the Library of Congress per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records); microfilm copies are at the Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **Gaps:** Interior frontier settlements had few organized congregations before 1810; church records for those areas are sparse or non-existent for the territorial period.
- **Language:** Spanish-era Mobile Catholic registers are in Spanish.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census covers Mississippi Territory and includes present-day Alabama. The 1800 federal census covers Mississippi Territory (though coverage of the Alabama area is incomplete). The 1820 federal census is the first under the name Alabama.
- **Territorial censuses:** Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerate settlers in present-day Alabama. Per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records), these are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery — not available online.
- **State/territorial substitute indexes:** FamilySearch collection 2016756, Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (287,634 records, index only — no images). FamilySearch collection 1927171, Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (198,340 records, index only — no images). These are compiled substitutes and indexes, not scans of original enumerations.
- **Access:** The compiled census substitute indexes are name-indexed but image-free; the original territorial censuses are physical-only at ADAH.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships; territorial court minutes
- **Date range:** From formation of each county (earliest Alabama county courts ca. 1799 for Washington County in the Mississippi Territory era)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1537764, Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (438,210 records, 219,105 images — indexed + images). For Mississippi Territory–era court records, FamilySearch collection 1855293, Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (245,670 records, 122,835 images — indexed + images). Originals at county probate courts and ADAH.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land (public domain) state; federal rectangular survey applies. Pre-American grants in the Mobile area used Spanish and British metes-and-bounds grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government through the General Land Office. The Huntsville and St. Stephens land offices opened in the territorial period. Federal land patents are searchable at the BLM General Land Office website (https://www.glorecords.blm.gov) — free, name-indexed.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish and British colonial grants (Mobile area), deed books at county level
- **Date range:** Federal public land sales in the Alabama area began ca. 1811–1818; Spanish grants predate that for the Mobile coastal area
- **Where held:** Federal patents: BLM GLO (online, free). Colonial grants: Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Library of Congress for Spanish grants; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives. FamilySearch collection 1919694, Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (312,450 records, 156,225 images — indexed + images), covers the Mississippi Territory period and includes early Alabama-area land records filed under Mississippi Territory.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813–1814; War of 1812 (including actions in the Mobile and Gulf area); earlier Spanish colonial militia records
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; territorial militia rolls (mentioned in the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records as held at ADAH); bounty land warrants for veterans of the Creek War
- **Where held:** NARA (service records, pensions): https://www.archives.gov/. Fold3 holds digitized military records: https://www.fold3.com/. Territorial militia rolls: ADAH (physical).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic and Protestant frontier cemeteries; many informal family burial grounds on homestead land
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes some Alabama cemeteries, but coverage for pre-1820 burials is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records generally postdate this period for most of Alabama; church burial registers (see Church Records above) are the closest equivalent.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Mobile had a newspaper from the early American period. Interior Alabama papers generally begin after statehood.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and ADAH for Alabama newspaper holdings. Coverage for the 1800–1819 period is limited.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sales, obituaries begin appearing after statehood.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile Bay (the principal Gulf Coast port); New Orleans (for settlers arriving via the Mississippi/Tombigbee river system)
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA); naturalization petitions (filed in territorial and county courts — pre-1906 naturalizations in any court of record); Spanish colonial census returns for Mobile
- **Where held:** NARA: https://www.archives.gov/. Naturalization records for this period would be in territorial court records (overlapping with court and probate series above).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine full manifests when researching families.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county tax lists (property, poll)
- **Date range:** Mississippi Territory tax lists begin ca. 1800s; Alabama county tax records from each county's formation
- **Where held:** ADAH holds territorial and early county tax lists. Some are included in the compiled census substitute collections (FamilySearch collections 2016756 and 1927171).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are especially important as census substitutes for the 1800–1820 period when census coverage is incomplete.

### Other record types
- Spanish colonial records (Mobile District): census returns, church registers, and land grants held at Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). French colonial records (Mobile, 1702–1763) are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 1598408) | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (612,345 records, images) | Marriage records from county formation | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1537764) | Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (438,210 records, images) | Wills, estates, guardianships | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764 |
| FamilySearch (collection 2016756) | Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (287,634 records, index only) | Census and tax list index; no images | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1986396) | Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (156,789 records, images) | Baptisms, marriages, burials pre-civil registration | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1919694) | Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (312,450 records, images) | Territorial-era land records filed under Mississippi | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1855293) | Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (245,670 records, images) | Territorial-era court records | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1927171) | Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (198,340 records, index only) | Territorial census and substitute index; no images | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171 |
| FamilySearch (collection 2034891) | Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950 (87,654 records, images) | Church records covering Mississippi Territory | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891 |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents for Alabama | Federal public land grants 1811–1819 | Free — https://www.glorecords.blm.gov |
| NARA | Military records, pension files, passenger lists | Service records, Creek War pensions | https://www.archives.gov/ |
| Fold3 | Digitized military records | War of 1812, Creek War service | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |

The area now called Alabama was, around 1800, part of the Mississippi Territory (created 1798), which makes Mississippi Territory the jurisdiction to search first. Within that territory, the records that survive and are accessible online are mostly indexed collections with images: FamilySearch holds Mississippi Territorial and State Land Records from 1798, Mississippi County Court Records from 1799, and Alabama Church Records from 1803 and County Marriages from 1809 — all name-searchable with attached images. The territorial censuses themselves — taken in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 and covering what is now Alabama — are physical records held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery and are not online. For the Mobile coastal area before 1813, the authority was Spain; those registers and land grants are in Spanish and held primarily at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood) (1790–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory established 1817 from Mississippi Territory; Alabama statehood 14 December 1819. Mississippi Territory was itself established in 1798 from land ceded by Georgia and Spain.
- **Administrative center:** Territorial capital was Washington, Mississippi (then St. Stephens for Alabama Territory; Montgomery became state capital later)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) → Alabama Territory (1817–1819) → State of Alabama (1819–)
- **Population during period:** Sparse and rapidly growing after the Creek War of 1813–1814. The 1810 federal census recorded the Territory of Mississippi; the 1820 census is the first to enumerate Alabama as a state.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton planting, fur trade; Mobile a port hub under successive colonial regimes
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations throughout the interior; Anglo-American settlers arriving primarily from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia (especially after 1814); French and Spanish Creole communities at Mobile
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders and Baptist congregations followed the frontier settlements; Catholic parishes at Mobile (French and Spanish legacy)
- **Key historical events:** Creek War 1813–1814 (opened interior Alabama to American settlement); transfer of Mobile from Spain to the U.S. in 1813; Mississippi Territory divided 1817 to create Alabama Territory

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: Present-day Alabama was disputed territory. The northern interior was claimed by Georgia (ceded 1802). The Mobile District was Spanish West Florida.
- 1798: Mississippi Territory created, covering roughly present-day Mississippi and Alabama south of Tennessee.
- 1804: Territory enlarged to include the old District of Washington (present-day southwest Alabama).
- 1813: United States seized Mobile from Spain; Mobile District incorporated into Mississippi Territory.
- 1817: Mississippi Territory divided along roughly the present Mississippi–Alabama state line. Mississippi became the 20th state; Alabama Territory created from the eastern half.
- 1819: Alabama achieved statehood. County formation within Alabama was rapid during 1818–1820; early records are often under the first county organized in a district, not the county that later contained the place.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed in Alabama during the territorial period. Alabama's statewide birth and death registration system was not in place during 1790–1819. Marriage records were kept by county courts from each county's formation (the earliest Alabama county marriages in FamilySearch collection 1598408 begin 1809). The FamilySearch Wiki page for Alabama Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and gives no specific registration start date that can be cited.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage bonds and licenses from the formation of each county (Baldwin County from 1809 is the earliest in the FamilySearch collection). No civil birth or death records from the territorial period are known.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (originals); FamilySearch collection 1598408, Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950, has 612,345 records with images (indexed + images).
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths entirely absent from civil registration for this period. Pre-1809 marriages not found in FamilySearch collections.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary vital record source for this period. Spanish Catholic registers at Mobile cover the 1780–1813 period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile); Methodist (circuit riders); Baptist (frontier congregations from ca. 1808)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; Methodist conference minutes; Baptist church minute books
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1986396, Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (156,789 records, 78,394 images — indexed + images). For the Mobile Catholic registers specifically (Spanish-era), records are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville and the Library of Congress per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records); microfilm copies are at the Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **Gaps:** Interior frontier settlements had few organized congregations before 1810; church records for those areas are sparse or non-existent for the territorial period.
- **Language:** Spanish-era Mobile Catholic registers are in Spanish.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census covers Mississippi Territory and includes present-day Alabama. The 1800 federal census covers Mississippi Territory (though coverage of the Alabama area is incomplete). The 1820 federal census is the first under the name Alabama.
- **Territorial censuses:** Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerate settlers in present-day Alabama. Per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records), these are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery — not available online.
- **State/territorial substitute indexes:** FamilySearch collection 2016756, Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (287,634 records, index only — no images). FamilySearch collection 1927171, Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (198,340 records, index only — no images). These are compiled substitutes and indexes, not scans of original enumerations.
- **Access:** The compiled census substitute indexes are name-indexed but image-free; the original territorial censuses are physical-only at ADAH.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships; territorial court minutes
- **Date range:** From formation of each county (earliest Alabama county courts ca. 1799 for Washington County in the Mississippi Territory era)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1537764, Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (438,210 records, 219,105 images — indexed + images). For Mississippi Territory–era court records, FamilySearch collection 1855293, Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (245,670 records, 122,835 images — indexed + images). Originals at county probate courts and ADAH.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land (public domain) state; federal rectangular survey applies. Pre-American grants in the Mobile area used Spanish and British metes-and-bounds grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government through the General Land Office. The Huntsville and St. Stephens land offices opened in the territorial period. Federal land patents are searchable at the BLM General Land Office website (https://www.glorecords.blm.gov) — free, name-indexed.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish and British colonial grants (Mobile area), deed books at county level
- **Date range:** Federal public land sales in the Alabama area began ca. 1811–1818; Spanish grants predate that for the Mobile coastal area
- **Where held:** Federal patents: BLM GLO (online, free). Colonial grants: Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Library of Congress for Spanish grants; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives. FamilySearch collection 1919694, Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (312,450 records, 156,225 images — indexed + images), covers the Mississippi Territory period and includes early Alabama-area land records filed under Mississippi Territory.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813–1814; War of 1812 (including actions in the Mobile and Gulf area); earlier Spanish colonial militia records
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; territorial militia rolls (mentioned in the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records as held at ADAH); bounty land warrants for veterans of the Creek War
- **Where held:** NARA (service records, pensions): https://www.archives.gov/. Fold3 holds digitized military records: https://www.fold3.com/. Territorial militia rolls: ADAH (physical).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic and Protestant frontier cemeteries; many informal family burial grounds on homestead land
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes some Alabama cemeteries, but coverage for pre-1820 burials is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records generally postdate this period for most of Alabama; church burial registers (see Church Records above) are the closest equivalent.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Mobile had a newspaper from the early American period. Interior Alabama papers generally begin after statehood.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and ADAH for Alabama newspaper holdings. Coverage for the 1800–1819 period is limited.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sales, obituaries begin appearing after statehood.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile Bay (the principal Gulf Coast port); New Orleans (for settlers arriving via the Mississippi/Tombigbee river system)
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA); naturalization petitions (filed in territorial and county courts — pre-1906 naturalizations in any court of record); Spanish colonial census returns for Mobile
- **Where held:** NARA: https://www.archives.gov/. Naturalization records for this period would be in territorial court records (overlapping with court and probate series above).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine full manifests when researching families.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county tax lists (property, poll)
- **Date range:** Mississippi Territory tax lists begin ca. 1800s; Alabama county tax records from each county's formation
- **Where held:** ADAH holds territorial and early county tax lists. Some are included in the compiled census substitute collections (FamilySearch collections 2016756 and 1927171).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are especially important as census substitutes for the 1800–1820 period when census coverage is incomplete.

### Other record types
- Spanish colonial records (Mobile District): census returns, church registers, and land grants held at Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). French colonial records (Mobile, 1702–1763) are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide, 1860–1900

### Geographic Scope
The anthracite coal region spans five core counties: **Schuylkill**, **Luzerne**, **Lackawanna**, **Carbon**, and **Northumberland**. The survey focused on Schuylkill County as the primary county; the remaining four each warrant their own separate guide.

---

### Key Finding: Vital Records Gap
Pennsylvania had **no statewide birth or death registration until the twentieth century**. For the 1860–1890s window, **Catholic parish registers are the only practical source** for births, baptisms, marriages, and deaths of Irish families. Schuylkill County Catholic parishes fall under the **Diocese of Philadelphia** (the Diocese of Allentown was not created until 1961), so records are accessed through that diocese's archive.

---

### FamilySearch Holdings — Schuylkill County
- Five digitized volumes exist on FamilySearch for Schuylkill County.
- **Four of the five are browse-only** (no name index) — you must page through them manually.
- The one partially indexed volume covers **deed records**, not vital or church records.

---

### Specialized Coal-Region Index
The most important specialized finding aid is the:

> **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898**

This index names roughly **41,000 colliery workers** across the lower anthracite field and **often records the parish of origin for Irish miners**. Important caveat: it centers on **Luzerne and Lackawanna counties** rather than Schuylkill, so it is most useful if your ancestors worked in those counties or migrated between them.

---

### Naturalization Records
Before 1906, naturalization could be granted by **any court of record**, not just federal courts. You must search multiple courts — Court of Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, etc. — rather than one central repository.

---

### FamilySearch Wiki — Current Status
The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Schuylkill County and for Pennsylvania Vital Records and Church Records returned only **generic placeholder content** during this survey. Check those pages directly, as their content may be updated.

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. **Search the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** for your Irish surnames, noting any parish-of-origin entries.
2. **Browse the unindexed Schuylkill County church volumes** on FamilySearch page-by-page.
3. **Contact the Diocese of Philadelphia archives** for Catholic registers not yet digitized.
4. **Search naturalization records** across multiple Schuylkill County courts (pre-1906).
5. Run the **research-plan** skill to build a prioritized search sequence using this guide.
6. Request a separate locality guide for **Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland** counties as needed.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860-1900)

*Primary survey county: Schuylkill. The other core anthracite counties — Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland — each require their own locality guide.*

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880) → 172,927 (1900)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; collieries, breakers, and related trades drove rapid population growth throughout the period
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic immigrant community from the 1840s onward; also Welsh, English, German, and (later in the period) Eastern European miners
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish miners), Welsh Congregationalist, Methodist Episcopal, Welsh Baptist, German Lutheran and Reformed, Episcopal
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials 1875-1877 (generated court and newspaper records naming coal-region Irish); Long Strike of 1875; rapid company town growth throughout the period

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County has had stable boundaries since its formation in 1811; no splits or absorptions during the 1860-1900 period
- Records before 1811 are held in the parent counties, Berks and Northampton

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania had no statewide birth or death registration during the 1860-1895 period; county-level marriage registration evidenced from 1885 (FamilySearch collection 1921317, "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950"). Statewide death certificates begin 1906 (collection 2255317). The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey, so specific registration-level dates cannot be cited from it; the collection date ranges are the basis for these figures.
- **What exists:** County marriage records from 1885 at county level; death certificates from 1906 at state level (postdates most of the target window). No indexed birth records exist for this period.
- **Where held:** County marriages 1885-1950 in FamilySearch collection 1921317 (524,189 records, indexed, free); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 in collection 1571957 (312,045 records, indexed, free); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 in collection 1502909 (198,765 records, indexed, no images, free)
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration 1860-1895; marriage registration below county level not confirmed from tool results; no vital registration of any kind for most of the 1860s-1880s
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial); Welsh Nonconformist chapel registers; Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments (1853 onward, listing occupation and sometimes nativity); cemetery records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (parishes established 1840-1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrants), Welsh Congregationalist, Methodist Episcopal, Welsh Baptist, German Lutheran, German Reformed, Episcopal
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; some parishes also kept registers of the poor and sick
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has digitized one volume of Schuylkill County church records, DGS 007936751 (1842-1895, 187 images, browse-only, English and German). Catholic registers pre-1961 fall under the Diocese of Philadelphia (Diocese of Allentown erected 1961); diocesan archives are in Philadelphia. Welsh Nonconformist and Methodist records may be held by local congregations or the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Gaps:** The single digitized church volume (DGS 007936751) is browse-only and must be scrolled image by image; it contains both English and German entries. Not all parishes are represented. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Church Records returned only generic content during this survey.
- **Language:** English and German both present in DGS 007936751

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 enumerations cover Schuylkill County; 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed nationwide. Ancestry holds the Schuylkill County 1850 federal census (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/). Federal census years 1860-1900 are in national FamilySearch census collections, not returned as county-specific digitized volumes in this survey.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct an official state census during this period
- **Other enumerations:** Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments from 1853 function as a quasi-census for household heads, listing occupation and sometimes nativity — a critical substitute for the missing 1890 federal census
- **Access:** Federal census 1860-1880 and 1900 are name-indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Tax assessments are physical records; digitization status not confirmed by tool results.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate), letters of administration (intestate), guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has digitized one Schuylkill County probate volume, DGS 007936749 (1851-1930, 412 images, browse-only, 0% name-indexed). Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 also available as FamilySearch collection 1999196 (3,200,560 images, browse-only).
- **Access:** Both probate resources are browse-only — no name search available online; must be scrolled image by image. Physical originals held at the Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey; the land-granting authority and which office holds patents cannot be cited from tool results for this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records
- **Date range:** Deed records digitized on FamilySearch from 1815 (DGS 007936752, 543 images, 22% name-indexed — the only partially indexed Schuylkill County volume in this survey)
- **Where held:** DGS 007936752 on FamilySearch (partially searchable by name). Physical deed books at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Civil War), draft registrations
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal service and pension records. The Molly Maguires trials (1875-1877) generated court records that name many Irish coal-region men; these are held at the Schuylkill County Courthouse and may be partially transcribed in local histories.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous Catholic and Protestant cemeteries throughout the coal patches and boroughs
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have partial coverage of Schuylkill County cemeteries; neither was returned as a curated external link for this place and period in the tool results
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are held by individual cemetery associations and Catholic parishes; not confirmed as digitized

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville) published from 1825 and covered the coal region throughout the 1860-1900 period; it is a prime source for obituaries, marriage notices, accident reports, and Molly Maguires coverage
- **Where held:** Microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society and the State Library of Pennsylvania; some digitization may exist but not returned as a confirmed online resource in tool results
- **Content value:** Extremely high for Irish coal-region families — obituaries commonly named Irish townland of origin; accident reports named decedents and witnesses

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden, then Ellis Island from 1892) were the primary arrival ports for Irish migrants to the coal region
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, declarations of intention, naturalization petitions, certificates of citizenship
- **Naturalization records at Schuylkill County level:** FamilySearch has digitized one naturalization volume, DGS 007936750 (1849-1915, 298 images, browse-only, 0% name-indexed). Pre-1906 naturalization petitions could be filed in any court of record — Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, or federal court.
- **State-level naturalization:** DGS 008120443 (Pennsylvania, Naturalization Records 1790-1915, 351 images, 15% name-indexed) is the most searchable naturalization resource returned by tools.
- **Where held:** Physical naturalization records at the Schuylkill County Courthouse and NARA Philadelphia. NARA holds passenger lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Naturalization declarations often named the Irish townland or county of origin — these are critical for linking coal-region immigrants back to Irish records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments (from 1853); county property and personal property tax
- **Date range:** State assessments from 1853 onward list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; digitization status not confirmed by tool results
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessments serve as a partial substitute for census years and especially for the missing 1890 federal census; nativity fields can confirm Irish origin

### Other record types
- **Mine and colliery records:** Distinguish company payroll ledgers (which name individual workers with occupation, wage, and sometimes parish of origin) from mine-inspection and accident reports (organized by colliery, not by person). The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898 covers the lower anthracite field (~41,000 workers from Luzerne and Lackawanna counties) — not Schuylkill specifically, but still worth checking for relatives who moved across the region.
- **Company town records:** Mining companies maintained employment and housing records; survival is uneven. Check the Hagley Museum and Library and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania for corporate archives.
- **Molly Maguires court records:** The 1875-1877 trials generated extensive records naming coal-region Irish men; transcripts and newspaper coverage are at the Schuylkill County Historical Society.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, indexed); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (1571957, 312,045 records, indexed); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (1502909, 198,765 records, indexed, no images); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 (1999196, browse-only images); 5 Schuylkill County digitized volumes (DGS 007936749-53) | Marriage records; probate; partial deed, naturalization, church records | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) | 1850 United States Federal Census — Schuylkill County | Migration context immediately before the target period | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 5 digitized volumes for Schuylkill County (1860-1900); summary confirms this is the complete set. A separate state-level naturalization volume (DGS 008120443) adds one partially indexed resource.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville, PA | Deed books, probate files, court records including naturalization petitions, marriage licenses | In-person; some records accessible by mail request |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville, PA | Local histories, newspaper files (Miners' Journal), Molly Maguires materials, cemetery records | In-person; contact for hours |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg, PA | Triennial tax assessments, state-level records, military records | In-person / online finding aids |
| Diocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill County pre-1961 | Contact diocesan archives |
| NARA Philadelphia (700 Market Street) | Passenger lists, pre-1906 naturalization records, federal census | In-person / online request |
| Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington, DE | Coal company corporate archives (employment, payroll) | In-person / contact for holdings |

## Records NOT online
- Birth records (no statewide registration 1860-1895; local and church records not fully digitized)
- Death records (no statewide death certificates until 1906; local church burial registers partially browse-only)
- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (physical at Pennsylvania State Archives)
- Miners' Journal newspaper (microfilm at historical society; limited online presence confirmed by tool results)
- Mine and colliery payroll books (company archives; uneven survival)
- Sexton and cemetery records (held by individual associations)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Schuylkill County record set was destroyed or lost. The near-total destruction of the 1890 federal census is nationwide, not specific to this county. Absence from online search results is a coverage gap, not confirmed loss — physical repositories named above should be consulted.

## Research tips
- **Use the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898 for relatives who worked in Luzerne or Lackawanna County collieries**, not for Schuylkill County workers specifically. The index names occupation, wage rate, and parish of origin where stated — critical for Irish immigrant identification. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Coal Region Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
- **Seek Catholic baptismal and burial registers via the Diocese of Philadelphia**, which held jurisdiction over Schuylkill County parishes throughout the 1860-1900 period and through 1960. After 1961, contact the Diocese of Allentown. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records
- **Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments from 1853 list occupation and sometimes nativity** — these are the closest thing to an intercensal record for coal-region residents and are especially valuable for the period between census years and for the missing 1890 federal census. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records
- **Check naturalization records in multiple courts.** Pre-1906 declarations and petitions could be filed in Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, or federal courts; DGS 007936750 (browse-only) and DGS 008120443 (15% indexed) are starting points, but physical records at the Schuylkill County Courthouse must also be searched.
- **The Miners' Journal (Pottsville) is a prime source for Irish coal-region families.** Obituaries commonly named the Irish townland of origin, and accident and trial coverage (especially Molly Maguires 1875-1877) names many coal-region men not found in surviving vital records.
- **Search Berks and Northampton County records for events before 1811**, since Schuylkill County was not formed until that year from those two parent counties.
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Schuylkill County Genealogy, Pennsylvania Vital Records, Pennsylvania Church Records, and all four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic placeholder content during this survey — re-run the locality guide before relying on their absence; these pages may exist with specific guidance.
